experiments.name: Compare the effects of acids, bases and indicators
experiments.process: Referring to Figure 10-21, add indicators such as litmus and phenolphthalein to the test tubes containing acid (such as dilute hydrochloric acid) and alkali (such as dilute sodium hydroxide solution), or use pH test paper to test and compare the color changes.
experiments.phenomena: Acidic solution and alkaline solution cause the indicator to show different colors. For example, phenolphthalein is colored in alkaline solution and colorless in acidic solution.
experiments.conclusion: Acid and alkali can make the indicator show different colors, which can be used to judge the acidity and alkalinity of the solution.

experiments.name: Experiment on removing iron nail rust with dilute hydrochloric acid
experiments.process: Put two rusty iron nails into two test tubes, then add about 2 mL of dilute hydrochloric acid and observe the phenomenon. When it is observed that the rust on the surface of the iron nail has been removed and it becomes shiny, take out the iron nail in one of the test tubes and wash it. Continue to observe the phenomenon in the other test tube. After a while, take out the iron nails, wash them, and compare the two iron nails.
experiments.phenomena: The rust on the surface of the iron nail gradually disappears and the iron nail becomes bright; iron nails soaked for a long time may undergo further corrosion, which is different from iron nails taken out after being soaked for a short time.
experiments.conclusion: Dilute hydrochloric acid can remove rust, indicating that acid has unique chemical properties such as rust removal.

experiments.name: Reaction of sodium hydroxide with copper sulfate solution and hydrochloric acid
experiments.process: Add about 2 mL of copper sulfate solution into the test tube, then add a few drops of sodium hydroxide solution and observe the phenomenon. Then add dilute hydrochloric acid to the test tube and continue to observe the phenomenon.
experiments.phenomena: After adding sodium hydroxide solution dropwise, a blue precipitate (copper hydroxide) is generated; after adding dilute hydrochloric acid, the blue precipitate dissolves and the solution returns to a clear colored solution.
experiments.conclusion: As an alkali, sodium hydroxide can react with the metal salt copper sulfate solution to form an insoluble hydroxide precipitate; the generated hydroxide can react with acid and dissolve, indicating that alkali can react with acid, reflecting the chemical properties of alkali.

experiments.name: Neutralization reaction of hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide and evaporation to dryness observation
experiments.process: Add about 1 mL of sodium hydroxide solution into the test tube and add a few drops of phenolphthalein solution. Then slowly drip in dilute hydrochloric acid with a dropper while shaking the test tube until the color of the solution turns colorless. Take about 1 mL of the colorless solution, place it in an evaporating dish and heat it to evaporate the liquid to dryness, and observe the phenomenon.
experiments.phenomena: Sodium hydroxide solution turns red after adding phenolphthalein; continue to add dilute hydrochloric acid dropwise until the solution just turns colorless. After evaporating to dryness, there is solid residue (salt) at the bottom of the evaporating dish.
experiments.conclusion: Acid and alkali can neutralize each other to form salt and water; the color change of phenolphthalein can be used to judge whether neutralization is achieved; the residue after evaporation to dryness proves the formation of salt.

experiments.name: Reaction of calcium hydroxide powder with water, acid and phenolphthalein
experiments.process: Add the same amount of calcium hydroxide powder to each of the two test tubes (use the handle of a medical spoon to pick up one end), then add 1 mL of water to each, and shake; then add 1 to 2 drops of phenolphthalein solution to each, and observe the phenomenon. Continue to add about 1 mL of water to one test tube and shake; add about 1 mL of dilute hydrochloric acid to the other test tube and shake; compare the phenomena in the two test tubes.
experiments.phenomena: After adding water, part of the calcium hydroxide dissolves, and the solution becomes slightly alkaline; after adding dropwise phenolphthalein, the solution takes on the characteristic color of alkaline. When water is added continuously, the alkalinity of the solution weakens and the color becomes lighter; when dilute hydrochloric acid is added, the color of the solution fades and the solid gradually dissolves.
experiments.conclusion: Calcium hydroxide can be dissolved in water (limited), and the solution is alkaline and can change the color of phenolphthalein. It is an alkali. Calcium hydroxide can react with acid and cause the color of the indicator to fade, indicating that it has the typical chemical properties of a base.

exercises.name: Determine the reaction between carbonate or bicarbonate salts and hydrochloric acid
exercises.stem: Write the chemical equations for the reactions of sodium carbonate and sodium bicarbonate with hydrochloric acid respectively, and explain whether these reactions are metathesis reactions and why.
tests: Reaction of salts containing carbonate or bicarbonate and hydrochloric acid
Use "gas or precipitation generation" to identify carbonate-containing salts
exercises.answer: Na2CO3 + 2HCl = 2NaCl + CO2↑ + H2O; NaHCO3 + HCl = NaCl + CO2↑ + H2O. Both reactions are metathesis reactions, because two compounds exchange components with each other in the solution to generate two other compounds (salt and water). At the same time, gas CO2 is generated, which is consistent with the metathesis reaction and its occurrence conditions.
exercises.analysis: Write the reaction based on the equation given in the textbook, and then compare it with the definition of metathesis reaction and the condition of "there is gas, precipitation, or water in the product" to judge.

experiments.name: Experiment 11-1: Reaction of sodium carbonate and sodium bicarbonate with hydrochloric acid
instrument: 0.5 g sodium carbonate or equivalent sodium bicarbonate
Test tubes containing clear lime water
experiments.process: Add 2 mL hydrochloric acid to the test tube containing 0.5 g of sodium carbonate, quickly plug the mouth of the test tube with a rubber stopper with a catheter, and pass the other end of the catheter into a test tube containing clear lime water to observe the phenomenon. Then repeat the experiment using sodium bicarbonate instead of sodium carbonate and analyze the phenomenon.
experiments.phenomena: Bubbles are generated in the original test tube, and the lime water passed through the tube becomes turbid.
experiments.conclusion: Both sodium carbonate and sodium bicarbonate can react with hydrochloric acid to produce carbon dioxide gas, water and sodium chloride.

experiments.name: Experiment 11-2: Reaction of sodium carbonate solution and clear lime water
instrument: A small amount of sodium carbonate solution
experiments.process: Drop clear lime water into a test tube containing a small amount of sodium carbonate solution, observe and analyze the phenomenon.
experiments.phenomena: A white precipitate appears and the solution becomes turbid.
experiments.conclusion: The metathesis reaction between sodium carbonate solution and calcium hydroxide solution produces water-insoluble calcium carbonate precipitate and sodium hydroxide solution.

experiments.name: Experiment 11-3: Reaction of copper sulfate solution with sodium hydroxide and barium chloride solution
experiments.process: Add copper sulfate solution dropwise into two test tubes containing a small amount of sodium hydroxide solution and barium chloride solution respectively, observe the phenomenon and fill in the form.
experiments.phenomena: When combined with NaOH solution, a blue precipitate of Cu(OH)2 is formed; when combined with a BaCl2 solution, a white precipitate of BaSO4 is formed.
experiments.conclusion: Both reactions are metathesis reactions, and the insoluble precipitate generated is the condition for the metathesis reaction to occur.

experiments.name: Purification of coarse salt
experiments.process: Dissolve coarse salt in an appropriate amount of water, let it stand or heat to dissolve, then filter to remove insoluble impurities such as sediment, and then evaporate and crystallize the filtrate to remove some soluble impurities to obtain relatively pure sodium chloride crystals.
experiments.phenomena: The solution becomes clear after filtration, and crystals precipitate after evaporation.
experiments.conclusion: Crude salt can be initially purified through steps such as dissolution, precipitation, filtration, evaporation, and crystallization.

exercises.stem:
Determine whether a metathesis reaction can occur between the following substances. If a reaction can occur, write the chemical equation of the reaction.
(1) Sodium carbonate solution and calcium chloride solution
(2) Potassium hydroxide solution and hydrochloric acid
(3) Sodium hydroxide solution and potassium chloride solution
(4) Potassium carbonate solution and hydrochloric acid
(5) Copper sulfate solution and barium chloride solution
exercises.answer:
(1) Can happen: Na2CO3 + CaCl2 → CaCO3↓ + 2NaCl
(2) Can occur (neutralization reaction can also be regarded as metathesis): KOH + HCl → KCl + H2O
(3) Cannot occur: 2Na+ + 2OH− + 2K+ + 2Cl− It is a soluble strong electrolyte before and after the reaction, and no precipitation, gas or weak electrolyte is generated.
(4) It can happen: K2CO3 + 2HCl → 2KCl + H2O + CO2↑
(5) Can occur: CuSO4 + BaCl2 → BaSO4↓ + CuCl2
exercises.analysis: According to the conditions of the metathesis reaction: there must be precipitation, gas or weak electrolyte (water) in the product. Analyze the solubility and state of the products one by one to determine whether the reaction can proceed and write a chemical equation.

exercises.stem: Urea is the most important type of nitrogen fertilizer. It contains high nitrogen and does not leave any harmful substances in the soil. Try to calculate the mass fraction of nitrogen element in urea CO(NH2)2 (approximate relative atomic mass: C=12, O=16, N=14, H=1).
tests: Quantitative calculation of the mass fraction of elements in a compound
exercises.answer: Relative molecular mass of urea: M[CO(NH2)2] = 12 + 16 + 2×(14 + 2×1) = 60; where the mass of nitrogen is 2×14 = 28. Mass fraction of nitrogen = 28 ÷ 60 × 100% ≈ 46.7%.
exercises.analysis: First calculate the relative molecular mass of urea, then find the total mass of nitrogen, and finally use "element mass ÷ total mass of compound × 100%" to obtain the mass fraction.

experiments.phenomena: Nitrogen fertilizers and potassium fertilizers are mostly white crystals, easily soluble in water; phosphate fertilizers are mostly gray-white powder, mostly insoluble or partially soluble in water.
experiments.conclusion: Nitrogen fertilizers, phosphate fertilizers and potassium fertilizers can be preliminarily distinguished through differences in appearance and solubility.

experiments.name: Comparative experiment on the properties of sodium carbonate and sodium bicarbonate
instrument: pH test paper or pH meter
experiments.process: ①Observe the color and state of the two solids; ②Dissolve in cold water and hot water respectively, and observe the difference in dissolution speed and solubility; ③Measure the pH value of each saturated solution; ④Add hydrochloric acid dropwise to the two solutions, and observe whether bubbles are generated and the degree of reaction.
experiments.phenomena: Both are white solids; both are soluble in water, and dissolve faster in hot water; sodium carbonate solution has a higher pH and is strongly alkaline, while sodium bicarbonate solution is weakly alkaline; adding hydrochloric acid will produce bubbles, and the sodium carbonate reaction will be more violent.
experiments.conclusion: Sodium carbonate is highly alkaline and reacts more violently with acid; sodium bicarbonate is weakly alkaline. Both can react with acid to release CO2 and can be used as leavening agents, but their uses and safety are different.

exercises.name: The properties utilized by the coarse salt purification method
exercises.stem:
In this experiment, the method of dissolution-filtration-evaporation is used to remove insoluble impurities from coarse salt. Considering the properties of sodium chloride, answer:
(1) Which two physical properties of sodium chloride are mainly used in this purification process?
(2) Can the salt obtained only by this experimental method be regarded as a pure substance? Briefly explain why.
tests: Solubility and Volatility of Sodium Chloride
Physical method purification and pure substance judgment
Select purification methods based on material properties
exercises.answer:
(1) Mainly utilizes the two physical properties of sodium chloride: "easily soluble in water" and "non-volatile when heated (not taken away with water vapor)".
(2) It cannot be regarded as a pure substance. Because coarse salt may contain some soluble impurities, these impurities are dissolved in water like sodium chloride and remain in the solid after the water is evaporated, so the resulting salt is still a mixture, but it is purer than coarse salt.
exercises.analysis: The question stem points to the key principles of this experiment. Dissolution-filtration-evaporation can remove insoluble impurities, but it is powerless against soluble impurities. Students need to answer the question based on the two physical properties of the substance, "solubility" and "volatility". At the same time, they need to understand that physical purification does not guarantee an absolutely pure substance.

experiments.phenomena: When the solute mass is small, it can be completely dissolved; when it is close to or exceeds the solubility, part of the sodium chloride will no longer dissolve and form a saturated solution.
experiments.conclusion: Whether the solubility limit has been reached can be judged by whether the solution can be completely dissolved, and the concentration can be calculated in conjunction with the mass fraction.

experiments.name: Removal of insoluble impurities in coarse salt
experiments.process: 1) Dissolution: weigh 5.0 g of coarse salt. Gradually add the coarse salt into a beaker containing 10 mL of water. Stir with a glass rod while adding until the coarse salt is no longer dissolved. Record the mass of the remaining coarse salt and calculate the dissolved amount. Observe whether the salt water is turbid. 2) Filtration: Filter the turbid salt water according to the device in Figure 11-13. Observe the residue on the filter paper and the color of the filtrate. If the filtrate is still turbid, filter it again. 3) Evaporation: Pour the obtained clarified filtrate into an evaporating dish, heat it with an alcohol lamp and stir continuously to prevent local overheating from causing droplets to splash. Stop heating when more solids are produced, use the residual heat to evaporate the solution to dryness, and observe the appearance of the salt. 4) Calculate the yield: transfer the solid to paper and weigh it, recover it to the designated container, calculate the yield of refined salt, and compare the appearance with that of coarse salt.
experiments.phenomena: The coarse salt is partially dissolved during the dissolution stage, and turbid salt water appears in the cup; after filtration, insoluble impurities remain on the filter paper, and the filtrate becomes clear or lighter in color; during the evaporation process, the liquid level gradually decreases, and finally white or nearly white solid salt is precipitated in the evaporation dish.
experiments.conclusion: Use the properties of sodium chloride to be easily soluble in water but impurities are insoluble, and sodium chloride does not evaporate with water vapor. The insoluble impurities in the coarse salt can be preliminarily removed through dissolution, filtration, and evaporation operations, and the yield of refined salt can be calculated; the salt obtained may still contain soluble impurities and is not necessarily pure.

exercises.name: A classmate used newly prepared Cu(OH)2 to test three solutions A, B, and C. After heating, a brick-red precipitate appears in solution A, solution B has no obvious change, and solution C forms a blue precipitate but does not change color when heated. The three known solutions are glucose solution, sucrose solution and salt solution. Please determine what kind of solution A, B, and C are, and explain the basis for your judgment.
exercises.stem: A classmate used newly prepared Cu(OH)2 to test three solutions A, B, and C. After heating, a brick-red precipitate appears in solution A, solution B has no obvious change, and solution C forms a blue precipitate but does not change color when heated. The three known solutions are glucose solution, sucrose solution and salt solution. Please determine what kind of solution A, B, and C are, and explain the basis for your judgment.
tests: Use characteristic reactions to detect organic matter
exercises.answer: A is glucose solution, B is sucrose solution, and C is salt solution. Basis: Glucose can heat with freshly prepared Cu(OH)2 to form a brick-red Cu2O precipitate, which is a characteristic reaction; sucrose cannot undergo this reaction under unhydrolyzed conditions, and only presents a blue suspension of Cu(OH)2; there is no reducing organic matter in the salt solution, and only a blue precipitate of Cu(OH)2 is generated or maintained without the appearance of a brick-red precipitate.
exercises.analysis: This question examines the characteristic reactions of glucose and the analysis of experimental phenomena. According to the textbook: "Glucose reacts with newly prepared copper hydroxide to form a brick-red cuprous oxide precipitate... These two reactions can be used to test glucose." Only when a glucose-containing solution is heated with Cu(OH)2 will a brick-red precipitate appear. Sucrose does not show reducing properties when it is not hydrolyzed. Table salt is an inorganic salt and does not undergo a reducing reaction with Cu(OH)2.

exercises.name: Distinguish between major elements and trace elements and determine whether they are necessary
exercises.stem:
Read the following narrative:
(1) Elements whose content exceeds 0.01% in the human body are called macroelements; elements whose content is less than 0.01% are called trace elements.
(2) Macroelements are all essential elements for the human body, and only a few of the trace elements are essential elements for the human body.
(3) The contents of selenium, iodine and fluorine in the human body are very small, but they are necessary to maintain normal life activities.
(4) For essential elements for the human body, the more intake, the better for human health.
Which of the above statements are correct? and explain the reasons.
tests: The appropriate amount of element intake
Distinguish between major elements and trace elements
exercises.answer:
Correct are (1) and (3).
Reason:
(1) Consistent with the definitions of major elements and trace elements in the textbook.
(2) The mistake is that the statement "all major elements are essential elements for the human body, and only a few of the trace elements are essential for the human body" is too absolute. The textbook statement is "major elements and some trace elements are essential for the human body." It does not deny that some trace elements are necessary, nor does it say that "only a few" trace elements are necessary.
(3) The textbook clearly states that selenium, iodine, and fluorine are essential trace elements. Although the content is very small, they are necessary to maintain life activities.
(4) It contradicts the conclusion that "either insufficient or excessive intake of essential elements is detrimental to human health" and is therefore wrong.
exercises.analysis: This question tests students' understanding of the concepts of macroelements and trace elements, as well as the concepts of "essential elements for the human body" and "appropriate intake". Key points: Remember the 0.01% dividing line; note that "major elements" and "essential elements" are not the same concept; understand the scientific concept of dosage that "deficiency" and "excess" are not good for health.

exercises.name: Disease prevention measures in iodine-deficient areas
exercises.stem:
The water and soil in a certain mountainous area are severely deficient in iodine, and the incidence of goiter among local residents is very high. Answer based on what you have learned:
(1) What is the main role of iodine in the human body?
(2) What are the main causes of this endemic disease?
(3) Please propose a simple and effective prevention and control measure and explain the reasons.
tests: The role of iodine in the human body
Endemic diseases and element content in water and soil
Strategies for obtaining essential elements from food
Analyze the relationship between elemental content in the environment and endemic diseases
exercises.answer:
(1) Iodine is an important component of thyroid hormone. Iodine deficiency can cause goiter. Iodine deficiency in young children can affect growth and development and cause slow thinking.
(2) The lack of iodine in the local water and soil leads to insufficient iodine intake from drinking water and food for residents for a long time, causing iodine deficiency and resulting in endemic goiter and other endemic diseases.
(3) Prevention and control measures: Promote the use of iodized salt. Reason: The textbook points out that iodized salt can be made to increase the intake of iodine to ensure human health; salt is a daily necessity, and adding an appropriate amount of iodine to salt is economical and convenient, and can provide long-term and stable iodine supplementation.
exercises.analysis: This question comprehensively examines concepts such as "the role of iodine in the human body", "endemic diseases and element content in water and soil", "food additives and element supplements". When answering, you should grasp the cause and effect chain of "iodine deficiency-goiter-iodized salt prevention and treatment".

exercises.stem:
Among the following statements about "solution", which one is correct ( )
A. The solution must be a transparent and pure substance
B. A solution is a uniform, stable mixture of solute and solvent.
C. As long as the solid is put into water and stirred, a solution will definitely be obtained
D. A solution can only contain one solute
exercises.answer: B
exercises.analysis: According to the textbook, "One or several substances are dispersed into another substance to form a uniform, stable mixture, called a solution. A solution is composed of a solute and a solvent." It can be seen that B is correct; a solution is a mixture and not a pure substance (Exclude A), not all solids can be dissolved (Exclude C), and there can be several solutes in the solution (Exclude D).

exercises.name: Add equal volumes of vegetable oil to two test tubes, and add equal volumes of water to each. Test tube A is only shaken, and test tube B is first added with an appropriate amount of detergent and then shaken. After standing for a period of time, test tube A was observed to re-stratify, while test tube B still remained milky and turbid. Please write down the names of the two concepts embodied by this phenomenon and give their definition points respectively.
exercises.stem: Add equal volumes of vegetable oil to two test tubes, and add equal volumes of water to each. Test tube A is only shaken, and test tube B is first added with an appropriate amount of detergent and then shaken. After standing for a period of time, test tube A was observed to re-stratify, while test tube B still remained milky and turbid. Please write down the names of the two concepts embodied by this phenomenon and give their definition points respectively.
exercises.answer:
Concept 1: emulsion - a mixture formed by small droplets dispersed into a liquid.
Concept 2: Emulsification - a phenomenon in which substances such as detergents disperse water-insoluble liquids into countless small droplets in water, thereby enhancing the stability of the emulsion.
exercises.analysis: Both test tubes A and B formed emulsions after shaking, but test tube A separated into layers after standing, indicating that the emulsions were generally unstable; test tube B formed a more stable emulsion under the action of detergent. This increase in stability is the emulsification phenomenon.

exercises.name:

exercises.stem:

exercises.name: Judgement of dispersion particle size and type
exercises.stem:
The diameter of the dispersed particles in a certain dispersion system is about 50 nm. Which of the following is correct ( ).
A. The dispersion must be a solution
B. The dispersion must be an emulsion or suspension
C. This dispersion is a colloid
D. The type of dispersion cannot be determined
and explain the reasons.
tests: Determine the type of dispersion system based on particle size
exercises.answer: Select C. Because the dispersion system with a diameter of 1 to 100 nm is a colloid, and 50 nm is within this range, the dispersion system is a colloid.
exercises.analysis: The textbook clearly points out: A dispersion particle whose diameter is less than 1 nm is a solution, a dispersion particle whose diameter is greater than 100 nm is an emulsion or suspension, and a dispersion whose diameter is 1 to 100 nm is a colloid. 50 nm is in line with the colloidal particle size range, so it should be judged as a colloid.

exercises.name: Use the Tyndall effect to determine the dispersion system
exercises.stem: Use a laser beam in a dark room to illuminate two liquid dispersions A and B in sequence. When observing in the direction perpendicular to the beam, it is found that A can see an obvious bright "path", but B cannot see this phenomenon. Try to judge what type of dispersion system A and B may belong to, and write down the basis.
tests: Use the Tyndall effect to distinguish colloids and solutions
exercises.answer: A may be a colloid and B may be a solution. Basis: When a light beam passes through a colloid, a bright "pathway" can be seen, which is the Tyndall effect caused by the scattering of light by colloidal particles; the diameter of the particles in the solution is less than 1 nm, and the scattering of light is extremely weak, so this bright "pathway" cannot be seen.
exercises.analysis: This question examines the concept and application of the Tyndall effect. According to the textbook description, only colloids will produce obvious Tyndall effect, while solutions are not easily observed, so the type of dispersion system can be judged based on the phenomenon.

experiments.name: Experiment 9-1 Sucrose dissolution
experiments.process: Add a spoonful of sucrose to 20 mL of water, stir with a glass rod, and observe whether the sucrose "disappears" and whether the solution is uniform and stable.
experiments.phenomena: Sucrose "disappears" quickly, forming a uniform sucrose solution with the same composition in any part.
experiments.conclusion: Sucrose dissolves in water to form a uniform and stable solution, indicating that the solution is a mixture of solute and solvent.

experiments.name: Experiment 9-4 Emulsification experiment of vegetable oil, water and detergent
experiments.process: Add 5 mL of water and a few drops of vegetable oil to each of the two test tubes and observe whether there is stratification. Add 4 to 5 drops of detergent to one of the test tubes. Plug the two test tubes tightly with rubber stoppers and shake them vigorously respectively, and observe the phenomenon after shaking. Let it sit for a few minutes and check to see if it separates. Pour off the liquid and rinse the test tubes with water to compare whether the inner walls of the two test tubes are clean.
experiments.phenomena: The test tube with only water and vegetable oil will appear a milky turbid liquid after shaking, and will stratify again after standing, and the inner wall of the test tube will be greasy and difficult to rinse; the test tube with detergent added will form a more stable emulsion, which will not stratify obviously after standing, and the test tube will be easier to rinse with water.
experiments.conclusion: Small droplets are dispersed into the liquid to form an emulsion. The emulsion is generally unstable; detergent can disperse oil into countless small droplets and enhance the stability of the emulsion. This phenomenon is called emulsification.

experiments.name: Use the Tyndall effect to distinguish Fe(OH)3 colloid and CuSO4 solution
instrument: Electric furnace or alcohol lamp for heating
experiments.process: 1. Take two 100 mL small beakers, add 40 mL distilled water and 40 mL CuSO4 solution respectively; 2. Heat the beaker containing distilled water to boiling, add 5 to 6 drops of FeCl3 saturated solution drop by drop to the boiling water, continue to boil until the liquid turns reddish brown, stop heating, and prepare Fe(OH)3 colloid; 3. Place the beaker containing the CuSO4 solution and Fe(OH)3 colloid in a dark place, illuminate the liquid in the beaker with a red laser pointer, and observe and record the phenomenon in the direction perpendicular to the beam.
experiments.phenomena: When the light beam passes through the Fe(OH)3 colloid, a bright "pathway" can be seen; however, when the light beam passes through the CuSO4 solution, this phenomenon cannot be seen.
experiments.conclusion: Colloids can significantly scatter light to produce the Tyndall effect. The particles in the solution have small diameters and extremely weak scattering. Therefore, the Tyndall effect can be used to distinguish colloids and solutions.

experiments.name: Sulfur dioxide soluble in water and acidity test (Experiment 5-1)
experiments.instrument: A test tube filled with SO2 and plugged with a rubber stopper, a sink, water, and pH test paper
experiments.process: Place the test tube filled with SO2 and plugged with a rubber stopper upside down in the water, open the rubber stopper under the water surface, and observe the rise of the liquid level in the test tube; when the liquid level no longer changes significantly, plug the test tube mouth tightly underwater, take out the test tube, and use pH test paper to measure the pH of the solution in the test tube.
experiments.phenomena: The liquid level in the test tube rises, indicating that SO2 is dissolved in water in large quantities; the pH test paper shows that the solution is acidic.
experiments.conclusion: SO2 is easily soluble in water, and the solution is acidic, indicating that SO2 is an acidic oxide and reacts with water to form H2SO3.

exercises.name: Determine conductivity and electrolyte
exercises.stem:
A classmate used a conductivity device to test the conductivity of dry NaCl solid, NaCl solution and distilled water. The result was that dry NaCl solid and distilled water were not conductive, but NaCl solution was conductive. Answer based on experimental phenomena:
(1) Is NaCl an electrolyte? Give reasons.
(2) Explain the difference in conductivity between NaCl solid and NaCl solution from the perspective of microscopic particles.
tests: Determine whether a substance is an electrolyte
Explain conductivity from a microscopic particle perspective
exercises.answer:
(1) NaCl is an electrolyte. Because NaCl can conduct electricity in an aqueous solution, it meets the definition of "a compound that can conduct electricity in an aqueous solution or molten state is called an electrolyte."
(2) Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in NaCl solid are closely arranged according to certain rules and cannot move freely, so they are not conductive. When NaCl is dissolved in water, it is ionized under the action of water molecules into hydrated Na⁺ and hydrated Cl⁻ that can move freely. They move in a direction under the action of an electric field to form an electric current, so the NaCl solution can conduct electricity.
exercises.analysis: This question examines the definition of electrolyte and the explanation of conductivity from a microscopic ion perspective. When answering the question, first use the original words about the electrolyte in the textbook to determine NaCl, and then explain the difference between solid and solution in terms of "whether ions can move freely."

exercises.name: Write the ionic equation for the reaction of Na2SO4 and BaCl2
exercises.stem:
Na2SO4 dilute solution reacts with BaCl2 dilute solution to form BaSO4 precipitate and NaCl solution.
(1) Write the chemical equation for this reaction.
(2) Write the ionic equation for this reaction and indicate which ions are bystander ions.
exercises.answer:
(1) Na2SO4 + BaCl2 = 2NaCl + BaSO4↓.
(2) Ba²⁺ + SO4²⁻ = BaSO4↓. The spectator ions are Na⁺ and Cl⁻, which always exist in the solution as ions before and after the reaction and do not participate in the formation of precipitation.
exercises.analysis: First write the balanced chemical equation, then write the strong electrolyte in ionic form, delete the same Na⁺ and Cl⁻ on both sides of the equation, and you can get the ionic equation. Ions that can identify deleted ions are spectator ions.

exercises.name: Understand the acid from the ionization perspective
exercises.stem:
According to the following ionization equation:
HCl = H⁺ + Cl⁻
H2SO4 = 2H⁺ + SO4²⁻
HNO3 = H⁺ + NO3⁻
(1) Summarize the common characteristics of acids when they ionize.
(2) Use this essence to explain why HCl is an acid but NaCl is not an acid.
tests: Judge the acid from the ionization perspective
exercises.answer:
(1) The cations generated when these substances are ionized in aqueous solution are all H⁺, which is a common feature of acids.
(2) The cations generated when HCl is ionized are all H⁺, which is consistent with the saying "A compound in which all cations generated during ionization are hydrogen ions is called an acid", so HCl is an acid; NaCl is ionized into Na⁺ and Cl⁻, and the cations generated are Na⁺ instead of H⁺, which does not conform to the ionizing nature of acids, so NaCl is not an acid.
exercises.analysis: Closely following the definition of the ionization nature of acids in the textbook, first abstract the point that "all cations are H⁺", and then compare the ionization equations of HCl and NaCl to make a judgment.

exercises.name: Calculate the ionization constant of ammonia water
exercises.stem: At a certain temperature, in ammonia water with a solute concentration of 0.20 mol·L⁻¹, when the ionization equilibrium is reached, the ionized NH3·H2O is 1.7×10⁻³ mol·L⁻¹. Try to calculate the ionization constant Kb of NH3·H2O at this temperature.
tests: Use the equilibrium concentration to calculate the ionization constant
exercises.analysis: Write the ionization equation: NH3·H2O ⇌ NH4⁺ + OH⁻. List each particle concentration according to "Start-Change-Equilibrium": starting c(NH3·H2O)=0.20 mol·L⁻¹, c(NH4⁺)=0, c(OH⁻)=0; change: all ±1.7×10⁻³; equilibrium: c(NH3·H2O)=0.20−1.7×10⁻³≈0.20 mol·L⁻¹, c(NH4⁺)=1.7×10⁻³ mol·L⁻¹, c(OH⁻)=1.7×10⁻³ mol·L⁻¹. Substituting Kb = c(NH4⁺)·c(OH⁻)/c(NH3·H2O) we get Kb ≈ (1.7×10⁻³)² / 0.20 ≈ 1.4×10⁻⁵.

experiments.name: Comparative experiment on the conductivity of solid NaCl, KNO3 and their solutions (Experiment 1-2)
experiments.process: Add dry NaCl solid, KNO3 solid and distilled water to the three beakers respectively, connect the circuit as shown in the figure, insert the graphite electrode into the three beakers in sequence and turn on the power supply to observe the conductivity. Then dissolve a little of NaCl solid and KNO3 solid in water to make a solution, then insert the electrode into the NaCl solution and KNO3 solution, turn on the power and observe the conductivity.
experiments.phenomena: Dry NaCl solid, KNO3 solid and distilled water are not conductive, but NaCl solution and KNO3 solution are conductive.
experiments.conclusion: NaCl, KNO3, etc. do not conduct electricity in the dry solid state, but they can conduct electricity in aqueous solutions. They are electrolytes; the conductivity of electrolyte solutions is related to the presence of freely moving ions in them.

experiments.name: Ion change experiment of the reaction between Na2SO4 and BaCl2 solution (Experiment 1-3)
experiments.process: Add 2 mL BaCl2 dilute solution to the test tube containing 2 mL Na2SO4 dilute solution (the two react completely), observe the phenomenon, and analyze the ion species in the solution before and after the reaction based on the ionization equation.
experiments.phenomena: A white precipitate is generated, and a white precipitate of BaSO4 appears in the solution.
experiments.conclusion: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ do not participate in the reaction. SO4²⁻ reacts with Ba²⁺ ionicly to form an insoluble white precipitate of BaSO4. The essence of the reaction is Ba²⁺ + SO4²⁻ = BaSO4↓, which is an ionic reaction.

exercises.stem: It is known that in a certain phosphorus oxide, phosphorus has a valence of +5 and oxygen has a valence of -2. Write the chemical formula of this phosphorus oxide.
tests: Use chemical valence to derive chemical formulas
The principle that the algebraic sum of element valences is zero
exercises.answer: P2O5
exercises.analysis: Write the element symbols P and O, write left for positive valence and right for negative valence; find the least common multiple of 10, the absolute value of the combined valence of the two elements; divide 10 by the number of atoms of the absolute value of each element: P is 10/5=2, O is 10/2=5; get the chemical formula P2O5; check again (+5)×2+(-2)×5=0, which conforms to the principle that the algebraic sum is zero.

exercises.name: Comparison of metallic properties of sodium and magnesium
exercises.stem: Recall the experimental phenomenon of the reaction between sodium and water, and write a chemical equation. Combined with the experimental fact that "magnesium basically does not react with cold water and reacts slowly with hot water", compare the metallicity of sodium and magnesium and explain the reasons.
tests: Compare the metallicity by reacting with water
exercises.answer:
The reaction phenomenon between sodium and water: sodium swims rapidly on the water surface, reacts violently, releases a large number of bubbles, and the resulting solution can turn phenolphthalein red.
Chemical equation: 2Na + 2H2O = 2NaOH + H2↑.
Compare: Sodium is more metallic than magnesium. Reason: Sodium reacts violently with cold water, while magnesium hardly reacts with cold water and reacts slowly in hot water, indicating that sodium is more likely to lose electrons and is more metallic.
exercises.analysis: The metal that reacts more violently with water at the same temperature has stronger metallicity. Comparing metallicity by using the ease of reaction between metals and water is a typical application of metallicity gradient in the same period.

experiments.name: Experiment 2-1 Physical properties of sodium and reaction with air
instrument: Container containing sodium (containing paraffin oil or kerosene)
experiments.process: Use tweezers to take a small piece of sodium, use filter paper to absorb the kerosene on the surface, and then cut off the skin at one end with a knife. Observe the luster and color of the sodium, and pay attention to the changes in the surface of the newly cut sodium.
experiments.phenomena: Sodium is very soft and can be cut with a knife; it has a silver-white metallic luster after the outer skin is cut, and the newly cut bright surface quickly darkens.
experiments.conclusion: Sodium is soft in texture and has a silvery white metallic luster. Its surface is easily oxidized in the air to form sodium oxide.

experiments.name: Experiment 2-2 The reaction of sodium heating in the air
experiments.process: Heat the dry crucible, and at the same time cut a piece of sodium as big as a mung bean and quickly put it into the hot crucible. Continue to heat for a while, remove the alcohol lamp after the sodium melts, and observe the phenomenon.
experiments.phenomena: Sodium first melts when heated, and then reacts violently with oxygen to emit a yellow flame and produce a light yellow solid.
experiments.conclusion: Sodium burns violently when heated in air to produce light yellow solid sodium peroxide.

experiments.name: Experiment on the reaction of sodium and water
experiments.process: Add some water into the beaker, add a few drops of phenolphthalein solution, and then put a piece of sodium as big as a mung bean into the water. Observe the phenomenon from the position of the sodium in the water, shape changes, and solution color changes.
experiments.phenomena: Sodium moves violently on the water surface or in the water and gradually becomes smaller, accompanied by heat generation, bubbles are generated, and the solution turns red due to phenolphthalein.
experiments.conclusion: Sodium reacts violently with water, releases heat, and generates sodium hydroxide and hydrogen gas, making the solution alkaline.

experiments.name: Experiment 2-3 Reaction of sodium peroxide with water and carbon dioxide
experiments.process: Drop 1~2 mL of water into a test tube containing 1~2 g of solid sodium peroxide. Immediately insert the wooden stick with sparks into the test tube to check the generated gas. Touch the outer wall of the test tube with your hand and use pH test paper to test the acidity and alkalinity of the solution.
experiments.phenomena: Wooden strips with sparks re-ignite, the outer wall of the test tube becomes hot, and the pH test paper shows alkalinity.
experiments.conclusion: Sodium peroxide reacts with water to produce sodium hydroxide and oxygen. The reaction is exothermic and produces an alkaline solution.

experiments.name: Experiment 2-4 Compare the properties of Na2CO3 and NaHCO3
experiments.process: Add a small amount of Na2CO3 and NaHCO3 to the two test tubes respectively and observe the appearance; add a few drops of water respectively to shake and insert a thermometer to observe the temperature change; continue to add about 5 mL of water and shake to observe the dissolution; drop in phenolphthalein solution respectively to observe the phenomenon.
experiments.phenomena: Na2CO3 is a white powder, which agglomerates into crystals when exposed to a small amount of water and emits heat; NaHCO3 is a fine white crystal, which dissolves and absorbs heat when exposed to a small amount of water; both solutions can turn phenolphthalein red.
experiments.conclusion: Na2CO3 forms hydrated crystals when it meets water and releases heat; NaHCO3 dissolves endothermicly; both solutions are alkaline.

experiments.name: Experiment 2-5 Compare the thermal stability of Na2CO3 and NaHCO3
experiments.process: Heat Na2CO3 and NaHCO3 respectively, and observe whether there is decomposition and gas generation.
experiments.phenomena: Na2CO3 is not easily decomposed when heated; NaHCO3 produces gas and solid residues when heated.
experiments.conclusion: Na2CO3 is thermally stable, and NaHCO3 is easy to decompose when heated. Heating can be used to identify the two.

experiments.name: Experiment 2-6 Metal flame color test
experiments.process: Put the platinum wire embedded in the glass rod on the outer flame and burn it until the flame color returns; dip the platinum wire into the sodium carbonate solution and burn it on the outer flame, and observe the flame color; then wash the platinum wire with hydrochloric acid, burn it until it is colorless, then dip it into the potassium carbonate solution and burn it, and observe the flame color through the blue cobalt glass.
experiments.phenomena: Sodium carbonate makes the flame yellow; potassium carbonate turns purple under cobalt glass.
experiments.conclusion: Different metal compounds have characteristic flame colors in the flame color test, which can be used to identify metallic elements.

(Textbook Exercise Question 4) At room temperature, a bleaching solution can be obtained by passing Cl₂ into NaOH solution.
(1) The ionic equation of the above reaction is ________, and the active ingredient of the bleach solution is ________ (fill in the name).

exercises.stem:
(Textbook Exercise Question 4) At room temperature, a bleaching solution can be obtained by passing Cl₂ into NaOH solution.
(1) The ionic equation of the above reaction is ________, and the active ingredient of the bleach solution is ________ (fill in the name).
(2) The method of testing whether a solution contains Cl⁻ is ________, and the ionic equation for the reaction is ________.
tests: Reaction of chlorine and sodium hydroxide
Interference of carbonate on chloride ion test
Use precipitation reactions to detect ions and eliminate interference
exercises.answer:
(1) Cl₂ + 2OH⁻ = Cl⁻ + ClO⁻ + H₂O; the active ingredient is sodium hypochlorite (NaClO).
(2) First add an appropriate amount of dilute nitric acid to the solution to be tested for acidification, and then add AgNO₃ solution dropwise. If a white precipitate insoluble in dilute nitric acid is formed, the solution contains Cl⁻; the ionic equation is Cl⁻ + Ag⁺ = AgCl↓.
exercises.analysis: This question examines the disproportionation reaction between chlorine and NaOH and the detection principle of chloride ions. When writing an ionic equation, be careful to omit bystander ions such as Na⁺; part of the Cl element in Cl₂ is reduced to Cl⁻, and part is oxidized to ClO⁻. When testing Cl⁻, it is necessary to first acidify it with dilute nitric acid to remove possible interfering ions such as CO₃²⁻, and then use the characteristic reaction of Cl⁻ and Ag⁺ to generate insoluble AgCl for identification.

Chemical equation: Cl₂ + H₂O = HCl + HClO.
Reason: When chlorine gas dissolves in water, it partially reacts with water to form hypochlorous acid (HClO). Hypochlorous acid has strong oxidizing properties and can kill bacteria in the water and play a disinfecting role.
exercises.analysis: When answering, you should write down the reaction equation between chlorine gas and water, and explain that HClO has strong oxidizing properties and is the direct cause of sterilization and disinfection.

exercises.name: (Adapted from Question 7 (1) of the textbook exercise) In the laboratory, four bottles of chlorine gas with a volume of 100 mL were prepared by reacting MnO₂ with concentrated hydrochloric acid (the density of chlorine gas at normal temperature is 2.91 g/L). exercises.stem: (Adapted from Question 7 (1) of the textbook exercise) In the laboratory, four bottles of chlorine gas with a volume of 100 mL were prepared by reacting MnO₂ with concentrated hydrochloric acid (the density of chlorine gas at normal temperature is 2.91 g/L). What is the theoretical mass of MnO₂ required? Please list the main calculation steps.
tests: Laboratory preparation reaction of chlorine gas
exercises.answer:
4 bottles, each bottle is 100 mL, total volume V(Cl₂)=0.4 L.
The mass of chlorine gas is m(Cl₂)=ρV=2.91 g/L × 0.4 L = 1.164 g.
The amount of substance n(Cl₂)=m/M≈1.164 g ÷ 71 g·mol⁻¹≈0.0164 mol.
From the equation: MnO₂ + 4HCl (concentrated) △→ MnCl₂ + Cl₂ + 2H₂O, n(MnO₂)=n(Cl₂)=0.0164 mol.
The required mass of MnO₂ m(MnO₂)=n·M≈0.0164 mol × 86.9 g·mol⁻¹≈1.4 g (according to two significant figures).
exercises.analysis: This question comprehensively applies the gas density formula m=ρV and the quantity relationship of substances in the chemical equation. First find the mass and quantity of Cl₂, and then find the quantity and mass of MnO₂ based on the 1:1 quantity relationship between reactants and products. Note the approximate value of molar mass.

experiments.name: Hydrogen gas combustion in chlorine gas experiment (Experiment 2-7)
experiments.process: Ignite hydrogen in the air, then slowly extend the ignited hydrogen tube into a gas bottle filled with chlorine, and observe the combustion phenomenon and the interaction between the products and water vapor in the air.
experiments.phenomena: Pure H₂ burns quietly in Cl₂, emitting a pale flame, and the generated HCl gas combines with water vapor in the air to form a mist.
experiments.conclusion: Hydrogen and chlorine combine to form HCl under ignition conditions. The reaction is a redox reaction, indicating that chlorine has strong oxidizing properties.

experiments.name: Chlorine bleaching experiment on colored substances (Experiment 2-8)
instrument: Several gas collecting bottles containing dry chlorine gas
Dry colored paper or cloth strips
Moist colored paper or cloth strips
experiments.process: (1) Place a dry colored paper strip and a moist colored paper strip into two gas collecting bottles containing dry chlorine gas, cover them with glass pieces and observe the phenomenon; (2) Place colored flowers into a gas collecting bottle containing dry chlorine gas, cover them with glass pieces and observe the color change.
experiments.phenomena: Moist colored strips of paper and colored flowers gradually fade, while in dry conditions the bleaching effect is significantly dependent on moisture.
experiments.conclusion: Chlorine itself does not directly bleach. In the presence of water, chlorine reacts with water to form hypochlorous acid, which has strong oxidizing properties. Hypochlorous acid can make certain dyes and organic pigments fade, so chlorine water and solutions containing ClO⁻ can be used as bleaching agents.

experiments.name: Digital experiment of hypochlorous acid light decomposition
experiments.process: (1) Connect the pH sensor, chloride ion sensor and oxygen sensor to the data collector and computer respectively; (2) Insert the three sensors into the jar containing chlorine water; (3) Irradiate the chlorine water with strong light and start collecting data at the same time to record the changes in pH, Cl⁻ concentration and oxygen volume fraction during the illumination process.
experiments.phenomena: During the illumination process, the pH of chlorine water gradually decreases, the chloride ion concentration increases, and the oxygen volume fraction in the jar increases. The data change curve shows the decomposition trend of HClO.
experiments.conclusion: Hypochlorous acid decomposes under light to produce HCl and O₂, which verifies the reaction of 2HClO light → 2HCl + O₂↑.

experiments.name: Chloride ion detection experiment (Experiment 2-9)
experiments.process: Add 2 to 3 mL of dilute hydrochloric acid, NaCl solution, and Na₂CO₃ solution into the three test tubes respectively, add a few drops of AgNO₃ solution in each, and observe the precipitation; then add a small amount of dilute nitric acid and observe the precipitation changes.
experiments.phenomena: After dripping AgNO₃, white precipitates were formed in the three test tubes; the white precipitates in the first two test tubes were insoluble in dilute nitric acid and were AgCl precipitates; the white precipitates in the third test tube were dissolved in dilute nitric acid and were Ag₂CO₃ precipitates.
experiments.conclusion: Cl⁻ and Ag⁺ form an insoluble AgCl precipitate, which can be used as a test reaction for Cl⁻; CO₃²⁻ can also form a white precipitate with Ag⁺ and dissolve in dilute nitric acid. Therefore, when testing Cl⁻, it should be acidified with dilute nitric acid first to eliminate the interference of CO₃²⁻.

exercises.name: In agricultural production, it is often necessary to use a sodium chloride solution with a mass fraction of 16% for seed selection. To prepare 150 kg of this solution, what mass of sodium chloride and water are needed?
exercises.stem: In agricultural production, it is often necessary to use a sodium chloride solution with a mass fraction of 16% for seed selection. To prepare 150 kg of this solution, what mass of sodium chloride and water are needed?
tests: Prepare a solution of a certain concentration based on the mass fraction
exercises.answer: The mass of sodium chloride is 24 kg and the mass of water is 126 kg.
exercises.analysis: By the mass fraction of solute = (mass of solute / mass of solution) × 100%. Assuming the mass of the solute is m, then 16% = m / 150 × 100%, m = 150 × 16% = 24 kg. Mass of solvent (water) = mass of solution - mass of solute = 150 - 24 = 126 kg.

Use "solute mass conservation" to perform dilution calculations
exercises.answer: The mass of water required is 195 g.

exercises.name: Calculation of the mass required to prepare NaOH solution
exercises.stem: Prepare 500 mL of 0.1 mol/L NaOH solution. What is the mass of NaOH required?
tests: Prepare solutions based on the amount and concentration of substances
exercises.answer: 2 g
exercises.analysis: From c = n / V, n(NaOH) = c·V = 0.1 mol/L × 0.5 L = 0.05 mol. The molar mass of NaOH is 40 g/mol, then m = n·M = 0.05 mol × 40 g/mol = 2 g.

exercises.name: Calculate Substance concentration of NaOH solution
exercises.stem: In the experiment of "titrating a strong base of unknown concentration with a strong acid of known concentration", use an acid burette to fill 0.1000 mol/L HCl solution, use a basic buret to measure 25.00 mL of the NaOH solution to be measured into a Erlenmeyer flask, and add phenolphthalein indicator. The volumes of HCl recorded in the three titrations were: 19.96 mL, 20.04 mL, and 20.00 mL. Try to calculate the concentration of NaOH in the NaOH solution to be tested (assuming that the titration reaction is complete, the reaction between HCl and NaOH proceeds according to the chemical equation HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O).
tests: Neutralization reaction of strong acid and strong base
Use neutralization titration to calculate the concentration of substances in unknown solutions
exercises.answer: The average volume of three HCl volumes V(HCl) = (19.96 + 20.04 + 20.00) / 3 = 20.00 mL = 0.02000 L; n(HCl) = c(HCl) × V(HCl) = 0.1000 mol/L × 0.02000 L = 2.000×10⁻³ mol. From HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O, we know that n(NaOH) = n(HCl) = 2.000×10⁻³ mol. The volume of the NaOH solution to be measured is V(NaOH) = 25.00 mL = 0.02500 L, so c(NaOH) = n/V = 2.000×10⁻³ mol ÷ 0.02500 L = 0.0800 mol/L.
exercises.analysis: This question examines the basic method of calculating the concentration of an unknown solution using neutralization titration. Key points: The first step is to find the average volume of HCl from three experiments; the second step is to use the cV relationship to find n(HCl); the third step is to use the 1:1 metering relationship between HCl and NaOH to find n(NaOH); the fourth step is to use n/V to find the concentration of NaOH.

experiments.name: Experiment 9-8 Prepare a sodium chloride solution and calculate the mass fraction

experiments.phenomena: When the solute mass is small, it can be completely dissolved; when it is close to or exceeds the solubility, part of the sodium chloride will no longer dissolve and form a saturated solution.
experiments.conclusion: Whether the solubility limit has been reached can be judged by whether the solution can be completely dissolved, and the concentration can be calculated in conjunction with the mass fraction.

experiments.name: Prepare 100 mL of 1.00 mol/L NaCl solution
process: Calculate the mass of NaCl solid required.
Weigh the NaCl solid based on the calculation.
Put the weighed NaCl solid into the beaker, add an appropriate amount of distilled water, and stir with a glass rod to dissolve it completely.

Pour the solution in the beaker into the 100 mL volumetric flask along the glass rod, and wash the inner wall of the beaker and the glass rod 2 to 3 times with a small amount of distilled water. Pour the washing liquid into the volumetric flask, and shake gently to mix the solution evenly.

Continue to add distilled water. When the liquid level is 1~2 cm away from the scale line, use a rubber dropper to add drops until the concave liquid surface of the solution is tangent to the scale line. Cap the bottle and shake it upside down repeatedly.
Pour the prepared solution into the reagent bottle and label it.
experiments.conclusion: The solute mass can be calculated based on the quantity, concentration and volume of the substance, and solutions with specified concentration and volume can be accurately prepared using instruments such as volumetric flasks.

experiments.name: Inspection and use of volumetric flasks
process: Tie the stopper of the volumetric flask to the neck of the bottle with a strong string to prevent damage or loss.
Before use, check whether the volumetric flask is in good condition and whether there is any water leakage at the mouth of the bottle. Make sure there is no water leakage before use.
After use, wash and dry the volumetric flask. Place a piece of paper between the stopper and mouth of the glass ground bottle stopper to avoid adhesion.
experiments.conclusion: Proper maintenance and use of volumetric flasks can ensure accurate volume of solutions, thereby ensuring the accuracy of the concentration of the prepared solutions.

experiments.name: Prepare 100 mL of 1.00 mol/L NaCl solution
experiments.process: Calculate the mass of NaCl solid required to prepare 100 mL of 1.00 mol/L NaCl solution; weigh the required mass of NaCl solid on the balance; put the weighed NaCl solid into the beaker, then add about 40 mL of distilled water to the beaker, stir with a glass rod to completely dissolve the NaCl solid; inject the solution along the glass rod for 100 mL volumetric flask, wash the inner wall of the beaker and the glass rod 2 to 3 times with a small amount of distilled water, and pour the washing liquid into the volumetric flask; continue to add distilled water to the volumetric flask, and when it is 1 to 2 cm below the scale line, use a rubber-tipped dropper to add drops until the liquid level is tangent to the scale line; cap the bottle, turn it upside down repeatedly, and shake well; pour the prepared solution into the reagent bottle and label it.
experiments.phenomena: The NaCl solid gradually dissolves, and finally a uniform and clear NaCl solution is obtained. The liquid level in the volumetric flask can be accurately adjusted to the scale line.
experiments.conclusion: By correct calculation, weighing, dissolving, quantitative transfer and constant volume operations, a NaCl solution with a substance concentration of 1.00 mol/L and a volume of 100 mL can be prepared.

experiments.name: Prepare 100 mL 0.50 mol/L NaCl solution with 1.00 mol/L NaCl solution
experiments.process: Calculate the volume of 1.00 mol/L NaCl solution required to prepare 100 mL of 0.50 mol/L NaCl solution; use a graduated cylinder to measure the required volume of 1.00 mol/L NaCl solution and pour it into the beaker; add about 20 mL of distilled water, stir slowly with a glass rod to mix evenly; pour the solution into the volumetric flask along the glass rod, wash the inner wall of the beaker and the glass rod 2 to 3 times with a small amount of distilled water, and pour the washing liquid into the volumetric flask; continue to add distilled water to the volumetric flask, and when 1 to 2 cm below the scale line, use a rubber-tipped dropper to drip until the liquid level is tangent to the scale line; cap the bottle, turn it upside down repeatedly, and shake well; pour the prepared solution into the designated container.
experiments.phenomena: The original 1.00 mol/L NaCl solution becomes a 0.50 mol/L NaCl solution with a lower substance concentration after adding water and diluting the volume.
experiments.conclusion: By taking the original solution according to the calculated volume and performing a constant volume operation, the dilution method can be used to prepare a NaCl solution with the specified substance concentration and volume.

exercises.name: Purpose of washing beakers and glass rods
exercises.stem: When preparing NaCl solution using a volumetric flask, after injecting the solution in the beaker into the volumetric flask, why do we need to wash the inner wall of the beaker and the glass rod 2 to 3 times with distilled water, and also pour the washing liquid into the volumetric flask?
tests: Quantitative transfer of solids or solutions
exercises.answer: Because during the transfer process, some of the solution is still attached to the inner wall of the beaker and the glass rod. If it is not washed and transferred, it will cause loss of solute, which will make the actual amount of solute in the volumetric flask smaller and the concentration of the prepared solution lower. Wash several times with distilled water and transfer all the washing liquid into the volumetric flask to ensure the quantitative transfer of all solutes and ensure the accuracy of the concentration of the prepared solution.
exercises.analysis: This question examines the meaning of "quantitative transfer" and "quantitative washing and transfer" when preparing solutions. The amount of solute in the volumetric flask must be equal to the theoretically calculated value. If the residual solute on the beaker and glass rod is not washed out and transferred to the volumetric flask, the concentration will be small. Therefore, it is necessary to wash repeatedly with a small amount of distilled water to allow all the solute to enter the volumetric flask.

experiments.process: Add a small amount of FeCl3 solution and FeSO4 solution to the two test tubes respectively, and then drop into each NaOH solution, observe and describe the color of the precipitate and its change with time.
experiments.phenomena: A reddish-brown Fe(OH)3 precipitate is formed in the FeCl3 solution; a white flocculent Fe(OH)2 precipitate is first formed in the FeSO4 solution, which quickly turns gray-green, and a reddish-brown substance is formed after being left for a period of time.
experiments.conclusion: The soluble salt solution of iron reacts with alkali to generate the corresponding hydroxide precipitate, and Fe(OH)2 is easily oxidized to Fe(OH)3 by oxygen.

experiments.name: Color reaction between Fe3+ and KSCN ( Experiment 3-2)
experiments.process: Add a small amount of FeCl3 solution and FeCl2 solution to the two test tubes respectively, add a few drops of KSCN solution to each and observe the color change of the solution.
experiments.phenomena: FeCl3 solution containing Fe3+ turns red when encountering KSCN solution; the color of FeCl2 solution containing Fe2+ does not change significantly and remains original color.
experiments.conclusion: Fe3+ can form a red complex with SCN-, and this color reaction can be used to test the presence of Fe3+.

experiments.name: Mutual redox between Fe3+, Fe and Cl2 (Experiment 3-3)
experiments.process: Add excess iron powder to the test tube containing the FeCl3 solution and shake it. After the reaction, drop in the KSCN solution to observe the phenomenon; then pour the supernatant into another test tube, drip in chlorine water and observe the changes.
experiments.phenomena: After adding iron powder, the solution changed from brown to light green, indicating that Fe3+ was reduced to Fe2+; at this time, KSCN did not appear red when added dropwise. After adding chlorine water to the clear solution, the solution turns red, indicating that Fe2+ is oxidized to Fe3+ by Cl2.
experiments.conclusion: Fe3+ can be reduced to Fe2+ by iron, and Fe2+ can be oxidized to Fe3+ by Cl2, indicating that there is a reversible redox transformation relationship between Fe2+, Fe3+ and iron elements.

experiments.name: Use copper-clad boards to make patterns
experiments.process: Take a small piece of copper-clad plate, draw the designed pattern on the surface with an oil-based pen, and then immerse the copper-clad plate into a small beaker containing FeCl3 solution. After a period of time, take out the copper-clad board and wash it with water to observe the appearance of the pattern.
experiments.phenomena: The area covered by the oil pen maintains the copper luster, and the copper in the uncovered part is corroded away, forming copper lines or graphics corresponding to the pattern.
experiments.conclusion: FeCl3 solution can selectively corrode exposed copper, reflecting the oxidizing property of iron salts and its application in the production of printed circuit boards.

experiments.name: Check the iron element in spinach
experiments.process: Chop about 10 g of fresh spinach and grind it in a mortar. Pour it into a beaker and add about 30 mL of distilled water. Stir. Filter the turbid liquid. The filtrate obtained is the test sample. Take a small amount of sample in a test tube, add a small amount of oxidizing dilute nitric acid, then add a few drops of KSCN solution and shake, and observe the color change.
experiments.phenomena: If spinach contains iron, adding dilute nitric acid can oxidize Fe2+ to Fe3+, and then the solution will appear red after adding KSCN solution dropwise.
experiments.conclusion: By converting iron in food into Fe3+ and producing red color with KSCN, it can be qualitatively determined whether spinach and other foods contain iron.

exercises.name: Calculation of the amount and gas volume of substances reacting between sulfuric acid and iron filings
exercises.stem: 250 mL of 2 mol/L sulfuric acid reacts completely with sufficient iron filings. Calculate: (1) the amount of iron filings participating in the reaction; (2) the volume of H2 produced (standard conditions).
tests: The relationship between the amount of substance and the stoichiometric number
Establish quantitative ratios of substances based on chemical equations
Conversion between the amount concentration of a substance and the amount of a substance
Conversion between the amount of substance and gas volume
exercises.answer: (1) The amount of iron filings participating in the reaction is 0.50 mol; (2) The volume of H2 generated under standard conditions is 11.2 L.
exercises.analysis: First find n(H2SO4) from c and V: n = 0.25 L × 2 mol/L = 0.50 mol. From the equation Fe + H2SO4 = FeSO4 + H2, we know that n(Fe):n(H2SO4) = 1:1, so n(Fe) = 0.50 mol. Using Vm=22.4 L/mol under standard conditions, from n(H2) = n(H2SO4) = 0.50 mol, we get V(H2) = 0.50 mol × 22.4 L/mol = 11.2 L.

experiments.name: Reaction experiment between aluminum flakes and hydrochloric acid
experiments.process: Add about 5 mL of hydrochloric acid into the test tube, then put in a small piece of aluminum and observe the phenomenon that occurs after a period of time. Then place the lit wooden stick at the mouth of the test tube and continue to observe.
experiments.phenomena: Bubbles are generated in the test tube, and gas will be released after a period of time. The characteristic phenomenon of flammable gas can be observed at the mouth of the test tube with a lit wooden stick.
experiments.conclusion: The aluminum oxide film on the aluminum surface and the aluminum body can react with hydrochloric acid to generate AlCl3 and H2, indicating that both Al and Al2O3 can react with acid.

experiments.name: Experiment 3-5 Reaction of aluminum and NaOH solution
instrument: Aluminum sheet polished to remove oxide film
experiments.process: Add a small amount of NaOH solution to each of the two test tubes, put a small piece of aluminum into one of them, and put into the other an aluminum piece that has been polished with sandpaper to remove the surface oxide film, and observe the time and number of bubbles generated; after a period of time, use a lit wooden stick close to the mouth of the two test tubes to test the gas generated.
experiments.phenomena: A large number of bubbles will immediately appear in the test tube where the polished aluminum sheet is placed; there will be no bubbles in the test tube without polished aluminum sheet at first, and they will appear after a period of time. There are flammable gases released from the mouths of both test tubes, which can ignite or make the wood sticks burn more vigorously.
experiments.conclusion: Aluminum and its surface alumina can react with NaOH solution to generate sodium metaaluminate and hydrogen; the dense oxide film on the surface will delay the start of the reaction, and polishing to remove the film can speed up the reaction. Al2O3 behaves as an amphoteric oxide.

exercises.name:
Add a small amount of acidic KMnO4 solution to a test tube, and then add an appropriate amount of FeSO4 solution dropwise. After the purple color fades, continue to add 2 drops of KSCN solution, and the solution will turn blood red. Try to answer:
(1) What type of reaction does the fading of the purple color indicate? What are the major ion valence state changes involved?
(2) When KSCN is added and blood red appears after the purple fades, what kind of iron ions are present in the solution? What relationship does this experiment reflect between different valence states of the same element?
exercises.stem:
Add a small amount of acidic KMnO4 solution to a test tube, and then add an appropriate amount of FeSO4 solution dropwise. After the purple color fades, continue to add 2 drops of KSCN solution, and the solution will turn blood red. Try to answer:
(1) What type of reaction does the fading of the purple color indicate? What are the major ion valence state changes involved?
(2) When KSCN is added and blood red appears after the purple fades, what kind of iron ions are present in the solution? What relationship does this experiment reflect between different valence states of the same element?
tests: Oxidizing and reducing properties of ferrous salts
Oxidation-reduction reaction realizes the mutual conversion between substances with different valence states of the same element
Detect ions through characteristic color reactions
Use the fading of strong oxidants to determine the presence and degree of reaction of the reducing agent
exercises.answer:
(1) A redox reaction occurs: Fe2+ reduces MnO4− and itself is oxidized from Fe2+ to Fe3+. The valence state of Mn element decreases from +7, and the valence state of Fe element increases from +2 to +3.
(2) The blood red color indicates the presence of Fe3+ in the solution, because Fe3+ and SCN− form a blood red complex. This experiment shows that the mutual conversion between the same element (iron) and different valence compounds Fe2+ and Fe3+ can be achieved through redox reactions.
exercises.analysis: The question combines the two phenomena of KMnO4 fading and KSCN color development to test students' understanding of the core ideas of Fe2+ reducibility, Fe3+ test and "mutual transformation between different valence states of the same element".

experiments.name: The reaction between iron wire and copper sulfate solution demonstrates the reducibility of iron
experiments.process: Add 2 mL of CuSO4 solution into a test tube, and then place a piece of iron wire into the CuSO4 solution. After a while, take out the wire, observe the phenomenon and explain it.
experiments.phenomena: Red metallic copper precipitates on the surface of the iron wire, and the color of the solution becomes lighter or even discolored.
experiments.conclusion: Iron reduces Cu2+ to Cu and itself is oxidized to Fe2+, indicating that elemental iron has reducing properties.

experiments.name: FeCl3 reacts with copper flakes to explore the oxidation of ferrous salts
experiments.process: Put 3 mL of FeCl3 dilute solution into the test tube, add a few small pieces of copper, shake, and observe the phenomenon after a while.
experiments.phenomena: The surface of the copper sheet changes (there may be attachments), and the color of the solution changes.
experiments.conclusion: Fe3+ oxidizes Cu to Cu2+ and itself is reduced to Fe2+, indicating that the iron salt has oxidizing properties.

experiments.name: FeCl3 reacts with KI and starch to explore the oxidation of iron salts
experiments.process: Add a few drops of FeCl3 dilute solution to a test tube containing 3 mL of water, then add 3 drops of KI solution, and observe the phenomenon. Then add 2 drops of starch solution to the solution and observe the phenomenon.
experiments.phenomena: The color change of iodine or iodine occurs after adding KI; the solution turns blue after adding starch solution.
experiments.conclusion: Fe3+ oxidizes I- to generate I2. I2 and starch appear blue, verifying the oxidizing property of Fe3+.

experiments.name: FeCl2 reacts with zinc flakes to explore the oxidation of ferrous salts
experiments.process: Take 3 mL of FeCl2 solution and add it to the test tube, add a few small pieces of zinc flakes, shake, and observe the phenomenon after a while.
experiments.phenomena: Zinc sheet may have sediments or bubbles, and the color of the solution changes.
experiments.conclusion: Zinc reduces Fe2+ to Fe and itself is oxidized to Zn2+, indicating that Fe2+ behaves as an oxidant in this reaction.

experiments.name: FeSO4 reacts with acidic KMnO4 to explore the reducibility of ferrous salts and the transformation of Fe2+→Fe3+
experiments.process: Add a small amount of acidic KMnO4 solution to a test tube, then add a small amount of FeSO4 solution to the test tube and observe the color change of the solution. When the purple color of the solution fades, add another 2 drops of KSCN solution and observe the phenomenon.
experiments.phenomena: After adding FeSO4, the purple color of the KMnO4 solution gradually fades; after the purple color fades, blood red appears when KSCN is added.
experiments.conclusion: Fe2+ reduces MnO4- and is oxidized to Fe3+; then Fe3+ and KSCN form a blood-red complex, indicating that ferrous salts are reducing and can be converted into iron salts through redox reactions.

experiments.name: Fe3+ and KSCN Chromogenic test of iron ions
experiments.process: Add 2 mL of distilled water to a test tube, then add a few drops of FeCl3 dilute solution, then add a few drops of KSCN solution, and observe the phenomenon.
experiments.phenomena: The solution turns blood red.
experiments.conclusion: Fe3+ and SCN- form a blood-red complex, which can be used as a test reaction for Fe3+.

experiments.name: Reduced Fe3+ and then reacted with KSCN to explore Fe2+/Fe3+ conversion and inspection
experiments.process: Add a small amount of FeCl3 dilute solution to a test tube, then add an appropriate amount of iron powder, shake gently for a while, then add a few drops of KSCN solution and observe the phenomenon.
experiments.phenomena: After adding iron powder, part of Fe3+ was reduced, and then the degree of color development weakened or changed after adding KSCN.
experiments.conclusion: Iron powder reduces part of Fe3+ to Fe2+, which reduces the Fe3+ that can form a blood-red complex with KSCN, indicating that the conversion of Fe2+ and Fe3+ can be achieved through oxidation and reduction, and can be indirectly judged by the intensity of color development.

exercises.name: Selective judgment on the composition of atomic nucleus
exercises.stem:
Nucleus ( ).
A. Made of electrons and protons B. Made of protons and neutrons C. Made of electrons and neutrons D. Made of protons, neutrons and electrons
exercises.answer: B
exercises.analysis: The original text states that "the nucleus is composed of protons and neutrons." Electrons move outside the nucleus and are not part of the nucleus, so choose B.

exercises.name: The relationship between the number of protons and the number of electrons
exercises.stem:
The number of protons in an atom is equal to ( ).
A. The number of neutrons B. The number of electrons C. The sum of the number of neutrons and the number of electrons D. The difference between the number of neutrons and the number of electrons
tests: Determine the number of protons and the number of electrons outside the nucleus based on the nuclear charge.
exercises.answer: B
exercises.analysis: In an electrically neutral atom, the number of positive charges carried by the nucleus is equal to the number of negative charges carried by electrons outside the nucleus, so the number of protons = the number of electrons.

exercises.name:

A. The number of protons is different B. The number of neutrons is different C. The relative atomic mass is different D. The sum of the number of neutrons and the number of electrons outside the nucleus is different

exercises.answer: A
exercises.analysis: The textbook points out that "an element is a general term for a type of atoms with the same number of protons (i.e., the number of nuclear charges)." Therefore, the essential difference between different elements is that the number of protons is different. Choose A.

O means __________; 2H means __________.
exercises.stem:
Fill in the blanks: Write the meaning of the following symbols:
O means __________; 2H means __________.
tests: Distinguish the three concepts of atoms, molecules and elements
exercises.answer: O represents oxygen element or one oxygen atom; 2H represents two hydrogen atoms.
exercises.analysis: The textbook points out that the element symbol represents both an element and an atom of this element. For example, "O" represents both an oxygen element and an oxygen atom; the previous coefficient represents the number of atoms of that type, so 2H represents two hydrogen atoms.

tests: Use atomic number and nuclide symbol to find the number of protons, neutrons, and electrons
exercises.answer:
(1) ${}_{3}^{6}\mathrm{Li}$ and ${}_{3}^{7}\mathrm{Li}$; ${}_{6}^{14}\mathrm{C}$ and ${}_{7}^{14}\mathrm{N}$ are not isotopes of each other (note that one pair is enough, the conventional answer in the textbook is to take a pair of Li, here we take ${}_{3}^{6}\mathrm{Li}$ and ${}_{3}^{7}\mathrm{Li}$)
(2) ${}_{6}^{14}\mathrm{C}$ and ${}_{7}^{14}\mathrm{N}$
(3) ${}_{3}^{7}\mathrm{Li}$ and ${}_{6}^{14}\mathrm{C}$
exercises.analysis: According to the nuclide symbol A^Z X, the number of protons is Z and the number of neutrons is A−Z. To be isotopes of each other requires "the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons." The equal mass numbers only require the same A; the equal neutron numbers require A1−Z1 = A2−Z2.

exercises.name:
In 2016, IUPAC named element No. 117 Ts (Chinese name "瑑", pronounced tián). The number of electrons in the outermost shell of Ts is 7. Among the following statements, the incorrect one is ( ).
