exercises.stem:
In 2016, IUPAC named element No. 117 Ts (Chinese name "瑑", pronounced tián). The number of electrons in the outermost shell of Ts is 7. Among the following statements, the incorrect one is ( ).
A. Ts is an element of Group VIIA of the seventh cycle
B. Isotopic atoms of Ts have the same number of electrons
C. Ts has the weakest non-metallic properties among the elements in the same family
D. Ts with a neutron number of 176, its nuclide symbol is ${}^{176} \mathrm{Ts}$
tests: Predict properties based on the position of elements in the periodic table
Use atomic number and nuclide symbol to find the number of protons, neutrons, and electrons
exercises.answer: D
exercises.analysis: Atomic number 117, corresponding to the nuclear charge number 117, the number of electrons in the isotope is the same, so B is correct. Group VIIA has 7 outermost electrons and is located in period 7. A is correct. The non-metallic property weakens from top to bottom in the same family, with Ts at the bottom being the weakest, and C is correct. The number of neutrons is 176, the mass number is A=Z+N=117+176=293, the nuclide symbol should be ${}_{117}^{293}\mathrm{Ts}$, and D only writes 176, which is wrong.

experiments.name: Experiment on potassium burning in air
experiments.process: Heat the dry crucible and cut a piece of potassium as big as a mung bean at the same time. Use tweezers to pick it up and quickly put it into the hot crucible. Continue heating for a while. When the potassium melts, immediately remove the alcohol lamp and observe the phenomenon.
experiments.phenomena: Potassium burns in air, emits characteristic flame and generates oxides.
experiments.conclusion: Potassium can react violently with oxygen, indicating that the chemical properties of alkali metals are active and their reactivity increases with the downward movement within the family.

experiments.name: Experiments on the reaction of potassium and water
experiments.process: Add some water to the beaker and add a few drops of phenolphthalein solution. Cut a piece of potassium the size of a mung bean, pick it up with tweezers and put it into the water to observe the phenomenon.
experiments.phenomena: Potassium moves rapidly on the water surface and reacts violently. The solution generates alkali, causing phenolphthalein to turn red and release hydrogen gas.
experiments.conclusion: Potassium can react violently with water to generate hydrogen and strong alkali, indicating that alkali metals are stronger than sodium, verifying that the chemical properties of alkali metals are similar and progressive.

experiments.name: Inter-halogen replacement reaction experiment (chlorine water/bromine water and potassium bromide, potassium iodide solution)
experiments.process: Add 1 mL of chlorine water to the two test tubes containing 4 mL of KBr solution and 4 mL of KI solution respectively, shake, observe the color change of the solution and compare with the color of chlorine water; add 1 mL of bromine water to the test tube containing 4 mL of KI solution, shake, observe the color change and compare with the color of bromine water.
experiments.phenomena: Chlorine water changes the color of potassium bromide solution and potassium iodide solution, indicating that bromine or iodine is replaced; bromine water can change the color of potassium iodide solution but cannot replace chlorine.
experiments.conclusion: The more reactive halogen can replace the less reactive halogen in the halide solution, reflecting the gradual weakening of halogen oxidation from fluorine to iodine.

experiments.name: Comparative experiment on the reaction between magnesium and water
experiments.process: Take a small piece of magnesium strip, use sandpaper to remove the oxide film on the surface, and place it in a test tube. Add 2 mL of water to the test tube, add 2 drops of phenolphthalein solution, and observe the phenomenon. After a while, heat the test tube until the liquid boils, observe the phenomenon, and analyze the ease of the reaction between magnesium and water and the products compared with the reaction between sodium and water.
experiments.phenomena: Magnesium reacts slowly with water at room temperature, and the color of phenolphthalein is not obvious. After heating to boiling, magnesium can be seen to gradually react, and the solution becomes alkaline (phenolphthalein turns red).
experiments.conclusion: The reaction between magnesium and water is more difficult than that between sodium and water, indicating that the metallicity of magnesium is weaker than that of sodium, and the products are hydrogen gas and magnesium hydroxide solution (weakly alkaline).

exercises.name:
In 2016, IUPAC named element No. 117 Ts (Chinese name "瑑", pronounced tián). The number of electrons in the outermost shell of Ts is 7. Among the following statements, the incorrect one is ( ).
A. Ts is an element of Group VIIA of the seventh cycle
B. Isotopic atoms of Ts have the same number of electrons
C. Ts has the weakest non-metallic properties among the elements in the same family
D. Ts with a neutron number of 176, its nuclide symbol is ${}^{176} \mathrm{Ts}$
exercises.stem:
In 2016, IUPAC named element No. 117 Ts (Chinese name "瑑", pronounced tián). The number of electrons in the outermost shell of Ts is 7. Among the following statements, the incorrect one is ( ).
A. Ts is an element of Group VIIA of the seventh cycle
B. Isotopic atoms of Ts have the same number of electrons
C. Ts has the weakest non-metallic properties among the elements in the same family
D. Ts with a neutron number of 176, its nuclide symbol is ${}^{176} \mathrm{Ts}$
tests: Predict properties based on the position of elements in the periodic table
Use atomic number and nuclide symbol to find the number of protons, neutrons, and electrons
exercises.answer: D
exercises.analysis: Atomic number 117, corresponding to the nuclear charge number 117, the number of electrons in the isotope is the same, so B is correct. Group VIIA has 7 outermost electrons and is located in period 7. A is correct. The non-metallic property weakens from top to bottom in the same family, with Ts at the bottom being the weakest, and C is correct. The number of neutrons is 176, the mass number is A=Z+N=117+176=293, the nuclide symbol should be ${}_{117}^{293}\mathrm{Ts}$, and D only writes 176, which is wrong.

C. The highest positive valence of a main group element is equal to the atomic number of the element
D. The sum of the absolute values of the highest positive valence and the lowest negative valence of chlorine is greater than 8
tests: Gradient law of properties of elements of the same period
The relationship between the highest positive valence of main group elements and the group order
The relationship between the valency and structure of non-metallic elements

exercises.answer: B
exercises.analysis: According to the textbook: "In the same cycle, although the number of electron layers outside the nucleus of each element is the same, from left to right, the number of nuclear charges increases, the atomic radius gradually decreases, the ability to lose electrons gradually weakens, and the ability to gain electrons gradually increases. Therefore, the metallicity gradually weakens, and the non-metallicity gradually weakens. Enhancement. "The direction of item A is opposite and wrong; item C should be that the highest positive valence of the main group element is equal to the group number, not the atomic number; item D is based on "the sum of the absolute values of the highest positive valence of the non-metal element and its negative valence is equal to 8", chlorine is +7 and -1, and the sum of the absolute values is 8. Therefore, only B is correct.

experiments.name: Comparative experiment on the reaction between magnesium and water
experiments.process: Take a small piece of magnesium strip, use sandpaper to remove the oxide film on the surface, and place it in a test tube. Add 2 mL of water to the test tube, add 2 drops of phenolphthalein solution, and observe the phenomenon. After a while, heat the test tube until the liquid boils, observe the phenomenon, and analyze the ease of the reaction between magnesium and water and the products compared with the reaction between sodium and water.
experiments.phenomena: Magnesium reacts slowly with water at room temperature, and the color of phenolphthalein is not obvious. After heating to boiling, magnesium can be seen to gradually react, and the solution becomes alkaline (phenolphthalein turns red).
experiments.conclusion: The reaction between magnesium and water is more difficult than that between sodium and water, indicating that the metallicity of magnesium is weaker than that of sodium, and the products are hydrogen gas and magnesium hydroxide solution (weakly alkaline).

experiments.name: Comparative experiment on the reaction of Al(OH)₃ with acid and alkali
experiments.process: Add 2 mL of 1 mol/L AlCl₃ solution into the test tube, and then add ammonia dropwise until white flocculent Al(OH)₃ precipitation no longer occurs. Divide the Al(OH)₃ precipitate into two test tubes, add 2 mol/L hydrochloric acid dropwise to one test tube, and drop 2 mol/L NaOH solution to the other test tube. Shake while adding dropwise, and observe changes in precipitation. Then use 2 mL of 1 mol/L MgCl₂ solution instead of AlCl₃ to do the same experiment for comparison.
experiments.phenomena: Al(OH)₃ can be dissolved in acid or strong alkali solution, while Mg(OH)₂ is only soluble in acid but not in strong alkali.
experiments.conclusion: Al(OH)₃ can react with both acid and strong alkali solution, and is an amphoteric hydroxide; Mg(OH)₂ only shows alkalinity and is a medium-strong base, indicating that although aluminum is a metal, it shows certain non-metallic properties.

exercises.name: Determine whether the reaction contains only non-polar covalent bonds
exercises.stem:
Among the following substances, the one that only contains non-polar covalent bonds is ( ).

A.NaOH
B.NaCl
C. H2
D. H2S
tests: Judge the type of chemical bonds (ionic bonds, covalent bonds, polar bonds and non-polar bonds)
exercises.answer: C
exercises.analysis: Non-polar covalent bonds require that they be formed by the same type of atoms and that the shared electron pair is not biased to either side. H—H in H2 is a non-polar covalent bond; NaOH and NaCl contain ionic bonds, and H2S is a polar covalent bond, so only H2 is all non-polar bonds.

tests: Judge the type of chemical bonds (ionic bonds, covalent bonds, polar bonds and non-polar bonds)
exercises.answer: D

exercises.name: Judge what is said about chemical bonds
exercises.stem:
Which of the following statements about chemical bonds is incorrect ( ).

A. A chemical bond is a force
B. Chemical bonds can combine ions or atoms
C. During a chemical reaction, chemical bonds within the reactant molecules are broken and chemical bonds within the product molecules are formed.
D. Non-polar bonds are not chemical bonds
tests: The essence of chemical reactions (chemical bond perspective)
exercises.answer: D
exercises.analysis: Chemical bonding is essentially a force that causes particles to attract each other. It can exist between ions and atoms. Chemical reactions are essentially the breaking of old bonds and the formation of new bonds. Non-polar covalent bonds are also a type of chemical bond, hence the error "non-polar bonds are not chemical bonds".

exercises.name: Compare covalent bonds and ionic bonds
exercises.stem: What is the difference between covalent bond and ionic bond? Please give an example.
tests: Judge the type of chemical bonds (ionic bonds, covalent bonds, polar bonds and non-polar bonds)
exercises.answer: Ionic bond is the interaction formed by electrostatic interaction between oppositely charged ions, such as the interaction between Na+ and Cl− to form NaCl; Covalent bond is the interaction formed between atoms by sharing electron pairs, such as the bonding method in H2, Cl2, HCl molecules. The former contains obvious ionic structures and is mostly found in compounds formed by metals and non-metals; the latter is mostly seen in bonds between non-metal atoms.
exercises.analysis: Compare the bonding particles (ions vs atoms), bonding methods (electrostatic attraction vs shared electrons) and typical examples (NaCl vs H2O, CO2, etc.) based on the definitions of ionic bonds and covalent bonds in the textbook.

exercises.name: They are also three-atom molecules. Water molecules are polar while carbon dioxide molecules are non-polar. Please explain from the perspective of molecular structure and bond polarity.
exercises.stem: They are also three-atom molecules. Water molecules are polar while carbon dioxide molecules are non-polar. Please explain from the perspective of molecular structure and bond polarity.
tests: Determine the polarity of bonds and the polarity of molecules
exercises.answer: The O—H bond in H2O is a polar bond, and the molecule has a curved structure (V shape). The dipole moments of the two O—H bonds cannot cancel each other out, resulting in the positive and negative electric centers of the molecule not coinciding, so it is a polar molecule. The C-O bond in CO2 is also a polar bond, but the molecule has a linear structure. The two C=O bonds are in opposite directions and equal in size. The vector sum of their dipole moments is zero, and the positive and negative electric centers overlap, so CO2 is a non-polar molecule.
exercises.analysis: This question comprehensively examines the judgment method of "bond polarity and molecule polarity", and the type and spatial configuration of the bond need to be considered at the same time.

exercises.name: Compare the structure and properties of ice and dry ice
exercises.stem:
Ice and dry ice are both colorless solids, but their structures and properties are significantly different. Answer according to the textbook content:
(1) Which type of crystal do ice and dry ice belong to?
(2) Briefly explain the difference in the main forces between water molecules in ice and CO₂ molecules in dry ice.
(3) Use microstructure to explain: Dry ice is denser than ice, but its melting point is lower than ice and it easily sublimates under normal pressure.
tests: Infer the macroscopic properties of substances from the microstructure
exercises.answer:
(1) Ice is a molecular crystal, and dry ice (solid CO₂) is also a molecular crystal.
(2) The main force between water molecules in ice is hydrogen bonding (van der Waals forces also exist); only van der Waals forces exist between CO₂ molecules in dry ice.
(3) Each water molecule in ice forms an approximate tetrahedral structure with 4 adjacent water molecules through directional hydrogen bonds, with low space utilization, large gaps, and low density; CO₂ molecules in dry ice only attract each other by van der Waals forces, and the molecules can be densely packed. One molecule is surrounded by 12 adjacent molecules, with fewer gaps and higher density. On the other hand, van der Waals forces are weaker than hydrogen bonds, so dry ice has a lower melting point than ice and can easily sublimate under normal pressure.
exercises.analysis: This question tests the understanding of the types of internal forces in molecular crystals, the concept of molecular close packing, and the structure-property relationship. The key is to grasp the two microscopic characteristics of "ice has hydrogen bonds and a tetrahedral structure with large gaps, and dry ice is densely packed with van der Waals forces", which are respectively related to density, melting point, and sublimation properties.

exercises.name: NaCl and CsCl are both ionic crystals. Why do they have higher melting points and boiling points?
exercises.stem: NaCl and CsCl are both ionic crystals. Why do they have higher melting points and boiling points?
exercises.answer: In NaCl and CsCl crystals, there are strong ionic bonds between cations and anions, making the crystals hard and difficult to compress. To change them from a solid to a liquid or gaseous state, sufficient energy must be provided to break these strong ionic bonds, so NaCl and CsCl have higher melting and boiling points.
exercises.analysis: This question requires explaining the macroscopic melting and boiling point from the perspective of microscopic forces. It should be noted that there are strong electrostatic interactions between counter-charged ions in ionic crystals, forming strong ionic bonds; melting and vaporization need to overcome this force, so the melting and boiling points are high. You can contact the specific values ​​provided in the text to deepen your understanding.

experiments.name: Make a spatial structure model of the molecule
experiments.process: Use plasticine or clay to represent atoms and toothpicks to represent chemical bonds. Build a spatial structure model of H₂, Cl₂, H₂O, CO₂, NH₃, CH₄ and other molecules according to the given bond lengths and bond angles, and use four balloons tied together with rubber bands to simulate the tetrahedral structure of methane.
experiments.phenomena: The model intuitively presents the spatial shapes and bond angles of different molecules; the four balloons are naturally arranged in a tetrahedron shape.
experiments.conclusion: The physical model helps to intuitively understand the spatial structure and bond angle size of the molecule. The balloon model illustrates that the four equivalent bonds will be as far apart as possible to form a tetrahedral structure.

experiments.name: Study on the microscopic mechanism of the adhesive force of gecko feet
experiments.process: Observe the microstructure of gecko feet using an electron microscope and find that they are covered with a large number of nanoscale fine hairs; measure the adsorption force of the fine hairs per unit area through mechanical experiments; use computer simulation to analyze the interaction between the fine hairs and the wall surface, and determine that its essence is van der Waals force; and then imitate adhesive materials based on this structure.
experiments.phenomena: When a cent is covered with about 1 million fine hairs, it can lift about 20 kg of objects; the bionic tape has strong adhesion.
experiments.conclusion: The adsorption force between gecko feet and the wall mainly comes from the van der Waals force between the fine hairs and the wall. Bionic design can prepare new adhesive materials based on this.

exercises.name: Comparison and phenomenon analysis of halogen oxidation
exercises.stem: Put 3 drops of NaBr solution, NaI solution and newly prepared chlorine water into the 3 holes of the drip plate respectively, then add 3 drops of newly prepared chlorine water to each of the NaBr solution and NaI solution; add NaI solution and bromine water to the other two holes, and then drop 3 drops of bromine water into the NaI solution. A change in color of the solution was observed. Try to write the chemical equation of the relevant reaction, and compare the oxidizing properties of Cl2, Br2, and I2 accordingly.
tests: Compare oxidation or activity through displacement reaction
exercises.answer:
Reaction equation:
Cl2 + 2NaBr = 2NaCl + Br2
Cl2 + 2NaI = 2NaCl + I2
Br2 + 2NaI = 2NaBr + I2
Oxidizing strength: Cl2 > Br2 > I2.
exercises.analysis: Judge the strength of oxidation by observing whether the more active halogen can displace another halogen from its halide solution: Cl2, which can oxidize Br- and I- to Br2 and I2, is the most oxidizing; Br2 can oxidize I- to I2, indicating that Br2 is more oxidizing than I2.

exercises.name: Comparison of metallic properties of sodium and magnesium
exercises.stem: Recall the experimental phenomenon of the reaction between sodium and water, and write a chemical equation. Combined with the experimental fact that "magnesium basically does not react with cold water and reacts slowly with hot water", compare the metallicity of sodium and magnesium and explain the reasons.
tests: Compare the metallicity by reacting with water
exercises.answer:
The reaction phenomenon between sodium and water: sodium swims rapidly on the water surface, reacts violently, releases a large number of bubbles, and the resulting solution can turn phenolphthalein red.
Chemical equation: 2Na + 2H2O = 2NaOH + H2↑.
Compare: Sodium is more metallic than magnesium. Reason: Sodium reacts violently with cold water, while magnesium hardly reacts with cold water and reacts slowly in hot water, indicating that sodium is more likely to lose electrons and is more metallic.
exercises.analysis: The metal that reacts more violently with water at the same temperature has stronger metallicity. Comparing metallicity by using the ease of reaction between metals and water is a typical application of metallicity gradient in the same period.

experiments.name: Experiment on the reaction of sodium and water

experiments.phenomena: Sodium moves violently on the water surface or in the water and gradually becomes smaller, accompanied by heat generation, bubbles are generated, and the solution turns red due to phenolphthalein.
experiments.conclusion: Sodium reacts violently with water, releases heat, and generates sodium hydroxide and hydrogen gas, making the solution alkaline.

experiments.phenomena: After adding chlorine water to the NaBr and NaI solutions, a color similar to the characteristic colors of Br2 and I2 appears; after adding bromine water to the NaI solution, a color similar to I2 appears.
experiments.conclusion: The oxidizing property of chlorine water is stronger than that of bromine water and iodine element, and the oxidizing property of bromine water is stronger than that of iodine element, reflecting the gradual change of the oxidation property of halogen with the position in the family.

experiments.name: Metallicity experiment comparing the reaction of sodium and magnesium with water
experiments.instrument: test tube, test tube rack, test tube clamp, measuring cylinder, rubber dropper, alcohol lamp, matches, magnesium bar

experiments.phenomena: Sodium reacts violently with cold water, rapidly releasing hydrogen gas and generating NaOH; magnesium hardly reacts with cold water, but slowly produces a small amount of bubbles when in contact with hot water, and white matter is formed on the surface.
experiments.conclusion: The metallicity of sodium is stronger than that of magnesium. In the same period, the metallicity generally weakens from left to right as the atomic number increases.

experiments.name: Comparison of the reaction of MgCl2 and AlCl3 with NaOH Hydroxide alkalinity experiment
experiments.instrument: test tube, test tube rack, rubber dropper, 1 mol/L NaOH Solution, phenolphthalein solution
experiments.process: Design an experiment to mix MgCl2 solution and NaOH solution to observe the precipitation of Mg(OH)2 and its behavior in excess NaOH; mix AlCl3 solution and NaOH solution to observe the formation of Al(OH)3 precipitation and its dissolution in excess NaOH.
experiments.phenomena: MgCl2 and NaOH form a white Mg(OH)2 precipitate, which is insoluble in excess NaOH; AlCl3 and NaOH form a white Al(OH)3 precipitate, which gradually dissolves in excess NaOH.
experiments.conclusion: Mg(OH)2 is more basic than Al(OH)3, indicating that the metallicity of magnesium is stronger than that of aluminum, and the metallicity weakens from left to right in the same period.

exercises.analysis: A should respond to water absorption rather than volatility; B The essence of the reaction is the oxidation of concentrated sulfuric acid; C The blackening of paper is mainly due to the strong dehydration of concentrated sulfuric acid that carbonizes organic matter; D is correct, concentrated sulfuric acid can dry some gases through water absorption.

experiments.name: Sulfur dioxide soluble in water and acidity test (Experiment 5-1)
experiments.instrument: A test tube filled with SO2 and plugged with a rubber stopper, a sink, water, and pH test paper
experiments.process: Place the test tube filled with SO2 and plugged with a rubber stopper upside down in the water, open the rubber stopper under the water surface, and observe the rise of the liquid level in the test tube; when the liquid level no longer changes significantly, plug the test tube mouth tightly underwater, take out the test tube, and use pH test paper to measure the pH of the solution in the test tube.
experiments.phenomena: The liquid level in the test tube rises, indicating that SO2 is dissolved in water in large quantities; the pH test paper shows that the solution is acidic.
experiments.conclusion: SO2 is easily soluble in water, and the solution is acidic, indicating that SO2 is an acidic oxide and reacts with water to form H2SO3.

experiments.name: The bleaching effect of sulfur dioxide (Experiment 5-2)
experiments.instrument: Test tubes, SO2 solution obtained in Experiment 5-1, magenta solution, heating device
experiments.process: Take 2 mL of the solution obtained in Experiment 5-1, add 1 to 2 drops of magenta solution, shake and observe the color change; then heat the test tube (pay attention to ventilation), and then observe the change of the solution.
experiments.phenomena: After adding magenta, the color of the solution fades or becomes significantly lighter; the color partially recovers after heating.
experiments.conclusion: SO2 has a bleaching effect because it forms unstable colorless substances with certain colored substances. These substances are easy to decompose, and the colored substances can restore their original color.

experiments.name: Reaction of concentrated sulfuric acid and copper (Experiment 5-3)
experiments.instrument: Test tube, rubber stopper with catheter, copper wire, concentrated sulfuric acid, heating device, magenta solution
experiments.process: Insert a copper wire with the lower end rolled into a spiral shape on the side of the rubber stopper with a catheter; add 2 mL of concentrated sulfuric acid to the test tube, plug the rubber stopper, bring the copper wire into contact with the concentrated sulfuric acid and heat it, and pass the generated gas into the magenta solution; pull the copper wire outward to terminate the reaction, and after cooling, slowly pour the contents of the test tube into another test tube containing a small amount of water, and observe the color of the solution.
experiments.phenomena: When heated, gas is produced, causing the magenta solution to fade (generating SO2); the solution in the test tube changes from colorless to blue (generating CuSO4 solution).
experiments.conclusion: Under heating conditions, concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with copper to produce copper sulfate, sulfur dioxide and water. Concentrated sulfuric acid oxidizes copper and reduces itself to SO2. Therefore, concentrated sulfuric acid has strong oxidizing properties and is an oxidizing agent.

experiments.name: The detection of sulfate ions (Experiment 5-4)
experiments.instrument: Three test tubes, dilute sulfuric acid, Na2SO4 solution , Na2CO3 solution, BaCl2 solution, dilute hydrochloric acid
experiments.process: Add a small amount of dilute sulfuric acid, Na2SO4 solution and Na2CO3 solution to the three test tubes, add a few drops of BaCl2 solution each, and observe the phenomenon; then add a small amount of dilute hydrochloric acid, shake, and observe the phenomenon.
experiments.phenomena: After adding BaCl2 to the three test tubes, white precipitates appeared; after adding dilute hydrochloric acid, the precipitate in the test tube containing Na2CO3 dissolved and CO2 was released, and the white precipitate BaSO4 in the solution containing SO4^{2-} was insoluble in dilute hydrochloric acid.
experiments.conclusion: In the solution, SO4^{2-} and Ba^{2+} generate a white BaSO4 precipitate that is insoluble in dilute hydrochloric acid. BaCl2 can be used to test the presence of sulfate ions; CO3^{2-} will also generate a white precipitate but can react with dilute hydrochloric acid to release CO2, so it needs to be acidified before testing to eliminate interference.

exercises.name: The purpose of adding hydrochloric acid in coarse salt purification
exercises.stem:
In the experiment of "removing impurity ions from coarse salt using chemical precipitation method", step 7 requires "add hydrochloric acid dropwise to the obtained filtrate, stir with a glass rod until no bubbles emerge, and use pH test paper to check to make the filtrate neutral or slightly acidic." Try to answer:
(1) What is the main purpose of adding hydrochloric acid in step 7?
(2) Why should the filtrate be controlled to be neutral or slightly acidic, but not significantly alkaline?
tests: Adjustment and control of solution acidity and alkalinity
Reaction of hydrochloric acid and carbonate (or hydroxide)
Control the dosage of reagents to be slightly excessive
exercises.answer:
(1) The purpose is to remove residual CO3^{2-}, HCO3^- or OH^- caused by excess Na2CO3, NaOH, etc. in the solution, and generate CO2↑ and water by reacting with hydrochloric acid, while neutralizing excess alkali so that the solution no longer bubbles, eliminates strong alkalinity, and reduces the impact on the purity and crystallization of refined salt.
(2) If the solution is significantly alkaline, it means that there is still a lot of CO3^{2-} or OH^-, which will continue to affect the purity and properties of the refined salt; adjusting to neutral or slightly acidic can not only eliminate alkalinity and carbonate, but also avoid being too acidic to cause equipment corrosion or introducing too much H^+ to cause new impurities.
exercises.analysis: This question tests students’ understanding of the intention of the experimental procedures. Step 7: Add hydrochloric acid dropwise and observe the bubbles until they stop. At the same time, use pH test paper to detect. This is to remove excess carbonate/hydroxide radicals and control the pH of the solution to prevent alkaline impurities from remaining in the crude salt. This reflects the control of solution conditions in material separation and purification.

experiments.name: Removal of Impurity Ions from Coarse Salt by Chemical Precipitation
process: Use a balance to weigh 5.0 g of coarse salt and dissolve it in 20 mL of distilled water to obtain crude brine.
Add excess BaCl2 solution dropwise to the crude brine to allow SO4^{2-} and Ba^{2+} to react completely to form BaSO4 precipitate, and let it stand.
After letting it stand, add a small amount of BaCl2 dropwise to the upper supernatant along the wall of the beaker to check whether SO4^{2-} is completely precipitated.

Add excess NaOH solution dropwise to allow Mg^{2+} and OH^- to completely react to form Mg(OH)2 precipitate; then add excess saturated Na2CO3 solution dropwise to allow Ca^{2+}, Ba^{2+} and CO3^{2-} to completely react to form precipitate.
Use a similar method to step 3 to check whether Mg^{2+}, Ca^{2+} and Ba^{2+} are completely precipitated.
Let it stand and then filter to remove the formed precipitate and insoluble impurities.
Add hydrochloric acid dropwise into the filtrate, stir until no bubbles appear, and check with pH paper to make the filtrate neutral or slightly acidic.
Pour the filtrate into an evaporating dish, heat and evaporate, and use the residual heat to evaporate to dryness.
Cooling to obtain refined salt with impurity ions removed.
phenomena: After adding BaCl2, white turbid BaSO4 precipitates, and the upper layer of the solution gradually becomes clear.
Addition of NaOH produced a white Mg(OH)2 precipitate.
After adding Na2CO3, carbonate precipitation occurs and the solution becomes turbid.
When hydrochloric acid is added dropwise, bubbles appear and gradually stop bubbling.
Heat and evaporate, and solid crystals gradually precipitate in the evaporation dish.
conclusion: Impurities such as Ca^{2+}, Mg^{2+}, SO4^{2-} in coarse salt can be removed through selective precipitation to obtain purer refined salt.
Chemical precipitation method combines dissolution, filtration, evaporation and other operations and is a commonly used method for separation and purification of substances.

exercises.name: Analysis of valence state changes of sulfur-containing substances

Point out the valence state changes of sulfur in these three processes respectively, and explain which process reflects the oxidation of sulfur and which process reflects the reduction of sulfur.
tests: Use the redox reaction to achieve valence state transformation
exercises.answer: ① S in Na2S has a valence of -2. When reacting with acidic KMnO4, S(-2) is oxidized by a strong oxidant to generate high-valence sulfur-containing substances (such as S(0), S(+4) or S(+6)). The valence of sulfur increases and the sulfur is oxidized. ② S in concentrated sulfuric acid has a valence of +6. When reacting with Cu, SO2 is generated, in which S has a valence of +4. The valence of sulfur decreases and the sulfur is reduced. ③ When Fe reacts with S, the S in the elemental sulfur has a valence of 0, and the S in the generated FeS has a valence of -2. The valence of sulfur decreases and the sulfur is reduced.
exercises.analysis: This question tests students' ability to judge the valence of sulfur in different compounds, and to use the rise and fall of valence to analyze redox reactions. By comparing the valence of sulfur before and after the reaction, when the valence state increases, it is oxidized, and when the valence state decreases, it is reduced.

exercises.name: Determine whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic
exercises.stem: Under the conditions of 25 ℃ and 101 kPa, the reaction of hydrogen and chlorine combining to form hydrogen chloride is: H₂(g)+Cl₂(g)=2HCl(g). Breaking the chemical bond of 1 mol H₂ requires absorbing 436 kJ of energy, breaking the chemical bond of 1 mol Cl₂ requires absorbing 243 kJ of energy, and forming the chemical bond of 2 mol HCl releases 862 kJ of energy. Based on these data, determine whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic and explain the reason.
tests: Energy change of chemical bond rupture and formation
Judge reaction type based on energy changes
Use chemical bond energy to explain the energy changes of chemical reactions
exercises.answer: This reaction is exothermic. Because the energy absorbed during the reaction is 436 kJ+243 kJ=679 kJ, and the energy released is 862 kJ. The energy released is greater than the energy absorbed. The difference is 862 kJ−679 kJ=183 kJ. The reaction releases a net energy of 183 kJ to the environment, so it is an exothermic reaction.
exercises.analysis: This question is based on the principle that chemical bond breaking is endothermic and bond formation is exothermic. Compare the total endothermic and total exothermic heat in the reaction, and determine the thermal effect of the reaction from the energy budget.

exercises.name: Explain the working principle and components of the primary battery.
exercises.stem: Explain the working principle and components of the primary battery based on multiple experiments in the "Conversion of Chemical Energy into Electrical Energy" experimental activity.
tests: Analyze the redox process based on experimental phenomena
exercises.answer: A primary battery is a device that converts chemical energy into electrical energy using spontaneous redox reactions. In the electrolyte solution, the more active metal electrode (such as zinc) undergoes an oxidation reaction and loses electrons. The electrons flow to another electrode (such as copper or graphite) through an external circuit. On the electrode, the oxidizing particles (such as H⁺) in the electrolyte obtain electrons and undergo a reduction reaction, thus forming a continuous current. The basic components of a primary battery include: electrodes of two different materials, an electrolyte solution, and an external circuit (wire, ammeter, etc.) that connects the two electrodes into a closed circuit.
exercises.analysis: When answering the question, first summarize the redox process and directional movement of electrons that occur in the primary battery, and then summarize the constituent elements: two different electrodes, electrolyte solution and external circuit. The "principle" and "elements" can be divided into sections to express the answer more clearly.

exercises.answer:

exercises.analysis: From the reaction equation N₂+3H₂⇌2NH₃, it can be seen that the consumption of N₂ is a−c, and the generated NH₃ is 2(a−c). exercises.name: Explain the working principle and components of the primary battery.
exercises.stem: Explain the working principle and components of the primary battery based on multiple experiments in the "Conversion of Chemical Energy into Electrical Energy" experimental activity.
tests: Analyze the redox process based on experimental phenomena
exercises.answer: A primary battery is a device that converts chemical energy into electrical energy using spontaneous redox reactions. In the electrolyte solution, the more active metal electrode (such as zinc) undergoes an oxidation reaction and loses electrons. The electrons flow to another electrode (such as copper or graphite) through an external circuit. On the electrode, the oxidizing particles (such as H⁺) in the electrolyte obtain electrons and undergo a reduction reaction, thus forming a continuous current. The basic components of a primary battery include: electrodes of two different materials, an electrolyte solution, and an external circuit (wire, ammeter, etc.) that connects the two electrodes into a closed circuit.
exercises.analysis: When answering the question, first summarize the redox process and directional movement of electrons that occur in the primary battery, and then summarize the constituent elements: two different electrodes, electrolyte solution and external circuit. The "principle" and "elements" can be divided into sections to express the answer more clearly.

exercises.answer: In a primary battery containing dilute sulfuric acid, it is theoretically feasible to use iron sheets instead of zinc sheets, because iron is more metallic and chemically active than copper, and can be oxidized in dilute sulfuric acid and lose electrons, forming a potential difference with the copper sheets, causing electrons to flow from iron to copper, forming a primary battery and generating current. However, compared with zinc sheets, iron is more susceptible to corrosion and rust, and has poor stability during actual use. Factors such as the corrosion resistance of the material and the electrode potential difference need to be weighed.
exercises.analysis: First determine the position of iron and copper in the activity order (Fe is more active than Cu), which shows that iron can serve as an "oxidized electrode" in the battery. Then contact the conditions of the primary battery: there is a sufficient potential difference and an oxidation-reduction reaction can occur in the electrolyte, and it can be concluded that a primary battery can be formed. Finally, practical factors such as material corrosion resistance are added.

exercises.answer:

Concentration: When other conditions are the same, increasing the concentration of reactants will increase the reaction rate. Example: Concentrated hydrochloric acid reacts more violently with magnesium than dilute hydrochloric acid.

exercises.stem:
In a closed container, a mol N₂ and b mol H₂ are introduced. When the reaction reaches equilibrium under certain conditions, c mol N₂ remains in the container.
(1) What is the amount of material that forms NH₃ when equilibrium is reached?
(2) What is the conversion rate of H₂ when equilibrium is reached?
(3) If the volume of the container is reduced to 1/2 of the original, then the forward reaction rate ____, the reverse reaction rate ____, and the conversion rate of N₂____ (fill in "increase", "decrease" or "unchanged").
tests: The effect of pressure on the gas phase equilibrium
Use the amount and conversion rate of the substance to describe the equilibrium state
exercises.answer:
(1) 2(a - c) mol
(2) Conversion rate of H₂ = 3(a - c) / b
(3) The forward reaction rate increases, the reverse reaction rate increases, and the conversion rate of N₂ increases
exercises.analysis: From the reaction equation N₂+3H₂⇌2NH₃, it can be seen that the consumption of N₂ is a−c, and the generated NH₃ is 2(a−c). The consumption of H₂ is 3(a−c), so the conversion rate is 3(a−c)/b. Decreasing the volume is equal to increasing the pressure, and the equilibrium moves to the side with less gas substance (in the direction of generating NH₃). Both the forward and reverse reaction rates increase with the increase in pressure, and the N₂ conversion rate increases at the new equilibrium.

experiments.phenomena: Test tubes in hot water baths develop milky turbidity more quickly, while test tubes in cold water baths develop turbidity more slowly.

exercises.name:
The molecular formula of an organic compound is C6H6. It is not oxidized by acidic potassium permanganate solution at room temperature, nor does it undergo an addition reaction with bromine water. However, in the presence of FeBr3, it can undergo a substitution reaction with bromine to produce colorless liquid bromobenzene. Try to answer:
(1) Which type of hydrocarbon does this organic matter belong to?
(2) Explain what is special about its molecular structure, which leads to the above chemical properties.
exercises.stem:
The molecular formula of an organic compound is C6H6. It is not oxidized by acidic potassium permanganate solution at room temperature, nor does it undergo an addition reaction with bromine water. However, in the presence of FeBr3, it can undergo a substitution reaction with bromine to produce colorless liquid bromobenzene. Try to answer:
(1) Which type of hydrocarbon does this organic matter belong to?
(2) Explain what is special about its molecular structure, which leads to the above chemical properties.
tests: Infer the molecular structure and properties through experimental phenomena
exercises.answer:
(1) The organic compound is benzene, which is an aromatic hydrocarbon.
(2) The benzene molecule has a planar regular hexagonal structure. All 6 carbon atoms are sp2 hybridized. The C–C bond lengths are equal and are between single bonds and double bonds. The unhybridized p orbitals of each carbon atom are perpendicular to the ring plane and overlap each other in parallel to form a closed large π bond. The π electrons are delocalized, making the benzene molecular structure highly symmetrical and stable. Therefore, under normal conditions, benzene is not easily oxidized by acidic potassium permanganate, nor is it easy to add to bromine, but mainly undergoes a substitution reaction.
exercises.analysis: This question points to benzene, an aromatic hydrocarbon, by giving the molecular formula C6H6 and typical reaction phenomena (not oxidized by acidic potassium permanganate, not added to bromine water, and substituted with bromine under the catalysis of FeBr3), and requires that benzene’s large π-bonded planar six-membered ring structure be used to explain its stability and chemical properties.

experiments.name: Comparative experiments on the reactions of methane and chlorine under different light conditions
experiments.instrument: Two test tubes, saturated NaCl solution, methane gas, chlorine gas, iron stand, aluminum foil
experiments.process: 1. Take two test tubes and collect half the test tube CH4 and half the test tube Cl2 respectively by draining the saturated NaCl solution; 2. Fix the two test tubes with an iron stand; 3. Cover one test tube with aluminum foil and place the other test tube in a bright place (avoid direct sunlight); 4. Let it stand for a while and compare the phenomena in the two test tubes.
experiments.phenomena: In a test tube without light, the mixed gas of methane and chlorine does not react at room temperature; in a test tube with light, the color of the gas gradually becomes lighter, oily droplets appear on the wall of the test tube, and the water level in the test tube rises.
experiments.conclusion: Under light conditions, a substitution reaction between methane and chlorine occurs, producing chlorinated products such as methyl chloride and hydrogen chloride, indicating that the substitution reaction between methane and chlorine requires light conditions.

experiments.name: Experiment 7-2 Oxidation reaction of ethylene
experiments.instrument: Ignition device, test tube filled with acidic potassium permanganate solution, ethylene generator or gas source
experiments.process: (1) Ignite pure ethylene and observe the combustion phenomenon; (2) Pour ethylene into a test tube containing acidic potassium permanganate solution and observe the color change of the solution.
experiments.phenomena: Ethylene burns in the air with a bright flame accompanied by black smoke; ethylene can discolor acidic potassium permanganate solution.
experiments.conclusion: Ethylene can be oxidized by oxygen in the air to form carbon dioxide and water and release heat; the carbon-carbon double bonds in ethylene can be oxidized by strong oxidants such as acidic potassium permanganate, causing the solution to fade.

experiments.name: Experiment 7-3 Addition reaction of ethylene and bromine
experiments.instrument: Test tube containing bromine and carbon tetrachloride solution, ethylene gas and tube
experiments.process: Pour ethylene into a test tube containing bromine and carbon tetrachloride solution, continue to aerate and observe the color change of the solution.
experiments.phenomena: The solution of bromine in carbon tetrachloride fades from colored to colorless.
experiments.conclusion: An addition reaction occurs between ethylene and bromine. One of the double bonds is broken, and two bromine atoms are added to two carbon atoms to generate colorless 1,2-dibromoethane, which is an addition reaction.

experiments.name: Molecular Structure Exploration Activities of Hydrocarbons
experiments.instrument: Molecular structure model or model materials such as plasticine, clay, foam, toothpicks, etc.
experiments.process: (1) Based on the bonding rules of carbon atoms and the structural formulas of methane, ethylene, and acetylene, write the electronic formulas of the three and discuss the types of chemical bonds in the molecules; (2) Use model materials to build ball-and-stick models of methane, ethylene, and acetylene to demonstrate and describe the molecular structure characteristics.
experiments.phenomena: It is observed that methane has a tetrahedral structure and only contains single bonds; the ethylene molecule contains double bonds and the overall structure is planar; acetylene contains triple bonds and the molecule has a linear structure.
experiments.conclusion: The different C-C bond types (single bond, double bond, triple bond) in different hydrocarbons lead to obvious differences in molecular geometric structures and chemical properties.

exercises.name: Judgement of functional groups and organic matter categories
tests: Classify organic compounds based on functional groups
exercises.answer:
(1) ① Contains hydroxyl group (—OH); ② Contains carboxyl group (—COOH); ③ Contains ester group (—COOR); ④ Contains carbon-carbon double bond (C=C).
(2) ① Alcohols (ethanol); ② Carboxylic acids (carboxylic acid, acetic acid); ③ Esters (ethyl acetate); ④ Alkenes (ethylene).
exercises.analysis: This question first identifies the characteristic atomic groups in the structural formula: -OH is a hydroxyl group, corresponding to alcohol; -COOH is a carboxyl group, corresponding to carboxylic acid; -COOR is an ester group, corresponding to ester; C=C is a carbon-carbon double bond, corresponding to an alkene. The classification is completed based on the idea that "organic substances containing the same functional groups have similar properties, so organic substances can be classified according to the different functional groups contained in the organic molecules."

exercises.name: Inference of the products of ethanol oxidation
exercises.stem: Experiment 7-5 shows that ethanol can be oxidized to acetaldehyde by oxygen in the air under the conditions of heating and copper as a catalyst. Please write a chemical equation for this reaction and explain which type of organic matter is involved in this change.
tests: Cognition method of organic matter to infer properties from structure
exercises.answer:
Chemical equation: 2CH3CH2OH + O2 → 2CH3CHO + 2H2O.
This change is the conversion of alcohol (ethanol) into aldehyde (acetaldehyde) by oxidation under mild conditions.
exercises.analysis: Write directly according to the reaction equation given in the text; and then according to Table 7-2: ethanol belongs to alcohols and acetaldehyde belongs to aldehydes, indicating that it is the transformation of the functional group level of "alcohol → aldehyde", reflecting the change in properties caused by structural changes.

exercises.name: Determine the types of hydrocarbons and hydrocarbon derivatives
exercises.stem: Among the following organic compounds: methane (CH4), ethanol (CH3CH2OH), ethylene (CH2=CH2), and ethyl acetate (CH3COOCH2CH3), which category of organic compounds do they belong to?
tests: Classification of organic compounds based on carbon skeleton
Classify organic compounds based on functional groups
exercises.answer: Methane belongs to alkanes (hydrocarbons); ethanol belongs to alcohols (derivatives of hydrocarbons); ethylene belongs to alkenes (hydrocarbons); ethyl acetate belongs to esters (derivatives of hydrocarbons).
exercises.analysis: First determine whether it contains only C and H elements: if so, it is a hydrocarbon, and then distinguish alkanes, alkenes, and alkynes based on whether there are double bonds or triple bonds; if it contains other elements such as O, it is a derivative of hydrocarbons, and then it is determined as an alcohol, carboxylic acid, or ester based on the functional group (-OH, -COOH, -COOR, etc.).

exercises.name: Judge whether acetaldehyde can undergo silver mirror reaction
exercises.stem: It is known that acetaldehyde contains aldehyde groups in its molecule. Answer: Can acetaldehyde undergo silver mirror reaction? Give reasons.
tests: Use functional groups to infer the chemical properties of organic matter
exercises.answer: Acetaldehyde can undergo silver mirror reaction. Because the acetaldehyde molecule contains an aldehyde group, the aldehyde group can be oxidized to carboxylate or ammonium salt by [Ag(NH3)2]OH in the silver ammonia solution. At the same time, Ag+ is reduced to metallic silver, forming a silver mirror attached to the wall of the test tube.
exercises.analysis: According to "the aldehyde functional group plays a decisive role in the chemical properties of acetaldehyde" and "the silver mirror reaction is used to test the aldehyde group", acetaldehyde containing an aldehyde group should be able to undergo a silver mirror reaction with the silver ammonia solution.

exercises.name: Writing of reaction equations related to ethyl acetate
exercises.stem: Based on the "Preparation and Properties of Ethyl Acetate" experiment, write down: (1) the chemical equation of the esterification reaction of acetic acid and ethanol to produce ethyl acetate; (2) the hydrolysis reaction equation of ethyl acetate under acidic conditions; (3) the saponification reaction equation of ethyl acetate when heated in NaOH solution.
tests: Write chemical equations for organic reactions
exercises.answer:
(1) CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 + H2O
(2) CH3COOC2H5 + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + C2H5OH (acid as catalyst)
(3) CH3COOC2H5 + NaOH → CH3COONa + C2H5OH
exercises.analysis: This question tests the understanding of esterification reactions, acidic hydrolysis and alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of esters, and the writing of organic reaction equations. Note that esterification and acidic hydrolysis are reversible reactions, generally represented by "⇌"; alkaline hydrolysis generates carboxylates and alcohols, which are basically irreversible, and are represented by "→".

experiments.name: Reaction of ethanol and sodium (Experiment 7-4)
instrument: Sodium (metal sodium, the surface needs to be wiped dry with kerosene)
experiments.process: Add a small piece of freshly cut sodium into a test tube containing a small amount of absolute ethanol, quickly plug the rubber stopper with a pointed tube, use a small test tube to collect the gas generated and check its purity, then ignite it, and then cover the dry small beaker over the flame. After droplets appear on the wall of the beaker, quickly invert the beaker, add a small amount of clarified lime water, and compare it with the experimental phenomenon of the reaction between water and sodium.
experiments.phenomena: Gas is produced and can be ignited; droplets appear on the wall of the beaker, and after adding lime water, a phenomenon similar to the reaction between water and sodium can be observed (for example, the lime water becomes turbid, indicating that CO2 is involved in the subsequent process). The reaction is milder than the reaction between water and sodium.
experiments.conclusion: Ethanol can react with sodium to produce hydrogen gas and sodium ethoxide. This property is related to the hydroxyl group in its molecule, and the reaction is gentler than the reaction between water and sodium.

experiments.name: Catalytic oxidation of ethanol (Experiment 7-5)
instrument: Copper wire (the lower end is wound into a spiral shape)
experiments.process: Add a small amount of ethanol to the test tube, take a copper wire with the lower end wound into a spiral shape, burn it on an alcohol lamp and then insert it into the ethanol while it is hot. Repeat this several times. Pay attention to the reaction phenomenon and smell the smell of the liquid in the test tube.
experiments.phenomena: When ethanol is oxidized, a new liquid with a pungent or pungent odor is formed (acetaldehyde). The color change on the surface of the copper wire indicates that it plays a catalytic role.
experiments.conclusion: In the presence of heating and catalysts such as copper, ethanol can be oxidized to acetaldehyde and water by oxygen in the air, indicating that ethanol has the property of being mildly oxidized.

experiments.name: Esterification reaction of acetic acid and ethanol (Experiment 7-6)
instrument: Test tubes (for heating on the left side)
Test tube containing saturated Na2CO3 solution (right side)
experiments.process: Add 3 mL of ethanol into the test tube, slowly add 2 mL of concentrated sulfuric acid and 2 mL of acetic acid while shaking, and then add a few broken porcelain pieces. Connect the device and heat it carefully with an alcohol lamp so that the generated steam passes through the conduit to the liquid surface containing the saturated Na2CO3 solution. Observe the phenomenon and smell the smell.
experiments.phenomena: A colorless and transparent oily liquid appears on the upper layer of the liquid in the test tube on the right, and the fragrance can be smelled. Part of the gas reacts with the Na2CO3 solution to generate bubbles.
experiments.conclusion: Under the catalysis of heating and concentrated sulfuric acid, acetic acid and ethanol undergo an esterification reaction to produce fragrant ethyl acetate and water; this reaction is a reversible reaction, and ethyl acetate can be hydrolyzed by water into acetic acid and ethanol.

experiments.name: Infrared spectrum determines the molecular structure
experiments.process: Let a beam of infrared ray pass through the sample molecules to be measured, record the spectrum of the transmitted light intensity changing with the wave number or wavelength, and obtain several absorption peaks.
experiments.phenomena: A series of absorption peaks appear on the infrared spectrum chart. Different vibration modes correspond to peaks with different positions and intensities.
experiments.conclusion: By the position and intensity of the absorption peak, the chemical bonds and functional groups contained in the molecule can be judged. If O–H, C–H, and C–O vibration absorption occurs, it is inferred that it contains hydroxyl groups.

experiments.name: Preparation of ethyl acetate
experiments.process: Add 2 mL of ethanol to a test tube, slowly add 0.5 mL of concentrated sulfuric acid and 2 mL of acetic acid while shaking the test tube, and then add a few broken porcelain pieces. Add 3 mL of saturated Na2CO3 solution to another test tube and connect the device as shown. Heat the test tube containing ethanol and acetic acid over low heat, and pass the generated steam through the catheter to about 0.5 cm above the saturated Na2CO3 solution. After the reaction for a period of time, remove the test tube containing the Na2CO3 solution and stop heating. Shake the test tube and let it stand. After the solution is separated, observe the oily liquid on the upper layer and smell its smell.
experiments.phenomena: After heating, steam is generated and passed over the Na2CO3 solution. After shaking and standing, the solution is separated into layers, and an oily liquid appears on the upper layer with an aromatic smell.
experiments.conclusion: Acetic acid and ethanol undergo an esterification reaction under the catalysis of concentrated sulfuric acid and heating conditions to generate ethyl acetate. Ethyl acetate is oily, has an aromatic odor, is insoluble in water, and can form an upper organic phase on a saturated Na2CO3 solution.

exercises.name: A classmate used newly prepared Cu(OH)2 to test three solutions A, B, and C. After heating, a brick-red precipitate appears in solution A, solution B has no obvious change, and solution C forms a blue precipitate but does not change color when heated. The three known solutions are glucose solution, sucrose solution and salt solution. Please determine what kind of solution A, B, and C are, and explain the basis for your judgment.
exercises.stem: A classmate used newly prepared Cu(OH)2 to test three solutions A, B, and C. After heating, a brick-red precipitate appears in solution A, solution B has no obvious change, and solution C forms a blue precipitate but does not change color when heated. The three known solutions are glucose solution, sucrose solution and salt solution. Please determine what kind of solution A, B, and C are, and explain the basis for your judgment.
tests: Use characteristic reactions to detect organic matter
exercises.answer: A is glucose solution, B is sucrose solution, and C is salt solution. Basis: Glucose can heat with freshly prepared Cu(OH)2 to form a brick-red Cu2O precipitate, which is a characteristic reaction; sucrose cannot undergo this reaction under unhydrolyzed conditions, and only presents a blue suspension of Cu(OH)2; there is no reducing organic matter in the salt solution, and only a blue precipitate of Cu(OH)2 is generated or maintained without the appearance of a brick-red precipitate.
exercises.analysis: This question examines the characteristic reactions of glucose and the analysis of experimental phenomena. According to the textbook: "Glucose reacts with newly prepared copper hydroxide to form a brick-red cuprous oxide precipitate... These two reactions can be used to test glucose." Only when a glucose-containing solution is heated with Cu(OH)2 will a brick-red precipitate appear. Sucrose does not show reducing properties when it is not hydrolyzed. Table salt is an inorganic salt and does not undergo a reducing reaction with Cu(OH)2.

exercises.name: Exploration of the relationship between structural formula and spatial structure
exercises.stem: According to the structural formula of methylene chloride, speculate whether it has isomers and explain the reason.
tests: The relationship between structural formula and molecular spatial structure
Infer molecular space structure from structural formula
exercises.answer: Dichloromethane has no isomers. The reason is that the carbon atoms in the methylene chloride molecule form four covalent bonds and are connected to two chlorine atoms and two hydrogen atoms, forming an approximate regular tetrahedral structure in space. The positions of two hydrogen atoms and two chlorine atoms are equivalent. No matter how the positions of the same atoms are exchanged, new compounds with different properties will not be obtained. Therefore, there are no isomers with different structural formulas but the same molecular formula.
exercises.analysis: This question tests students to infer the spatial structure based on the structural formula and determine whether there may be different structural formulas. It is a comprehensive application of the chain of "structural formula - spatial structure - isomers".

exercises.analysis: Natural oils and fats often contain unsaturated fatty acid esters, which can add to bromine and cause bromine water to fade. Therefore, "neither can make bromine water fade" is wrong. A and C meet the definition, and B is because grease is a mixture and generally does not have a fixed melting and boiling point.

exercises.answer: C
exercises.analysis: The textbook points out that many sugar molecules can be represented by C_m(H_2O)_n, so they are called carbohydrates, but not all sugars conform to this general formula, such as deoxyribose; there are also substances that conform to this general formula but are not sugars, such as acetic acid. The essential structural characteristics of sugars are polyhydroxy aldehydes, polyhydroxy ketones and their dehydration condensates. The correct option is C.

C. This substance is a polysaccharide

tests: Classify sugars based on hydrolysis products
exercises.answer: B
exercises.analysis: According to the classification of sugars: monosaccharides cannot be hydrolyzed, and oligosaccharides can produce 2 to 10 mol of monosaccharides when hydrolyzed from 1 mol of sugar. The most common of these is disaccharide, and the 2 mol of monosaccharides produced must be disaccharides. The sugar is therefore a disaccharide.

exercises.name:
Protein is affected by certain factors, and its spatial structure changes (the primary structure remains unchanged), causing changes in its physical and chemical properties and biological activity. At this time, protein degeneration occurs ( ).
A. Hydrolysis B. Denaturation C. Salting out D. Dissolution
exercises.stem:
Protein is affected by certain factors, and its spatial structure changes (the primary structure remains unchanged), causing changes in its physical and chemical properties and biological activity. At this time, protein degeneration occurs ( ).
A. Hydrolysis B. Denaturation C. Salting out D. Dissolution
exercises.answer: B
exercises.analysis: Hydrolysis involves the breakage of peptide bonds and changes in primary structure; salting out is a reversible change in solubility; the question emphasizes changes in spatial structure but unchanged primary structure and changes in activity, which is in line with the definition of protein denaturation.

The following process does not involve protein denaturation ( ).

exercises.answer: C
exercises.analysis: Heating, formaldehyde, ethanol, and ultraviolet rays can all cause protein denaturation; grain brewing mainly involves starch fermentation rather than protein denaturation, so C does not involve protein denaturation.

experiments.name: Experiment 7-7: Reaction of glucose with Cu(OH)2 and silver ammonia solution
experiments.process: (1) Add 10% NaOH solution to the test tube, add CuSO4 solution dropwise to generate new Cu(OH)2, then add glucose solution and heat, observe the phenomenon. (2) Use AgNO3 solution and ammonia water to prepare a silver ammonia solution, add glucose solution, oscillate and heat in a water bath, and observe changes in the inner wall of the test tube.
experiments.phenomena: Heat with newly prepared Cu(OH)2 to form a brick red Cu2O precipitate; heat with silver ammonia solution to form a bright silver mirror on the inner wall of the test tube.
experiments.conclusion: Glucose can react with newly prepared Cu(OH)2 to form brick-red cuprous oxide precipitate, and can also react with silver ammonia solution to form silver mirror. These two types of reactions are characteristic reactions for testing glucose.

experiments.name: Experiment 7-8: Test of starch and test of hydrolyzate
experiments.process: (1) Drop iodine solution onto steamed buns or potatoes and observe the color change. (2) Add starch and dilute sulfuric acid solution to the test tube and heat it. After cooling, use NaOH solution to make it alkaline. Then add fresh Cu(OH)2 and heat it to observe the phenomenon.
experiments.phenomena: Iodine solution turns blue when it comes into contact with starch-containing steamed buns or potatoes; after acid hydrolysis and alkali neutralization, Cu(OH)2 is added and heated to produce a brick-red precipitation similar to the characteristic reaction of glucose.
experiments.conclusion: Iodine solution can test starch; starch is hydrolyzed under acid catalysis to eventually generate glucose, and its hydrolyzate can react with Cu(OH)2 to produce the characteristic reaction of glucose.

experiments.name: Experiment 7-9: Exploration of protein properties
experiments.process: (1) Add a few drops of lead acetate solution to the test tube containing the egg white solution and observe whether precipitation or color changes occur. (2) Add a few drops of concentrated nitric acid to the egg white solution and heat it to observe the color change. (3) Burn a small section of hair and silk fabric respectively on the flame of the alcohol lamp and smell the smell carefully.
experiments.phenomena: Egg white and lead acetate may form a precipitate; heating with concentrated nitric acid may cause significant discoloration; hair and silk fabrics may burn to produce a unique burnt odor of nitrogen-containing organic matter.
experiments.conclusion: Protein reacts with certain inorganic salts or strong acids to denature, change color and solubility; protein-containing silk and hair produce a special burnt smell when burned, indicating that the protein contains elements such as nitrogen and is prone to thermal decomposition.

experiments.name: Use the ball-and-stick model to verify whether methylene chloride has isomers
experiments.process: Based on the structural formula of methylene chloride, speculate its possible spatial arrangement. Try to build different ball-and-stick models to compare whether there are different spatial structures.
experiments.phenomena: Through model building, we found that only an equivalent spatial structure can be formed according to the structural formula of methylene chloride.
experiments.conclusion: Understand the correspondence between the structural formula and the molecular space structure, and determine whether there are isomers of methylene chloride.

experiments.name: Homemade soap (oil saponification reaction)
experiments.instrument: Edible oil, edible alkali (NaOH or KOH), water, heating device, stirrer, molding mold, etc.
experiments.process: Mix edible oil and alkali solution in a certain proportion, heat and stir to cause saponification of the oil; after the reaction, salt out and separate the soap, then wash to remove impurities and pour into a mold to form. After drying, the soap is obtained.
experiments.phenomena: A milky mixture appears during the reaction and gradually thickens. After standing, a solid soap block and a glycerin water layer appear; soap precipitates out during salting out.
experiments.conclusion: Grease is hydrolyzed in alkaline solution to produce glycerol and higher fatty acid salts, which are the main components of soap. It proves that saponification reaction can be used to prepare soap, and surfactants have decontamination effects.

experiments.name: Experiment 4-1 Testing the reducing property of glucose
experiments.process: (1) Prepare about 2 mL of silver ammonia solution in a clean test tube, add 1 mL of 10% glucose solution, shake, heat in a water bath, and observe whether a silver mirror is formed; (2) Add 2 mL of 10% NaOH solution to another test tube, add 5 drops of 5% CuSO4 solution, then add 2 mL of 10% glucose solution, heat, and observe whether a brick red precipitate is formed; (3) Conclusions were drawn by comparison with similar experiments with acetaldehyde.
experiments.phenomena: Silver mirror and brick red precipitates appeared in the test tube respectively.
experiments.conclusion: Glucose can reduce silver ammonia solution and copper hydroxide. It has reducing properties and is a reducing sugar.

experiments.name: Experiment 4-2 Reaction of cellulose and Cu(OH)2
experiments.process: Put a small amount of absorbent cotton in the test tube, add a few drops of distilled water and a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid, and stir into a paste; then add excess NaOH solution to neutralize it to alkalinity, add 3 drops of 5% CuSO4 solution, heat, observe and explain the phenomenon.
experiments.phenomena: After heating, color changes similar to those containing polyhydroxy compounds can be observed, indicating that the cellulose molecules still contain hydroxyl groups and can interact with Cu(OH)2.
experiments.conclusion: Cellulose molecules contain multiple hydroxyl groups and have similar chemical properties to starch. They can undergo reactions such as esterification and hydrolysis, but do not show reduction properties.

experiments.name: Protein denaturation experiment (Experiment 4-4)
experiments.instrument: 3 test tubes, egg white solution, heating device, silver nitrate solution, ethanol, distilled water
experiments.process: Add 2 mL of egg white solution to each of the three test tubes; heat one, add silver nitrate solution and ethanol to the other two, and observe the phenomenon; then add distilled water to the test tubes to observe whether the precipitate can be dissolved.
experiments.phenomena: Heating, adding silver nitrate or ethanol will cause the protein to precipitate and denature, and the precipitate cannot be redissolved after adding water.
experiments.conclusion: Under the action of physical (heating) and chemical factors (heavy metal salts, ethanol), proteins undergo irreversible denaturation and lose their original physiological activity.

exercises.name: Summarize the bonding characteristics of carbon atoms and the types of chemical bonds in hydrocarbon molecules
exercises.stem: Through the above construction of the ball-and-stick model of organic molecules, the bonding characteristics of carbon atoms and the types of chemical bonds in various hydrocarbon molecules are summarized.
tests: Types of chemical bonds in hydrocarbon molecules
Summarize the bonding characteristics of carbon atoms and the types of bonds in hydrocarbons
exercises.answer: Carbon atoms usually form 4 covalent bonds with other carbon atoms and hydrogen atoms. In methane, carbon atoms form 4 C–H single bonds with 4 hydrogen atoms; in ethane, there are C–C single bonds and C–H single bonds; in ethylene, there are C=C double bonds between two carbon atoms, and form C–H single bonds with hydrogen atoms; in acetylene, there are C≡C triple bonds between two carbon atoms, and form C–H single bonds with hydrogen atoms. Common types of chemical bonds in various types of hydrocarbon molecules include C–H single bonds, C–C single bonds, C=C double bonds, and C≡C triple bonds.
exercises.analysis: This question requires students to summarize the number of bonds formed by carbon atoms and the bond types that can be formed based on observing the ball-and-stick models of methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene, and classify several typical chemical bond types that appear in hydrocarbon molecules.

exercises.name: Exploration of the relationship between structural formula and spatial structure
exercises.stem: According to the structural formula of methylene chloride, speculate whether it has isomers and explain the reason.
tests: The relationship between structural formula and molecular spatial structure
Infer molecular space structure from structural formula
exercises.answer: Dichloromethane has no isomers. The reason is that the carbon atoms in the methylene chloride molecule form four covalent bonds and are connected to two chlorine atoms and two hydrogen atoms, forming an approximate regular tetrahedral structure in space. The positions of two hydrogen atoms and two chlorine atoms are equivalent. No matter how the positions of the same atoms are exchanged, new compounds with different properties will not be obtained. Therefore, there are no isomers with different structural formulas but the same molecular formula.
exercises.analysis: This question tests students to infer the spatial structure based on the structural formula and determine whether there may be different structural formulas. It is a comprehensive application of the chain of "structural formula - spatial structure - isomers".

experiments.conclusion: Deepen your understanding of the molecular structure of methane and appreciate the characteristics of four bonds between carbon atoms.

experiments.phenomena: It is found that the types of carbon-carbon bonds in ethane, ethylene and acetylene are different, and the corresponding molecular space structures are also different.
experiments.conclusion: Different types of carbon-carbon bonds (single bond, double bond, triple bond) cause hydrocarbon molecules to have different spatial structural characteristics.

experiments.conclusion: Hydrocarbons containing 4 carbon atoms may have various structural forms, reflecting the structural diversity of organic matter.

experiments.name: Make a spatial structure model of the molecule
experiments.process: Use plasticine or clay to represent atoms and toothpicks to represent chemical bonds. Build a spatial structure model of H₂, Cl₂, H₂O, CO₂, NH₃, CH₄ and other molecules according to the given bond lengths and bond angles, and use four balloons tied together with rubber bands to simulate the tetrahedral structure of methane.
experiments.phenomena: The model intuitively presents the spatial shapes and bond angles of different molecules; the four balloons are naturally arranged in a tetrahedron shape.
experiments.conclusion: The physical model helps to intuitively understand the spatial structure and bond angle size of the molecule. The balloon model illustrates that the four equivalent bonds will be as far apart as possible to form a tetrahedral structure.

exercises.name: Write the chemical equation for ethanol oxidation and esterification
exercises.stem:
There are two typical reactions involving ethanol in this experiment:
(1) Ethanol is oxidized in the presence of copper oxide to generate acetaldehyde and water;
(2) Ethanol and acetic acid are heated under the action of concentrated sulfuric acid to produce ethyl acetate and water.
Please write the chemical equations for these two reactions.
tests: Write chemical equations for organic reactions
exercises.answer:
(1) C2H5OH + CuO → CH3CHO + Cu + H2O
(2) CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 + H2O
exercises.analysis: This question tests students’ mastery of organic reaction types and writing chemical equations. Question (1) is a mild oxidation reaction of ethanol. It should be noted that CuO is reduced to Cu and water is generated. Question (2) is a typical esterification reaction. Note that the reaction is a reversible reaction, represented by a two-way arrow, and the conservation of elements must be ensured.

exercises.name: The role of concentrated sulfuric acid and Na2CO3 solution in the preparation of ethyl acetate
exercises.stem:
In the experiment of preparing ethyl acetate, a small amount of concentrated sulfuric acid was added to the mixture of ethanol and acetic acid and heated. Then the generated steam was passed into a test tube containing a saturated Na2CO3 solution. After shaking and standing, an oily liquid was observed in the upper layer.
(1) What role does concentrated sulfuric acid play in this experiment?
(2) What role does the saturated Na2CO3 solution play in this experiment?
(3) What is the oily liquid in the upper layer and what is its smell?
tests: The role of concentrated sulfuric acid in esterification reaction
The role of saturated Na2CO3 solution in post-esterification treatment
Analyze experimental phenomena to infer reaction types and products
exercises.answer:
(1) Concentrated sulfuric acid mainly acts as a catalyst in the esterification reaction, provides an acidic environment, and has a certain dehydration effect, which moves the equilibrium toward the production of ester.
(2) Saturated Na2CO3 solution is used to neutralize unreacted acetic acid and convert it into water-soluble sodium acetate, thereby facilitating the layered separation of ethyl acetate and the water layer, while also removing some residual acidity.
(3) The upper oily liquid is ethyl acetate, which has a fruit-like aroma.
exercises.analysis: By reviewing the experimental steps and phenomena, this question guides students to connect the acidity and dehydration of concentrated sulfuric acid and the neutralization effect of sodium carbonate solution, and understand the comprehensive design ideas of catalysis, post-treatment and layered separation in organic preparation experiments.

exercises.name: Writing of reaction equations related to ethyl acetate
exercises.stem: Based on the "Preparation and Properties of Ethyl Acetate" experiment, write down: (1) the chemical equation of the esterification reaction of acetic acid and ethanol to produce ethyl acetate; (2) the hydrolysis reaction equation of ethyl acetate under acidic conditions; (3) the saponification reaction equation of ethyl acetate when heated in NaOH solution.
tests: Write chemical equations for organic reactions
exercises.answer:
(1) CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 + H2O
(2) CH3COOC2H5 + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + C2H5OH (acid as catalyst)
(3) CH3COOC2H5 + NaOH → CH3COONa + C2H5OH
exercises.analysis: This question tests the understanding of esterification reactions, acidic hydrolysis and alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of esters, and the writing of organic reaction equations. Note that esterification and acidic hydrolysis are reversible reactions, generally represented by "⇌"; alkaline hydrolysis generates carboxylates and alcohols, which are basically irreversible, and are represented by "→".
