experiments.phenomena: Acetic acid reacts with corresponding reagents to release gas or cause the indicator to change color; the intensity of the phenomenon is different when compared with carbonic acid.
experiments.conclusion: Acetic acid has the properties of an acid, and the relative strength of its acidity and carbonic acid can be judged.

experiments.name: Prepare ethyl acetate and separate it into layers with Na2CO3 solution
experiments.process: Add 2 mL of ethanol to a test tube, then slowly add 0.5 mL of concentrated sulfuric acid and 2 mL of acetic acid while shaking the test tube, and then add a few pieces of broken porcelain. Add 3 mL of saturated Na2CO3 solution to another test tube and connect the device as shown. Heat the test tube containing ethanol and acetic acid over low heat, and the steam generated passes through the tube to about 0.5 cm above the saturated Na2CO3 solution. After stopping heating, remove the test tube containing the saturated Na2CO3 solution, shake it, and let it stand until the solution is separated into layers. Observe the upper oily liquid and smell it.
experiments.phenomena: Steam is generated after the reaction mixture is heated, bubbles appear in the Na2CO3 solution test tube, and a colorless or slightly scented oily liquid appears in the upper layer, which is obviously stratified with the lower aqueous solution, and has a fruity aroma.
experiments.conclusion: Ethanol and acetic acid are esterified under concentrated sulfuric acid catalysis and heating conditions to generate ethyl acetate; saturated Na2CO3 solution neutralizes unreacted acetic acid and promotes the stratified separation of ethyl acetate.

A. All metals can be smelted by heating to decompose the corresponding oxides
B. For some very active metals, molten electrolysis is commonly used in industry for smelting.
C. Coke, carbon monoxide, and hydrogen can only be used as fuel and cannot be used as reducing agents for metal smelting.

tests: Coke, carbon monoxide, hydrogen and other reducing agents are used to smelt metals

exercises.answer: B
exercises.analysis: The textbook points out: “For some very active metals, it is difficult to reduce them from their compounds using ordinary reducing agents. Electrolytic smelting is commonly used in industry.” This corresponds to option B. A is wrong because "some inactive metals can be decomposed by heating directly", not all metals; C is wrong because the textbook says "commonly used reducing agents include coke, carbon monoxide, hydrogen, etc."; D is wrong because the thermite reaction uses aluminum to reduce Fe2O3 to iron.

experiments.name: Thermal decomposition of mercury oxide produces mercury and oxygen
instrument: Test tube or crucible containing mercury oxide

experiments.process: Put an appropriate amount of mercury oxide solid into a heat-resistant container, continue to heat it to a certain temperature with an alcohol lamp or electric furnace, observe the changes in color and appearance of the solid, and use a gas collection device to collect the gas generated.
experiments.phenomena: The red or orange mercury oxide solid gradually decomposes to produce silvery-white metallic mercury, and colorless gas is produced (it can rekindle wooden sticks with Mars, proving to be oxygen).
experiments.conclusion: Mercury oxide decomposes under heating conditions to generate metallic mercury and oxygen. The reaction is 2HgO △→ 2Hg + O2↑, indicating that inactive metals can be smelted from their compounds through thermal decomposition.

experiments.name: Traditional experiment of making tofu
instrument: Brine (containing magnesium chloride, etc.) or coagulants such as gypsum
experiments.process: ① Soak the beans: Soak the soybeans until they fully absorb water and swell; ② Grind the beans: Add water and grind them to make soy milk; ③ Filtration: Filter with gauze to remove the bean dregs; ④ Cook the milk: Heat the soy milk to boiling and keep it for a while; ⑤ Brine: Slowly add the coagulant at a suitable temperature, stir gently, and observe the protein solidification; ⑥ Forming: Put the solidified tofu into a mold and press it into block tofu.
experiments.phenomena: After adding coagulant, the originally uniform soy milk appears white flocculent agglomeration, gradually forming a relatively solid tofu block and separating from the whey.
experiments.conclusion: Coagulants such as salt brine and gypsum cause the proteins in soy milk to coagulate from a colloidal state and form a network structure, thereby making tofu.

experiments.name: Comparative experiment on the properties of sodium carbonate and sodium bicarbonate
instrument: pH test paper or pH meter

exercises.name: Determine whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic
exercises.stem: Under the conditions of 25 ℃ and 101 kPa, the reaction of hydrogen and chlorine combining to form hydrogen chloride is: H₂(g)+Cl₂(g)=2HCl(g). Breaking the chemical bond of 1 mol H₂ requires absorbing 436 kJ of energy, breaking the chemical bond of 1 mol Cl₂ requires absorbing 243 kJ of energy, and forming the chemical bond of 2 mol HCl releases 862 kJ of energy. Based on these data, determine whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic and explain the reason.
tests: Energy change of chemical bond rupture and formation
Judge reaction type based on energy changes
Use chemical bond energy to explain the energy changes of chemical reactions
exercises.answer: This reaction is exothermic. Because the energy absorbed during the reaction is 436 kJ+243 kJ=679 kJ, and the energy released is 862 kJ. The energy released is greater than the energy absorbed. The difference is 862 kJ−679 kJ=183 kJ. The reaction releases a net energy of 183 kJ to the environment, so it is an exothermic reaction.
exercises.analysis: This question is based on the principle that chemical bond breaking is endothermic and bond formation is exothermic. Compare the total endothermic and total exothermic heat in the reaction, and determine the thermal effect of the reaction from the energy budget.

exercises.name: Write a thermochemical equation for the given facts
exercises.stem:
Based on the facts, write the thermochemical equation for the following reaction.
(1) 1 mol Cu(s) reacts with an appropriate amount of O₂(g) to form CuO(s), releasing 157.3 kJ of heat.
(2) 1 mol C₂H₄(g) reacts with an appropriate amount of O₂(g) to produce CO₂(g) and H₂O(l), releasing 1411.0 kJ of heat.
(3) 1 mol C(s) reacts with an appropriate amount of H₂O(g) to produce CO(g) and H₂(g), absorbing 131.5 kJ of heat.
exercises.answer:
(1) Cu(s)+½O₂(g)=CuO(s)    ΔH=-157.3 kJ/mol
(2) C₂H₄(g)+3O₂(g)=2CO₂(g)+2H₂O(l)    ΔH=-1411.0 kJ/mol
(3) C(s)+H₂O(g)=CO(g)+H₂(g)    ΔH=+131.5 kJ/mol
exercises.analysis: This question tests the writing of thermochemical equations. First write the balanced chemical equation, and then write the question "How many kJ is released (or absorbed) by the reaction of 1 mol of a substance" directly as ΔH. Pay attention to the sign: exotherm is negative and endotherm is positive. At the same time, the aggregation state of each substance should be noted so that the thermochemical equation satisfies the principle of "one-to-one correspondence between ΔH and the equation".

exercises.name: Use bond energy to calculate the thermochemical equation of NO generation reaction
exercises.stem: It is known that: (1) 946 kJ of energy is absorbed when the chemical bond in 1 mol N₂(g) is broken; (2) 498 kJ of energy is absorbed when the chemical bond in 1 mol O₂(g) is broken; (3) 632 kJ of energy is released when the chemical bond in 1 mol NO(g) is formed. Write a thermochemical equation for the reaction of N₂(g) with O₂(g) to form NO(g).
tests: Chemical bond energy changes and reaction heat
Estimate the heat of reaction based on the bond energy
exercises.answer: N₂(g)+O₂(g)=2NO(g) ΔH=+180 kJ/mol (approximately)
exercises.analysis: Estimate the heat of reaction based on the bond energy. Reaction: N₂+O₂→2NO, requires breaking 1 mol N≡N (absorption 946 kJ) and 1 mol O=O (absorption 498 kJ), total absorption 1444 kJ. When 2 mol of NO is produced, 2 mol of N–O bonds are formed, releasing 2×632=1264 kJ. The net endothermic Q=1444−1264=180 kJ, that is, ΔH≈+180 kJ/mol, indicates that the reaction is endothermic.

B. Only chemical reactions with increased entropy can proceed spontaneously

exercises.answer: D
exercises.analysis: The textbook points out that "most exothermic reactions can proceed spontaneously...some endothermic reactions can also proceed spontaneously", indicating that not only exothermic reactions can be spontaneous; at the same time, "some entropy decreasing processes can also proceed spontaneously", indicating that not only entropy increasing can be spontaneous. experiments.name: Measurement of reaction heat of neutralization reaction
instrument: Simple calorimeter (foam cup, inner cylinder, cup lid)
experiments.process:
(1) Use a graduated cylinder to measure 50 mL of 0.50 mol/L hydrochloric acid, pour it into the inner cylinder of the calorimeter, cover the cup, insert a thermometer, measure and record the temperature of the hydrochloric acid, rinse and dry the thermometer; use another graduated cylinder to measure 50 mL of 0.55 mol/L NaOH solution, use a thermometer to measure and record its temperature.
(2) Open the lid of the cup, quickly pour the NaOH solution into the inner cylinder of the calorimeter, cover the cup immediately, insert the thermometer, stir at a constant speed, pay close attention to the temperature changes, and record the maximum temperature t₂ as the system temperature after the reaction.
(3) Repeat the above steps three times, record and process the data: take the average temperature of the hydrochloric acid and NaOH solutions as t₁, find the temperature difference t₂−t₁, and find the average value of the three times.
(4) Calculate the reaction heat based on the temperature difference and specific heat capacity. It is approximately considered that the density and specific heat capacity of the solution are the same as water. Ignore the specific heat capacity of the calorimeter, calculate the heat release Q=(m₁+m₂)c(t₂−t₁), and convert it into the reaction heat when 1 mol H₂O is generated.
experiments.phenomena: The temperature of the solution increases after mixing, and the thermometer reading rises to a maximum value during the mixing process and then drops slightly.
experiments.conclusion: The neutralization reaction of hydrochloric acid and NaOH solution is an exothermic reaction; at 25 ℃ and 101 kPa, approximately 57.3 kJ of heat is released when a dilute solution of a strong acid and a dilute solution of a strong base are neutralized to form 1 mol H₂O.

experiments.name: Experiment on the effect of temperature on the decomposition rate of NO2/N2O4 Effect of chemical equilibrium (Experiment 2-3)
experiments.instrument: Two connected flasks, latex tube, spring clamp, mixed NO2 and N2O4 Gas, hot water, ice water
experiments.process: Pour the mixed gas of NO2 and N2O4 into two connected flasks, and clamp the latex tube with a spring clamp; immerse one flask in hot water and the other in ice water, and observe the color change of the mixed gas in the two bottles.
experiments.phenomena: The red-brown color in the flask soaked in hot water deepens, indicating that the NO2 concentration increases; the red-brown color in the flask soaked in ice water becomes lighter, indicating that the NO2 concentration decreases.
experiments.conclusion: For the exothermic equilibrium 2NO2(g) ⇌ N2O4(g), ΔH=-56.9 kJ·mol⁻¹, increasing the temperature equilibrium moves to the endothermic direction (NO2), decreasing the temperature equilibrium moves to the exothermic direction (N2O4). Generally speaking, increasing the temperature shifts the chemical equilibrium toward endothermic reactions, and lowering the temperature shifts the chemical equilibrium toward exothermic reactions.

Example answer:
Temperature: As the temperature increases, the reaction rate generally increases; as the temperature decreases, the reaction rate decreases. Example: If the reaction temperature between CaCO3 and dilute hydrochloric acid is increased appropriately, CO2 will be produced faster.
Concentration: When other conditions are the same, increasing the concentration of reactants will increase the reaction rate. Example: Concentrated hydrochloric acid reacts more violently with magnesium than dilute hydrochloric acid.
Surface area of ​​solid: increasing the surface area of ​​the solid increases the reaction rate. Example: Aluminum powder burns more violently than aluminum flakes in oxygen; flour dust can explode in the air.
Catalyst: Catalysts can significantly change the rate of a chemical reaction, often increasing the rate. Example: MnO2 is added when KClO3 is decomposed to produce O2; a catalyst is used to catalyze the oxidation of SO2 when industrially producing sulfuric acid.
exercises.analysis: This question requires students to summarize the influence of temperature, concentration, solid surface area and catalyst on reaction rate, and give daily or experimental examples to test the overall understanding and application of "factors affecting chemical reaction rate".

exercises.name: Calculate the average rate of ammonia synthesis reaction
tests: The relationship between chemical reaction rate and stoichiometric number
Quantitatively express the reaction rate by changing the concentration with time
exercises.analysis: This question examines the definition of reaction rate and its relationship with measurement numbers. First find the average rate from the concentration change, then find the concentration changes and corresponding rates of other substances based on the stoichiometric ratio of the chemical equation, and finally compare whether the proportional relationship between v and the stoichiometric number is the same.

exercises.name: Determine the effect of temperature on reaction rate
exercises.stem:
Other conditions being equal, the rate of a reaction at 25°C is v. If the temperature rises to 35°C, according to the empirical rules given in the textbook, the following reasonable estimates of the rate change are ( )
A. The rate must become 2v
B. The rate must become 3v
C. The speed is approximately between 2v~4v
D. The rate does not change with temperature
and briefly explain the reasons.
tests: Effect of temperature on reaction rate
Qualitative comparison of chemical reactions The magnitude of the rate
exercises.answer: C. For every 10°C increase in temperature, the chemical reaction rate usually increases by 2 to 4 times its original value. Therefore, when the temperature rises from 25°C to 35°C, the rate will generally increase between 2 and 4 times its original value. It is not a definite single value.
exercises.analysis: The key is to grasp the empirical rule that "for every 10°C increase, the rate usually increases by 2 to 4 times the original value." Understand that it is a range rather than an exact multiple, so A, B, and D are excluded.

exercises.name:
In a closed container, a mol N₂ and b mol H₂ are introduced. When the reaction reaches equilibrium under certain conditions, c mol N₂ remains in the container.

(2) What is the conversion rate of H₂ when equilibrium is reached?
(3) If the volume of the container is reduced to 1/2 of the original, then the forward reaction rate ____, the reverse reaction rate ____, and the conversion rate of N₂____ (fill in "increase", "decrease" or "unchanged").
exercises.stem:
In a closed container, a mol N₂ and b mol H₂ are introduced. When the reaction reaches equilibrium under certain conditions, c mol N₂ remains in the container.
(1) What is the amount of material that forms NH₃ when equilibrium is reached?
(2) What is the conversion rate of H₂ when equilibrium is reached?
(3) If the volume of the container is reduced to 1/2 of the original, then the forward reaction rate ____, the reverse reaction rate ____, and the conversion rate of N₂____ (fill in "increase", "decrease" or "unchanged").
tests: The effect of pressure on the gas phase equilibrium
Use the amount and conversion rate of the substance to describe the equilibrium state
exercises.answer:
(1) 2(a - c) mol
(2) Conversion rate of H₂ = 3(a - c) / b
(3) The forward reaction rate increases, the reverse reaction rate increases, and the conversion rate of N₂ increases
exercises.analysis: From the reaction equation N₂+3H₂⇌2NH₃, it can be seen that the consumption of N₂ is a−c, and the generated NH₃ is 2(a−c). The consumption of H₂ is 3(a−c), so the conversion rate is 3(a−c)/b. Decreasing the volume is equal to increasing the pressure, and the equilibrium moves to the side with less gas substance (in the direction of generating NH₃). Both the forward and reverse reaction rates increase with the increase in pressure, and the N₂ conversion rate increases at the new equilibrium.

experiments.name: Experiment on the effect of temperature on the decomposition rate of H2O2
experiments.instrument: 5% H2O2 solution, 1 mol/L FeCl3 solution, test tube, test tube clamp, beaker, cold water, hot water, graduated cylinder, rubber tip dropper
experiments.process: Add 2 mL of 5% H2O2 solution into two test tubes of the same size, and drop 2 drops of 1 mol/L FeCl3 solution at the same time. When an appropriate amount of bubbles appear in the test tubes, put one test tube into a beaker filled with cold water and the other test tube into a beaker filled with hot water. Observe the speed of bubble generation and compare.
experiments.phenomena: The bubbles in the test tube placed in hot water are generated faster and more violently, indicating that the reaction rate is greater at high temperature; the bubbles in the test tube placed in cold water are slower.
experiments.conclusion: Other conditions being equal, increasing temperature can increase the rate of chemical reactions.

experiments.name: Student-designed experiment on the effect of concentration on reaction rate
experiments.instrument: 0.1 mol/L hydrochloric acid, 1 mol/L Hydrochloric acid, marble fragments, test tubes, measuring cylinders, etc.
experiments.process: Keeping the conditions such as the mass and temperature of the marble fragments the same, add hydrochloric acid of different concentrations (such as 0.1 mol/L and 1 mol/L) to the marbles in the two test tubes respectively, and compare the reaction rates by observing the speed of bubble generation or the change in the collected gas volume over time.
experiments.phenomena: In high-concentration hydrochloric acid, bubbles are generated faster and more densely on the marble surface, and the reaction rate is greater; in low-concentration hydrochloric acid, the reaction is slower.
experiments.conclusion: When other conditions are the same, increasing the concentration of reactants increases the rate of chemical reaction.

experiments.name: Pressure sensor experiment on the reaction rate of magnesium and hydrochloric acid of different concentrations
experiments.instrument: Magnesium bars, hydrochloric acid of different concentrations, pressure sensors, data collectors, computers, reaction vessels
experiments.process: In a closed device, magnesium strips of the same mass are reacted with hydrochloric acid of different concentrations (1.0 mol·L⁻¹ and 0.5 mol·L⁻¹). Use a pressure sensor and a data collector to record the curve of pressure changing with time during the reaction, and use a computer to draw two curves for comparison.
experiments.phenomena: Under the conditions of high concentration hydrochloric acid, the pressure rises faster and the curve is steeper, indicating a larger reaction rate; under low concentration hydrochloric acid, the pressure rises more slowly.
experiments.conclusion: The greater the concentration of reactants, the faster the reaction rate between magnesium and hydrochloric acid.

experiments.name: Measurement of reaction heat of neutralization reaction
instrument: Simple calorimeter (foam cup, inner cylinder, cup lid)
experiments.process:
(1) Use a graduated cylinder to measure 50 mL of 0.50 mol/L hydrochloric acid, pour it into the inner cylinder of the calorimeter, cover the cup, insert a thermometer, measure and record the temperature of the hydrochloric acid, rinse and dry the thermometer; use another graduated cylinder to measure 50 mL of 0.55 mol/L NaOH solution, use a thermometer to measure and record its temperature.
(2) Open the lid of the cup, quickly pour the NaOH solution into the inner cylinder of the calorimeter, cover the cup immediately, insert the thermometer, stir at a constant speed, pay close attention to the temperature changes, and record the maximum temperature t₂ as the system temperature after the reaction.
(3) Repeat the above steps three times, record and process the data: take the average temperature of the hydrochloric acid and NaOH solutions as t₁, find the temperature difference t₂−t₁, and find the average value of the three times.
(4) Calculate the reaction heat based on the temperature difference and specific heat capacity. It is approximately considered that the density and specific heat capacity of the solution are the same as water. Ignore the specific heat capacity of the calorimeter, calculate the heat release Q=(m₁+m₂)c(t₂−t₁), and convert it into the reaction heat when 1 mol H₂O is generated.
experiments.phenomena: The temperature of the solution increases after mixing, and the thermometer reading rises to a maximum value during the mixing process and then drops slightly.
experiments.conclusion: The neutralization reaction of hydrochloric acid and NaOH solution is an exothermic reaction; at 25 ℃ and 101 kPa, approximately 57.3 kJ of heat is released when a dilute solution of a strong acid and a dilute solution of a strong base are neutralized to form 1 mol H₂O.

experiments.name: Qualitative and quantitative study of factors affecting the rate of chemical reactions (Experimental Exploration I)
experiments.process: Select 0.1 mol/L Na2S2O3 solution, H2SO4 solution of different concentrations, 5% H2O2 solution, 1 mol/L FeCl3 solution, distilled water and hot water, etc. to design a comparative experiment. Carry out the reaction under the conditions of changing only the concentration, changing only the temperature, adding or not adding a catalyst, record the phenomena and time, and fill in the experimental steps, comparison of experimental phenomena and conclusions in the form.

exercises.name: Determine whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic
exercises.stem: Under the conditions of 25 ℃ and 101 kPa, the reaction of hydrogen and chlorine combining to form hydrogen chloride is: H₂(g)+Cl₂(g)=2HCl(g). Breaking the chemical bond of 1 mol H₂ requires absorbing 436 kJ of energy, breaking the chemical bond of 1 mol Cl₂ requires absorbing 243 kJ of energy, and forming the chemical bond of 2 mol HCl releases 862 kJ of energy. Based on these data, determine whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic and explain the reason.
tests: Energy change of chemical bond rupture and formation
Judge reaction type based on energy changes
Use chemical bond energy to explain the energy changes of chemical reactions
exercises.answer: This reaction is exothermic. Because the energy absorbed during the reaction is 436 kJ+243 kJ=679 kJ, and the energy released is 862 kJ. The energy released is greater than the energy absorbed. The difference is 862 kJ−679 kJ=183 kJ. The reaction releases a net energy of 183 kJ to the environment, so it is an exothermic reaction.

exercises.analysis: The textbook points out: The chemical equilibrium state is a state in which the forward and reverse reaction rates are equal in a reversible reaction. At this time, the concentrations of the reactants and products no longer change, but the reaction does not stop. The forward and reverse reactions are still proceeding at equal rates. Therefore, "the forward and reverse reaction rates are both zero" error. A, B, and D all meet the description of "under given conditions, the degree of completion of the reversible reaction is maximized when equilibrium is reached."

exercises.name: Example 1: Calculation of the equilibrium constant and equilibrium concentration of HI generated by H2 and I2
exercises.stem:
At a certain temperature, a gaseous mixture containing 0.10 mol each of H2 and I2 is filled into a closed container with a volume of 10 L. After full reaction and reaching equilibrium, c(H2)=0.0080 mol·L⁻¹ is measured.
(1) Calculate the equilibrium constant for this reaction.
(2) At the above temperature, if 0.20 mol each of H2 and I2(g) is initially introduced into the container, try to find the concentration of each substance when reaching chemical equilibrium.
tests: The equilibrium system of HI generated by H2 and I2
Establish and apply the equilibrium concentration table
Use the equilibrium constant to judge the degree of reaction and conversion rate
exercises.answer: (1) K = 0.25; (2) At equilibrium, c(H2)=c(I2)=0.016 mol·L⁻¹, c(HI)=0.0080 mol·L⁻¹.
exercises.analysis:
(1) From the initial and equilibrium data, it can be obtained that starting c(H2)=c(I2)=0.010 mol·L⁻¹, the concentration of H2 at equilibrium is 0.0080 mol·L⁻¹, so 0.0020 mol·L⁻¹ is consumed, and I2 also consumes 0.0020 mol·L⁻¹, generating HI 0.0040 mol·L⁻¹. Substitute K = c²(HI)/[c(H2)c(I2)] = (0.0040)²/(0.0080×0.0080)=0.25.
(2) Initial c(H2)=c(I2)=0.020 mol·L⁻¹, assuming that the H2 concentration decreases by x during equilibrium, then the equilibrium concentrations are c(H2)=0.020−x, c(I2)=0.020−x, c(HI)=2x. Substituting the K expression: (2x)²/(0.020−x)²=0.25, we solve for x=0.0040. So c(H2)=c(I2)=0.016 mol·L⁻¹, c(HI)=0.0080 mol·L⁻¹.

exercises.name: Example 2: Calculation of the conversion rate using the equilibrium constant
exercises.stem:
In a closed container with constant volume, 2.0 mol CO and 10 mol H2O are mixed and heated to 830°C to achieve the following equilibrium:
CO(g)+H2O(g) ⇌ CO2(g)+H2(g)
The K of this reaction is now 1.0. Find the conversion rate of CO to CO2 when equilibrium is reached.
tests: Establish and apply the equilibrium concentration table
Use the equilibrium constant to judge the degree of reaction and conversion rate
exercises.answer: The conversion rate of CO to CO2 is 83%.
exercises.analysis: Suppose the amount of substance converted from CO to CO2 at equilibrium is x mol and the volume of the container is y L. The initial concentrations are 2.0/y, 10/y, 0, 0 respectively; the changing concentrations are all x/y; the equilibrium concentrations are (2.0−x)/y, (10−x)/y, x/y, x/y. From K = [c(CO2)c(H2)]/[c(CO)c(H2O)] = (x/y)²/[(2.0−x)(10−x)/y²] = 1.0, we get x² = (2.0−x)(10−x) = 20−12x+x², and the solution is x=5/3 mol. Conversion rate = (5/3 mol)/(2.0 mol)×100% ≈ 83%.

exercises.name: Summarize the factors that affect the movement of chemical equilibrium
exercises.stem: Combined with the phenomena of FeCl3 and KSCN, K2Cr2O7, CuCl2 and NO2/N2O4 experiments in this section, try to summarize the main factors that affect the movement of chemical equilibrium, and explain in which direction the equilibrium generally moves when these factors change.
tests: Effect of concentration on chemical equilibrium
Effect of temperature on chemical equilibrium
Summarize the factors affecting chemical equilibrium from experimental phenomena
exercises.answer:
Main factors:
(1) Concentration: When the concentration of a certain reactant is increased, the equilibrium moves to the side that consumes the reactant; when the concentration of a certain reactant is decreased, the equilibrium moves to the side that generates the substance. The same is true for products. When it increases, the balance moves to the side that consumes the product, and when it decreases, it moves toward the side that generates the substance.
(2) Temperature: As the temperature increases, the equilibrium moves toward the endothermic direction; as the temperature decreases, the equilibrium moves toward the exothermic direction. The above phenomenon can be explained by Le Chatelier's principle, that is, the equilibrium always moves in a direction that partially offsets external changes.
exercises.analysis: This question requires students to synthesize and abstract multiple experimental phenomena, extract the two key factors of concentration and temperature from the changes in solution color and gas color, and be able to use "increase/decrease" and "endotherm/release" to correspond to the direction of equilibrium movement, reflecting the ability to generalize from phenomena to rules.

experiments.name: Experiment 7-3 The reaction between quicklime and water releases heat

experiments.process: Add a small spoonful of dry quicklime to a test tube, then add about 2 mL of water, observe the phenomenon, and gently touch the outer wall of the test tube with your hand.
experiments.phenomena: You can feel the outer wall of the test tube getting hot.
experiments.conclusion: The reaction between quicklime and water releases heat, which is an exothermic reaction, indicating that chemical reactions are accompanied by changes in energy.

experiments.name: Experiment 7-4 Methane combustion and product verification
experiments.instrument: Methane gas source, tube, match or igniter, cold and dry beaker, clarified lime water
experiments.process: (1) Observe the color and state of methane, ignite the methane released from the tube, cover a cold and dry beaker over the flame, and observe the phenomenon of the beaker wall after a while. (2) Quickly turn the beaker upside down, pour a small amount of clarified lime water into the beaker, shake it, and observe the phenomenon.
experiments.phenomena: There are water droplets on the wall of the beaker, which become turbid after adding lime water and shaking.
experiments.conclusion: Explain that the combustion of methane produces water and carbon dioxide. The combustion of methane is an exothermic reaction and is a hydrocarbon combustion.

experiments.name: Temperature change experiment of the reaction between hydrochloric acid and magnesium (Experiment 6-1)
experiments.instrument: Test tubes, 2 mL 2 mol/L Hydrochloric acid, thermometer, polished magnesium strip with sandpaper
experiments.process: Add 2 mL of 2 mol/L hydrochloric acid into the test tube and measure its initial temperature; put a polished magnesium strip into the test tube, observe the phenomenon, and measure the change in solution temperature again.
experiments.phenomena: The temperature of the solution increased after the reaction, indicating that the reaction process was accompanied by the release of heat.
experiments.conclusion: The reaction between magnesium and hydrochloric acid is an exothermic reaction, and chemical reactions can release heat.

experiments.name: Endothermic experiment of the reaction of barium hydroxide and ammonium chloride (Experiment 6-2)
experiments.instrument: 20 g Ba(OH)2·8H2O crystal, 10 g NH4Cl crystal, beaker, wood chips, a few drops of water, glass rod, glass piece
experiments.process: Put the finely ground Ba(OH)2·8H2O and NH4Cl crystals into a beaker, place the beaker on a wood chip with a few drops of water, and stir quickly with a glass rod. After smelling the smell, quickly cover the beaker with a glass piece, touch the lower part of the cup wall with your hand, try to pick up the beaker with your hand, and observe the phenomenon.
experiments.phenomena: The lower part of the beaker becomes obviously cold, the water between the wood chips and the beaker condenses into ice, and the beaker is "frozen" on the wood chips.
experiments.conclusion: The reaction of barium hydroxide and ammonium chloride absorbs a large amount of heat and is an endothermic reaction.

experiments.name: The effect of the concentration of Fe3+ and SCN- on chemical equilibrium (Experiment 2-1)
experiments.instrument: 0.005 mol·L⁻¹ FeCl3 solution, 0.015 mol·L⁻¹ KSCN solution, test tube, iron powder, 1 mol·L⁻¹ KSCN solution dropper
experiments.process: Add 5 mL of 0.015 mol·L⁻¹ KSCN solution into a test tube containing 5 mL of 0.005 mol·L⁻¹ FeCl3 solution. The solution turns red. Divide the solution evenly into three test tubes a, b, and c; add a small amount of iron powder to b, add 4 drops of 1 mol·L⁻¹ KSCN solution to c, and compare the color changes with a.
experiments.phenomena: The original solution is red; the color of the test tube added with iron powder becomes lighter; the color of the test tube added with KSCN solution becomes darker.
experiments.conclusion: Changing the concentration of Fe³⁺ or SCN⁻ will cause the Fe³⁺ + 3SCN⁻ ⇌ Fe(SCN)3 equilibrium to shift, and the composition of the equilibrium mixture will change.

experiments.name: The effect of pressure on the chemical equilibrium of NO2/N2O4 (Experiment 2-2)
experiments.instrument: 50 mL syringe, mixed gas containing NO2 and N2O4, thin tube, rubber stopper
experiments.process: Use a syringe to inhale about 20 mL of mixed gas of NO2 and N2O4 (the piston is at I), and seal the end of the thin tube. Pull the piston from position I to position II and push it back, reciprocating several times, and observe the color change of the mixed gas.
experiments.phenomena: Pull out the piston: the volume increases, the pressure and concentration decrease, the color of the mixed gas first becomes lighter and then gradually becomes darker, indicating that more NO2 is generated; push the piston: the volume decreases, the pressure and concentration increase, the color of the mixed gas first becomes darker and then gradually becomes lighter, indicating that more NO2 is consumed.
experiments.conclusion: In the 2NO2(g) ⇌ N2O4(g) equilibrium system, decreasing the pressure (concentration) will shift the equilibrium to the side with a larger amount of gaseous substances (NO2); increasing the pressure will shift the equilibrium to the side with a smaller amount of gaseous substances (N2O4).

experiments.name: Experiment on the effect of temperature on the decomposition rate of NO2/N2O4 Effect of chemical equilibrium (Experiment 2-3)
experiments.instrument: Two connected flasks, latex tube, spring clamp, mixed NO2 and N2O4 Gas, hot water, ice water
experiments.process: Pour the mixed gas of NO2 and N2O4 into two connected flasks, and clamp the latex tube with a spring clamp; immerse one flask in hot water and the other in ice water, and observe the color change of the mixed gas in the two bottles.
experiments.phenomena: The red-brown color in the flask soaked in hot water deepens, indicating that the NO2 concentration increases; the red-brown color in the flask soaked in ice water becomes lighter, indicating that the NO2 concentration decreases.
experiments.conclusion: For the exothermic equilibrium 2NO2(g) ⇌ N2O4(g), ΔH=-56.9 kJ·mol⁻¹, increasing the temperature equilibrium moves to the endothermic direction (NO2), decreasing the temperature equilibrium moves to the exothermic direction (N2O4). Generally speaking, increasing the temperature shifts the chemical equilibrium toward endothermic reactions, and lowering the temperature shifts the chemical equilibrium toward exothermic reactions.

experiments.name: Comprehensive schematic experiment on pressure and temperature of NO2/N2O4 system
experiments.instrument: NO2 and N2O4 mixed gas, syringe or flask, water bath device
experiments.process: By changing the position of the syringe piston or changing the temperature of the water bath in which the flask is located, observe the changes in red-brown shade and summarize the effects of pressure and temperature on equilibrium.
experiments.phenomena: Pressure changes cause the color to change rapidly first and then gradually return to a new depth; temperature changes cause the color of hot water bottles to deepen and the color of ice water bottles to become lighter.
experiments.conclusion: Chemical equilibrium can respond to changes in external pressure and temperature and move in a direction that weakens such changes, consistent with Le Chatelier's principle.

C. ΔH>0, ΔS>0
D. ΔH<0, ΔS>0
tests: Free energy change and spontaneity criterion
The combined effect of enthalpy change and entropy change on spontaneity
Judge the spontaneity of the reaction based on the enthalpy change and entropy change
exercises.answer: D
exercises.analysis: It can be seen from ΔG=ΔH−TΔS that when ΔH<0 and ΔS>0, no matter what the temperature is, TΔS is positive, −TΔS is negative, ΔG must be negative, and the reaction must be spontaneous. Textbook "It can be inferred from the above relationship: when ΔH<0, ΔS>0, the reaction can proceed spontaneously; when ΔH>0, ΔS<0, the reaction cannot proceed spontaneously; when ΔH and ΔS have the same sign, spontaneity is related to temperature." Therefore, D is selected.

experiments.name: Experiment on the effect of temperature on the decomposition rate of NO2/N2O4 Effect of chemical equilibrium (Experiment 2-3)

exercises.stem:
In a closed container, a mol N₂ and b mol H₂ are introduced. When the reaction reaches equilibrium under certain conditions, c mol N₂ remains in the container.

tests: The effect of pressure on the gas phase equilibrium
Use the amount and conversion rate of the substance to describe the equilibrium state
exercises.answer:
(1) 2(a - c) mol
(2) Conversion rate of H₂ = 3(a - c) / b
(3) The forward reaction rate increases, the reverse reaction rate increases, and the conversion rate of N₂ increases
exercises.analysis: From the reaction equation N₂+3H₂⇌2NH₃, it can be seen that the consumption of N₂ is a−c, and the generated NH₃ is 2(a−c). The consumption of H₂ is 3(a−c), so the conversion rate is 3(a−c)/b. Decreasing the volume is equal to increasing the pressure, and the equilibrium moves to the side with less gas substance (in the direction of generating NH₃). Both the forward and reverse reaction rates increase with the increase in pressure, and the N₂ conversion rate increases at the new equilibrium.

exercises.stem:
In the sulfuric acid industry, SO₂ is oxidized to SO₃ via the reaction 2SO₂(g)+O₂(g)⇌2SO₃(g) (ΔH = −196.6 kJ/mol). The table below lists the conversion rates of SO₂ at equilibrium at different temperatures and pressures.

(1) From a theoretical analysis, in order to convert as much sulfur dioxide into sulfur trioxide as possible, what temperature and pressure should be selected?
(2) In actual production, the selected temperature is 400~500 ℃. What is the reason?
(3) In actual production, the pressure used is normal pressure. What is the reason?
(4) In actual production, excessive air is introduced. What is the reason?
(5) SO₂ in exhaust gas must be recovered. Why?
tests: In the sulfuric acid industry, SO₂ is oxidized to SO₃ reaction
Selection of conditions for exothermic reversible reactions
Optimization and compromise of industrial production conditions
Selecting the most favorable reaction conditions based on the principle of equilibrium movement
Comprehensive rate, balance and economics determine industrial operating conditions
Use experimental and tabular data to analyze the impact of reaction conditions
exercises.answer:
(1) Low temperature and high pressure.
(2) Although lowering the temperature is beneficial to improving the equilibrium conversion rate, the reaction rate is too low and uneconomical, so a compromise of 400~500 °C was chosen.
(3) It can be seen from the table that the conversion rate does not increase significantly when increasing from normal pressure to higher pressure, and high pressure will significantly increase equipment and energy consumption costs, so normal pressure can be used.
(4) Excess air provides excess O₂, which can push the balance toward the direction of generating SO₃ according to the principle of equilibrium movement, thereby improving the SO₂ conversion rate.
(5) SO₂ is toxic and can cause serious environmental pollution, and needs to be recycled to reduce emissions and improve resource utilization.
exercises.analysis: This question comprehensively examines the principle of equilibrium movement and the optimization of industrial conditions. Theoretically, the exothermic reaction is suitable for low temperature and high pressure, but the speed and investment cost need to be weighed. The introduction of excess reactants and the recovery of tail gas reflect the comprehensive consideration of material conversion rate and environmental protection.

exercises.name:
Hydrogen energy is a clean energy source with great development potential. The following reaction is one of the current methods for producing hydrogen on a large scale:
CO(g)+H₂O(g)⇌CO₂(g)+H₂(g), ΔH = −41.2 kJ/mol.
(1) In production, what measures can be taken to increase the conversion rate of CO and increase the yield of H₂ at the same time?
(2) In a closed container with a constant volume, 2.0 mol CO and 8.0 mol H₂O are mixed and heated to 830 °C to cause the above reaction. When equilibrium is reached, the conversion rate of CO is 80%. Calculate the equilibrium constant K for this reaction under these conditions.
exercises.stem:
Hydrogen energy is a clean energy source with great development potential. The following reaction is one of the current methods for producing hydrogen on a large scale:
CO(g)+H₂O(g)⇌CO₂(g)+H₂(g), ΔH = −41.2 kJ/mol.
(1) In production, what measures can be taken to increase the conversion rate of CO and increase the yield of H₂ at the same time?
(2) In a closed container with a constant volume, 2.0 mol CO and 8.0 mol H₂O are mixed and heated to 830 °C to cause the above reaction. When equilibrium is reached, the conversion rate of CO is 80%. Calculate the equilibrium constant K for this reaction under these conditions.
tests: Chemical equilibrium and equilibrium mixture composition
Selecting the most favorable reaction conditions based on the principle of equilibrium movement
Use the amount and conversion rate of the substance to describe the equilibrium state
exercises.answer:
(1) Use an appropriately lower temperature (on the premise of ensuring a sufficient reaction rate), increase the concentration of reactants (such as appropriately increasing CO or H₂O), and remove the products in a timely manner (such as absorbing CO₂ or releasing H₂). You can also use a suitable catalyst to speed up the rate of reaching equilibrium.
(2) Initial: n(CO)=2.0 mol, n(H₂O)=8.0 mol. 80% CO conversion consumes 1.6 mol. At equilibrium: n(CO)=0.4 mol, n(H₂O)=6.4 mol, n(CO₂)=1.6 mol, n(H₂)=1.6 mol. The total amount of material is 10.0 mol. The equilibrium concentration (or partial pressure) of each substance is proportional to the amount of the substance, and can be replaced by the amount of the substance at constant volume:
K = [CO₂][H₂]/([CO][H₂O]) = (1.6×1.6)/(0.4×6.4) = 2.56/2.56 = 1.0.
exercises.analysis: The first question examines the condition selection of the exothermic equilibrium system and the idea of ​​removing products to promote equilibrium; the second question is to find the equilibrium composition through the change in the amount of substances and the conversion rate, and then find the equilibrium constant according to the reaction formula.

exercises.name: Summarize the factors that affect the movement of chemical equilibrium
exercises.stem: Combined with the phenomena of FeCl3 and KSCN, K2Cr2O7, CuCl2 and NO2/N2O4 experiments in this section, try to summarize the main factors that affect the movement of chemical equilibrium, and explain in which direction the equilibrium generally moves when these factors change.
tests: Effect of concentration on chemical equilibrium
Effect of temperature on chemical equilibrium
Summarize the factors affecting chemical equilibrium from experimental phenomena
exercises.answer:
Main factors:
(1) Concentration: When the concentration of a certain reactant is increased, the equilibrium moves to the side that consumes the reactant; when the concentration of a certain reactant is decreased, the equilibrium moves to the side that generates the substance. The same is true for products. When it increases, the balance moves to the side that consumes the product, and when it decreases, it moves toward the side that generates the substance.
(2) Temperature: As the temperature increases, the equilibrium moves toward the endothermic direction; as the temperature decreases, the equilibrium moves toward the exothermic direction. The above phenomenon can be explained by Le Chatelier's principle, that is, the equilibrium always moves in a direction that partially offsets external changes.
exercises.analysis: This question requires students to synthesize and abstract multiple experimental phenomena, extract the two key factors of concentration and temperature from the changes in solution color and gas color, and be able to use "increase/decrease" and "endotherm/release" to correspond to the direction of equilibrium movement, reflecting the ability to generalize from phenomena to rules.

experiments.name: The effect of the concentration of Fe3+ and SCN- on chemical equilibrium (Experiment 2-1)

experiments.name: The effect of pressure on the chemical equilibrium of NO2/N2O4 (Experiment 2-2)

experiments.phenomena: Pull out the piston: the volume increases, the pressure and concentration decrease, the color of the mixed gas first becomes lighter and then gradually becomes darker, indicating that more NO2 is generated; push the piston: the volume decreases, the pressure and concentration increase, the color of the mixed gas first becomes darker and then gradually becomes lighter, indicating that more NO2 is consumed.
experiments.conclusion: In the 2NO2(g) ⇌ N2O4(g) equilibrium system, decreasing the pressure (concentration) will shift the equilibrium to the side with a larger amount of gaseous substances (NO2); increasing the pressure will shift the equilibrium to the side with a smaller amount of gaseous substances (N2O4).

experiments.name: The effect of NaOH and H2SO4 on Cr2O7²−/CrO4²− equilibrium experiment
experiments.process: Take a test tube, add 2 mL of 0.1 mol/L K2Cr2O7 solution, and observe the orange color; add 5 to 10 drops of 6 mol/L NaOH solution to the test tube, observe the color change, and determine the direction of equilibrium movement; then add 5 to 10 drops of 6 mol/L H2SO4 solution to the same test tube, observe the color change, and determine whether the equilibrium has moved and the direction of movement.

exercises.name: Determine conductivity and electrolyte
exercises.stem:
A classmate used a conductivity device to test the conductivity of dry NaCl solid, NaCl solution and distilled water. The result was that dry NaCl solid and distilled water were not conductive, but NaCl solution was conductive. Answer based on experimental phenomena:
(1) Is NaCl an electrolyte? Give reasons.
(2) Explain the difference in conductivity between NaCl solid and NaCl solution from the perspective of microscopic particles.
tests: Determine whether a substance is an electrolyte
Explain conductivity from a microscopic particle perspective
exercises.answer:
(1) NaCl is an electrolyte. Because NaCl can conduct electricity in an aqueous solution, it meets the definition of "a compound that can conduct electricity in an aqueous solution or molten state is called an electrolyte."
(2) Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in NaCl solid are closely arranged according to certain rules and cannot move freely, so they are not conductive. When NaCl is dissolved in water, it is ionized under the action of water molecules into hydrated Na⁺ and hydrated Cl⁻ that can move freely. They move in a direction under the action of an electric field to form an electric current, so the NaCl solution can conduct electricity.
exercises.analysis: This question examines the definition of electrolyte and the explanation of conductivity from a microscopic ion perspective. When answering the question, first use the original words about the electrolyte in the textbook to determine NaCl, and then explain the difference between solid and solution in terms of "whether ions can move freely."

exercises.name: Calculate the ionization constant of ammonia water
exercises.stem: At a certain temperature, in ammonia water with a solute concentration of 0.20 mol·L⁻¹, when the ionization equilibrium is reached, the ionized NH3·H2O is 1.7×10⁻³ mol·L⁻¹. Try to calculate the ionization constant Kb of NH3·H2O at this temperature.
tests: Use the equilibrium concentration to calculate the ionization constant
exercises.analysis: Write the ionization equation: NH3·H2O ⇌ NH4⁺ + OH⁻. List each particle concentration according to "Start-Change-Equilibrium": starting c(NH3·H2O)=0.20 mol·L⁻¹, c(NH4⁺)=0, c(OH⁻)=0; change: all ±1.7×10⁻³; equilibrium: c(NH3·H2O)=0.20−1.7×10⁻³≈0.20 mol·L⁻¹, c(NH4⁺)=1.7×10⁻³ mol·L⁻¹, c(OH⁻)=1.7×10⁻³ mol·L⁻¹. Substituting Kb = c(NH4⁺)·c(OH⁻)/c(NH3·H2O) we get Kb ≈ (1.7×10⁻³)² / 0.20 ≈ 1.4×10⁻⁵.

exercises.name: Judge the acidity and alkalinity of different types of salt solutions
exercises.stem: Make the following salt solutions into 0.1 mol/L solutions in water: NaCl, Na₂CO₃, NH₄Cl, KNO₃, CH₃COONa. (1) Determine their acidity and alkalinity (acidic, alkaline or neutral) respectively; (2) Point out which category each salt belongs to: strong acid and strong alkali salt, strong acid and weak alkali salt, or strong base and weak acid salt; (3) Explain why Na₂CO₃ solution can be used as a "base".
tests: Acidity and alkalinity of salt solutions
Determine the acidity and alkalinity of the salt solution based on the strength of the acid and alkali.
exercises.answer: (1) NaCl and KNO₃ solutions are neutral; NH₄Cl solutions are acidic; Na₂CO₃ and CH₃COONa solutions are alkaline. (2) NaCl and KNO₃ are salts of strong acid and strong base; NH₄Cl is salt of strong acid and weak base; Na₂CO₃ and CH₃COONa are salts of strong base and weak base. (3) Na₂CO₃ is a strong base and weak acid salt. CO₃²⁻ hydrolyzes in water to form OH⁻, making the solution alkaline. Therefore, Na₂CO₃ solution can be used as a "base" to neutralize acid and remove oil stains.
exercises.analysis: First judge the strength of the acids and bases that make up the salt, and classify the salts: NaCl and KNO₃ are generated from strong acids and strong bases; Na₂CO₃ and CH₃COONa are generated from strong bases and weak acids; NH₄Cl is generated from strong acids and weak bases. According to the rule: salt solutions of strong acids and strong bases are neutral, salt solutions of strong acids and weak bases are acidic, and solutions of strong bases and weak salts are alkaline. The alkaline nature of Na₂CO₃ solution is the hydrolysis of CO₃²⁻ to produce OH⁻.

exercises.name: The relationship between FeCl₃ hydrolysis and conditions
exercises.stem: It is known that FeCl₃ is a salt generated by strong acid and weak base. Its hydrolysis can be expressed as: Fe³⁺ + 3H₂O ⇌ Fe(OH)₃↓ + 3H⁺. (1) Determine the acidity and alkalinity of 0.01 mol/L FeCl₃ solution and explain the reason; (2) If the solution is heated, how will the hydrolysis equilibrium shift? How does the degree of hydrolysis change? (3) When preparing FeCl₃ solution, FeCl₃ crystals are often dissolved in concentrated hydrochloric acid and then diluted with water. Explain the purpose of doing so.
tests: FeCl₃ Acidity and hydrolysis of solution
The effect of reaction conditions on the hydrolysis of salts
Use the equilibrium shift principle to analyze salt hydrolysis
Determine the acidity and alkalinity of the salt solution based on the strength of the acid and alkali.
exercises.answer: (1) FeCl₃ is a strong acid and weak alkali salt. Fe³⁺ hydrolyzes in water to generate Fe(OH)₃ and H⁺, making c(H⁺)>c(OH⁻) in the solution, so the solution is acidic. (2) The hydrolysis of FeCl₃ is an endothermic reaction. Heating moves the equilibrium toward the forward reaction direction, increases the degree of hydrolysis, and generates more Fe(OH)₃ and H⁺. (3) Concentrated hydrochloric acid provides a higher H⁺ concentration, which shifts the hydrolysis equilibrium toward the reverse reaction direction, thereby inhibiting the hydrolysis of FeCl₃, allowing Fe³⁺ to exist stably in the solution, and preventing the generation of large amounts of Fe(OH)₃ colloids or precipitation.
exercises.analysis: Judge the acidity of the solution based on the fact that FeCl₃ is a salt of strong acid and weak alkali; then use the conclusion that "hydrolysis of salts is an endothermic reaction" and use the principle of equilibrium movement to analyze the direction of equilibrium movement when the temperature rises; finally, use the idea of ​​"increasing H⁺ concentration to inhibit hydrolysis" to explain the purpose of the preparation operation.

experiments.phenomena: The pH of NaCl and KNO₃ solutions is close to 7, which is neutral; the pH of NH₄Cl and (NH₄)₂SO₄ solutions is less than 7, which is acidic; the pH of Na₂CO₃ and CH₃COONa solutions is greater than 7, which is alkaline.
experiments.conclusion: Strong acid and strong base salt solutions are generally neutral, strong acid and weak base salt solutions are acidic, and strong base and weak acid salt solutions are alkaline.

experiments.name: The effect of reaction conditions on the hydrolysis equilibrium of FeCl₃
experiments.process: (1) Take 0.01 mol/L Put the FeCl₃ solution in several test tubes, use a pH meter to measure the pH, observe the color and whether there is Fe(OH)₃ colloid or precipitation; (2) Heat one of the tubes, observe the changes in pH and turbidity of the solution, and analyze the effect of temperature on hydrolysis; (3) Add a small amount of water to the other tube to dilute, observe the changes in pH and colloids, and analyze the effect of concentration changes on water (4) Add an appropriate amount of concentrated hydrochloric acid to the third branch of the solution, observe whether the hydrolysis products are reduced, and whether the solution becomes clear, explaining the inhibitory effect of increased H⁺ concentration on the hydrolysis balance; (5) Add a small amount of NaOH solution to the other branch, observe the phenomenon of large amounts of Fe(OH)₃ precipitates, and analyze the impact of product concentration changes on the balance.
experiments.phenomena: After heating or dilution, the pH of the FeCl₃ solution decreases or more Fe(OH)₃ colloids appear, and the degree of hydrolysis increases; after adding concentrated hydrochloric acid, the Fe(OH)₃ colloids in the solution decrease or even disappear, the solution becomes clear, and hydrolysis is inhibited; after adding NaOH, a large amount of Fe(OH)₃ precipitates are immediately generated.
experiments.conclusion: Salt hydrolysis is an endothermic reaction. Heating and dilution both promote the hydrolysis equilibrium to shift toward the generation of hydrolysis products, increasing the degree of hydrolysis. Increasing the H⁺ concentration (such as adding hydrochloric acid) can inhibit the hydrolysis of FeCl₃, and changing the concentration of reactants or products can cause the hydrolysis equilibrium to shift.

experiments.name: Comparison of dissolution of Mg(OH)2 in water and hydrochloric acid
experiments.process: Add appropriate amounts of distilled water and hydrochloric acid to two test tubes containing a small amount of Mg(OH)2 solid respectively, shake and observe the dissolution of Mg(OH)2.
experiments.phenomena: Mg(OH)2 is basically insoluble when distilled water is added dropwise; Mg(OH)2 gradually dissolves when hydrochloric acid is added dropwise, possibly accompanied by a weak exotherm and disappearance of turbidity.
experiments.conclusion: There is a precipitation-dissolution equilibrium between Mg(OH)2 and its saturated solution in pure water; after adding acid, the reaction between H⁺ and OH⁻ reduces the ion product Q of Mg(OH)2, and the equilibrium moves toward the dissolution direction, causing the precipitate to dissolve.

experiments.conclusion: The precipitate-dissolution equilibrium of AgCl, AgI, and Ag2S shifts in the presence of I⁻ and S²⁻ in the direction of generating precipitates with smaller solubility, indicating that the essence of the precipitation transformation is an equilibrium shift driven by solubility differences.

experiments.name: Conversion of Mg(OH)2 precipitation to Fe(OH)3 precipitation

experiments.conclusion: In the presence of Fe³⁺, the system is more inclined to generate less soluble Fe(OH)3 precipitates, and Mg(OH)2 is partially converted to Fe(OH)3, indicating that the precipitation transformation is controlled by the Ksp size of different hydroxides.

exercises.name: Calculation of the mass required to prepare NaOH solution
exercises.stem: Prepare 500 mL of 0.1 mol/L NaOH solution. What is the mass of NaOH required?
tests: Prepare solutions based on the amount and concentration of substances
exercises.answer: 2 g
exercises.analysis: From c = n / V, n(NaOH) = c·V = 0.1 mol/L × 0.5 L = 0.05 mol. The molar mass of NaOH is 40 g/mol, then m = n·M = 0.05 mol × 40 g/mol = 2 g.

exercises.name: Calculate Substance concentration of NaOH solution
exercises.stem: In the experiment of "titrating a strong base of unknown concentration with a strong acid of known concentration", use an acid burette to fill 0.1000 mol/L HCl solution, use a basic buret to measure 25.00 mL of the NaOH solution to be measured into a Erlenmeyer flask, and add phenolphthalein indicator. The volumes of HCl recorded in the three titrations were: 19.96 mL, 20.04 mL, and 20.00 mL. Try to calculate the concentration of NaOH in the NaOH solution to be tested (assuming that the titration reaction is complete, the reaction between HCl and NaOH proceeds according to the chemical equation HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O).
tests: Neutralization reaction of strong acid and strong base
Use neutralization titration to calculate the concentration of substances in unknown solutions
exercises.answer: The average volume of three HCl volumes V(HCl) = (19.96 + 20.04 + 20.00) / 3 = 20.00 mL = 0.02000 L; n(HCl) = c(HCl) × V(HCl) = 0.1000 mol/L × 0.02000 L = 2.000×10⁻³ mol. From HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O, we know that n(NaOH) = n(HCl) = 2.000×10⁻³ mol. The volume of the NaOH solution to be measured is V(NaOH) = 25.00 mL = 0.02500 L, so c(NaOH) = n/V = 2.000×10⁻³ mol ÷ 0.02500 L = 0.0800 mol/L.
exercises.analysis: This question examines the basic method of calculating the concentration of an unknown solution using neutralization titration. Key points: The first step is to find the average volume of HCl from three experiments; the second step is to use the cV relationship to find n(HCl); the third step is to use the 1:1 metering relationship between HCl and NaOH to find n(NaOH); the fourth step is to use n/V to find the concentration of NaOH.

exercises.name: Whether the Erlenmeyer flask needs to be rinsed and dried
exercises.stem: When performing a neutralization titration experiment with strong acids and strong alkali, does the titration Erlenmeyer flask need to be rinsed with the acid or alkali solution to be tested? Does the Erlenmeyer flask have to be kept dry before filling it with the solution to be tested? Please briefly explain your reasons.
tests: Requirements for the use of Erlenmeyer flask
exercises.answer: The Erlenmeyer flask used for titration only needs to be clean, and does not need to be rinsed with the acid or alkali solution to be measured, nor does it need to be completely dry. Because a small amount of distilled water in the Erlenmeyer flask will not change the amount of the titrated substance (acid or alkali), it will only slightly change the total volume, and will not affect the quantity relationship of the substance on which the titration is based; and the burette must be rinsed with the solution to be filled to avoid residual water or other solutions from diluting the standard solution, thereby changing the quantity concentration of its substance.
exercises.analysis: This question tests students’ understanding of “instrument rinsing” and their mastery of the essence of quantitative experiments. Key points: The titration calculation is based on the amount of the solute, not the total volume of the system; the water in the Erlenmeyer flask does not change the n of the solute, but the remaining water in the burette will change the c of the titrant.

exercises.name: Preparation method of FeCl₃ solution in the laboratory
exercises.stem: Based on the experimental results of "Add a small amount of FeCl₃ crystals to a test tube, then add 5 mL of distilled water, shake, and observe that the solution is turbid; then add 2 mL of concentrated hydrochloric acid to the test tube, shake, and the solution becomes clear." Answer: How to correctly prepare a relatively clear and stable FeCl₃ solution in the laboratory? and briefly explain the reasons.
tests: Analyze the hydrolysis of salts and the acidity and alkalinity of the solution based on the phenomenon
exercises.answer: When preparing, FeCl₃ crystals should be dissolved in a small amount of concentrated hydrochloric acid first, and then diluted to the required volume with distilled water after complete dissolution. Reason: FeCl₃ will be hydrolyzed to form Fe(OH)₃ when dissolved in water, making the solution turbid. However, a large amount of H⁺ in concentrated hydrochloric acid can inhibit the hydrolysis of Fe³⁺ and dissolve Fe(OH)₃ to obtain a clear solution.
exercises.analysis: The question tests the understanding and application of the principles of salt hydrolysis. The key is to realize that Fe³⁺ is easily hydrolyzed in water to form Fe(OH)₃, causing the solution to be turbid; adding concentrated hydrochloric acid provides a large amount of H⁺, which causes the hydrolysis equilibrium to shift in the opposite direction, and Fe(OH)₃ dissolves, making the solution clear. Therefore, the correct preparation sequence must be "acid first, then water" to inhibit hydrolysis.

experiments.name: FeCl₃ Solution preparation and hydrolysis phenomenon observation

experiments.phenomena: After adding water, the solution appears yellow-brown turbidity or precipitation, indicating that Fe³⁺ is hydrolyzed to generate Fe(OH)₃; after adding concentrated hydrochloric acid, the solution becomes clear, and the H⁺ released by hydrolysis is inhibited by a large amount of H⁺, and Fe(OH)₃ is dissolved.
experiments.conclusion: FeCl₃ dissolves in water and undergoes hydrolysis, and the solution becomes acidic; when preparing FeCl₃ solution, it should be dissolved with concentrated hydrochloric acid and then diluted.

experiments.phenomena: Flocculent precipitates appeared in the test tubes added with FeCl₃ or Al₂(SO₄)₃. After standing, the soil sank with the flocculent precipitates and the upper water became clear; the control test tubes without chemicals were still turbid.
experiments.conclusion: FeCl₃ and Al₂(SO₄)₃ are hydrolyzed in water to form Fe(OH)₃ and Al(OH)₃ flocculent precipitates, which can absorb soil and settle, and can be used as water purification agents.

experiments.conclusion: Slowly add FeCl₃ solution to boiling water and continue to boil, Fe(OH)₃ colloid can be produced by hydrolysis of salts.

exercises.name: Polarity and reaction of alkaline zinc-manganese batteries
exercises.stem:
In an alkaline zinc-manganese battery, one end of Zn is used as the negative electrode, one end of MnO₂ is used as the positive electrode, and the electrolyte is KOH. Try to answer:
(1) What is the electrode reaction that occurs at the negative electrode during discharge?
(2) What is the flow direction of electrons in the external circuit during discharge?
(3) Indicate whether the battery is a primary battery or a secondary battery, and briefly explain the reason.
tests: Write and balance electrode reactions and total reactions
Analyze the positive and negative electrodes and electrolytes from the battery structure
exercises.answer:
(1) Negative electrode reaction: Zn + 2OH⁻ - 2e⁻ = Zn(OH)₂.
(2) During discharge, electrons flow from the Zn electrode to the MnO₂ electrode through the external circuit, that is, from the negative electrode to the positive electrode.
(3) This battery is a primary battery. Because it cannot be recharged after discharge, and the active material cannot be restored by charging after being consumed, it is a type of dry battery in which the electrolyte in the primary battery is made into a gel.
exercises.analysis: According to the original text, we know that alkaline zinc-manganese battery is a primary battery, and the electrode reaction formula is given in the book. The principle of the galvanic cell is used to determine the flow of electrons from the negative electrode where the oxidation reaction occurs to the positive electrode where the reduction reaction occurs.

exercises.name: Main indicators for judging battery performance
exercises.stem: The textbook points out that there are several indicators to judge the quality of a battery or its suitability for a certain purpose. Please write at least three items and explain the meaning of two of them.
tests: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of batteries and applicable occasions based on performance indicators
exercises.answer:
Main indicators include: the amount of electrical energy that the battery can output per unit mass or unit volume (specific energy), the size of the output power (specific power), the length of time the battery can be stored, and whether the mass and volume are small, etc.
Meaning examples:
(1) Specific energy: The electrical energy that a battery per unit mass or volume can output during the discharge process. The larger the value, the higher the energy density and the more "durable" the battery.
(2) Specific power: The power that a battery can output per unit mass or unit volume. The larger the value, the greater the current it can provide in a short time, which is more suitable for occasions that require high power.
exercises.analysis: The answer comes directly from the textbook's description of judging the quality of batteries, and combines the concepts to explain specific energy and specific power.

exercises.stem: 2. From a principle analysis, what are the similarities between electrolytically refined copper and electroplated copper? Write the electrode reaction for electrolytic refining of copper.
tests: Analyze industrial processes based on the principle of electrolysis
exercises.answer: Similarities: Both use the principle of electrolysis to precipitate the copper in the electrolyte solution containing Cu²⁺ through electric current to form a dense metal layer on the cathode. Both are processes of depositing metal on the cathode. The electrode reaction of electrolytically refined copper is: anode: Cu − 2e⁻ = Cu²⁺; cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ = Cu.
exercises.analysis: This question tests students' ability to compare electroplating and electrolytic refining using electrolysis principles and electrochemical system views, and is required to write down a typical electrolytic refining copper electrode reaction, highlighting the characteristics of anode dissolution and cathode precipitation.

experiments.name: Zinc-copper-dilute sulfuric acid galvanic battery experiment (Experiment 6-3)
experiments.instrument: Beaker containing dilute sulfuric acid, zinc sheets, copper sheets, wires, and ammeters
experiments.process: (1) Insert the zinc sheet and the copper sheet into a beaker containing dilute sulfuric acid and observe the phenomenon; (2) Use a wire to connect the zinc sheet and the copper sheet, observe and compare the phenomenon before and after the wire connection; (3) Use a wire to connect an ammeter in series between the zinc sheet and the copper sheet, and observe whether the ammeter pointer deflects.
experiments.phenomena: After the zinc sheet is inserted into dilute sulfuric acid, bubbles are generated, but the copper sheet initially has no bubbles; after the wires are connected, bubbles appear on the copper sheet; when the ammeter is connected in series, the ammeter pointer deflects, indicating that there is current passing through the wire.
experiments.conclusion: The oxidation of zinc and the reduction of H+ are carried out in different areas through the device. Electrons move directionally through the external circuit to form an electric current, realizing the conversion of chemical energy into electrical energy. This device is a primary battery.

experiments.name: Electrolysis experiment of CuCl₂ solution (Experiment 4-2)
experiments.instrument: U-shaped tube, 25% mass fraction CuCl₂ solution, two graphite rods, power supply, wires, potassium iodide starch test paper
experiments.process: Inject 25% CuCl₂ solution into the U-shaped tube, insert two graphite rods as electrodes, and place the moist potassium iodide starch test paper near the graphite rod connected to the positive electrode of the DC power supply. Turn on the DC power supply and observe the phenomenon near the electrode and the color change of the test paper.
experiments.phenomena: The surface of the graphite rod connected to the negative electrode is gradually covered with a layer of red copper; bubbles are generated on the graphite rod connected to the positive electrode; the potassium iodide starch test paper turns blue, and gas with a pungent smell is produced.
experiments.conclusion: CuCl₂ solution is electrolyzed to generate metallic copper and chlorine gas under energized conditions, indicating that the current passes through the electrolyte solution and causes a redox reaction on the electrode.

experiments.name: Simple electroplating experiment (copper plating on iron)
instrument: Electroplating solution mainly prepared with CuSO4 solution
process: Use sandpaper to polish the iron plated parts, put them into 1 mol/L NaOH solution to remove oil stains, and then wash them with distilled water.
Place the iron plated parts in 20% hydrochloric acid to remove rust, take them out after a few minutes, and wash them with distilled water.
Connect the iron plated piece to the negative pole of the 2~3V DC power supply, and the copper piece to the positive pole of the DC power supply.
Immerse the two poles in parallel in the plating solution mainly composed of CuSO4 solution. The distance between the two poles is about 5 cm, and energize for 5 to 10 minutes.
Take out the iron plated parts and observe their surface changes.
experiments.phenomena: After being energized for a period of time, the surface of the iron plated part is covered with a metallic bright layer similar in color to copper, and the copper sheet gradually dissolves and becomes thinner.
experiments.conclusion: Under the action of direct current, Cu2+ gains electrons on the cathode (iron plated parts) and is reduced to metallic copper deposition. The anode (copper sheet) loses electrons and dissolves into Cu2+ and enters the solution, thereby realizing electroplating.

exercises.name: What is chemical corrosion of metals? What is electrochemical corrosion of metals? Give examples to illustrate the dangers of metal corrosion.
exercises.stem: What is chemical corrosion of metals? What is electrochemical corrosion of metals? Give examples to illustrate the dangers of metal corrosion.
exercises.answer: Chemical corrosion of metals refers to the corrosion caused by the direct chemical reaction of certain substances (such as O₂, Cl₂, SO₂, etc.) in the gas or liquid in contact with the metal and its surface. For example, steel is oxidized at high temperatures, oil pipelines are corroded by sulfur-containing compounds in crude oil, etc. Electrochemical corrosion of metals refers to the formation of galvanic cells when impure metals come into contact with electrolyte solutions, and relatively active metals are oxidized and dissolved as anodes in electrochemical reactions, such as the rust of steel in humid air and the hydrogen evolution corrosion of steel in acidic solutions. Metal corrosion will reduce the accuracy and sensitivity of machinery, equipment, instruments, and instruments until they are scrapped, and may lead to the collapse of bridges and building metal structures due to reduced strength, leakage of underground metal pipelines, damage to ship hulls, and other hazards.

exercises.name: In order to extend the service life of the boiler, zinc sheets are often welded to its inner wall. Please briefly describe the rationale behind this approach.
exercises.stem: In order to extend the service life of the boiler, zinc sheets are often welded to its inner wall. Please briefly describe the rationale behind this approach.
tests: Analyze the corrosion and protection of metals through the principle of galvanic cells
exercises.answer: Zinc is more active than iron. When zinc sheets are welded to the inner wall of the boiler, zinc, iron, and the electrolyte solution in the boiler form a primary battery. Zinc acts as the anode and is oxidized and dissolved. Iron acts as the cathode and is basically not corroded, thus protecting the inner wall of the boiler steel. This is the principle of cathodic protection of the sacrificial anode method.

exercises.name: Explain the basic principles of impressed current method to protect harbor steel pipe piles, and point out the role of high silicon cast iron in this system.
exercises.stem: Explain the basic principles of impressed current method to protect harbor steel pipe piles, and point out the role of high silicon cast iron in this system.
tests: Analyze the corrosion and protection of metals through the principle of galvanic cells
exercises.answer: The impressed current method is to place the harbor steel pipe piles and inert anodes (such as high-silicon cast iron) in seawater and connect them to the DC power supply, so that the steel pipe piles are connected to the negative electrode of the power supply and the high-silicon cast iron is connected to the positive electrode. After energization, the applied current forces electrons to flow to the steel pipe pile, making the steel pile become a cathode in the entire electrochemical system. The metal on its surface no longer loses electrons and dissolves, and the corrosion current drops to zero or close to zero, thus being protected. High-silicon cast iron serves as an inert auxiliary anode in this system. Its main function is to conduct electricity and complete the anode process in the solution, and it is basically not consumed.

experiments.instrument: Pickled and rust-removed iron nails, saturated salt water, test tubes, conduits, water columns
experiments.process: Soak the rust-removing iron nails in saturated salt water and put them into a test tube. Observe the changes in the water column in the tube after a few minutes and analyze the reasons.
experiments.phenomena: Changes in the height of the water column in the tube indicate changes in the gas composition and pressure in the test tube.
experiments.conclusion: Iron nails undergo oxygen-absorbing corrosion in the water film containing electrolyte and air environment, consuming oxygen and causing changes in gas pressure.

experiments.name: Electrochemical corrosion experiment of Zn with dilute hydrochloric acid and Cu²⁺ (Experiment 4-3 Part)
experiments.instrument: Zinc granules, two test tubes, equal volumes of dilute hydrochloric acid of equal concentration, dropper, copper sulfate solution
experiments.process: Put two zinc particles into test tubes containing equal amounts of dilute hydrochloric acid, and observe the phenomenon; then add 1 to 2 drops of copper sulfate solution to one of the test tubes, and observe and compare the phenomena of the two tubes again.
experiments.phenomena: In the test tube where CuSO₄ was added, bubbles increased, the reaction intensified, and copper precipitated on the zinc surface.
experiments.conclusion: Cu²⁺ participates in the formation of primary cells and accelerates the electrochemical corrosion of Zn, indicating that electrode materials and oxidants affect the corrosion rate.

experiments.name: Sacrificial anode method electrolysis experiment (Experiment 4-4 part)
experiments.instrument: Fe electrode, Zn electrode, acidified 3% NaCl solution, beaker, ammeter, wire, glue tip dropper, test tube, K₃[Fe(CN)₆] solution
experiments.process: Use Fe as the protective electrode and Zn as the auxiliary electrode. Immerse them in the acidified 3% NaCl solution and connect the circuit as shown in the figure. Observe the ammeter reading and the phenomena near the electrode. After a certain period of time, take the Fe electrode area solution, add K₃[Fe(CN)₆] solution, and observe the color change.
experiments.phenomena: Ammeter has pointer deflection; there are bubbles or dissolution near the Zn electrode; there is no obvious blue precipitate between the solution and K₃[Fe(CN)₆] near the Fe electrode.
experiments.conclusion: Zn is preferentially dissolved as an anode while Fe is protected as a cathode, embodying the principle of the sacrificial anode method.

experiments.name: Comparative experiment on corrosion of zinc-coated iron nails and copper wire-wrapped iron nails (Experiment 4-4 part)
experiments.instrument: Agar, beaker, petri dish, saturated saline, water, phenolphthalein solution, K₃[Fe(CN)₆] solution, two iron nails, zinc sheet, copper wire, sandpaper
experiments.process: Prepare an agar solution containing NaCl and indicator, pour it into two petri dishes; wrap polished iron nails with zinc coating and copper wire respectively and insert them into the two dishes to observe the color change and corrosion.
experiments.phenomena: Fe²⁺ and alkaline area changes are less likely to appear near iron nails wrapped with zinc; blue and red areas appear near iron nails wrapped with copper wire, and the iron is obviously rusted.
experiments.conclusion: When zinc and iron form a primary battery, zinc serves as the anode and protects the iron; when copper and iron form a primary battery, iron serves as the anode and is corroded at an accelerated rate.

experiments.name: Fe²⁺ test experiment

experiments.conclusion: The formation of blue KFe[Fe(CN)₆] precipitate can be used as evidence of the existence of Fe²⁺ and is a common method for testing Fe²⁺.
